spoiler alert I have to admire Beth Revis for her unique premise. But, like so many trilogies, the first book outshone the second book. I really was immersed in reading Across the Universe. However, I felt that the writing was terrible in A Million Suns. Either I have gotten pickier, or her writing has gotten worse. What's with all of the breaks in the paragraphs? She does this for emphasis, but it comes across forced and is a sad excuse for good writing. If she were a better writer she wouldn't need to make so many sentences one-liners for impact. Or should I say a sad attempt to make impact. It so often didn't work . This style bothered me frequently throughout reading the story and interrupted the fluidity of the novel. And like so many other reviews on here, I have to agree that the characters were what made this book so weak. They were inconsistent and bored me. I connected with them so much more in the previous book. Amy and Elder's personalities blurred together with the every other chapter point-of-view switch. Beth Revis lost Elder and Amy's voices in A Million Suns, which is unfortunate. And the villains' motivations were lame! Should I break into a new paragraph to emphasize that last sentence? The villains' reasons to kill were far-fetched and unbelievable. Orion killed the frozens because he thought they'd force the people to fight the monsters? Come on! To take someone's innocent life over the POSSIBILITY that some of them MIGHT want to land on the planet? BUT it's ok to wake teenage Amy and let her rationally decide, yet all of the rest of the educated scientists military personnel aren't capable of that? And don't even get me started on Doc's motivations to do all that he did. The healer killer who blindly followed Orion's will to reveal the videos to Amy but then tampers with them at the same time to throw her off? Really? Because THAT make sense. Also, the whole Luthor drama was a good part of the plot but seemed like it got resolved randomly and I had to ask why the heck that plotline was put in the story to begin with? Even Bartie seemed inconsistent. He was a good long-time friend to Elder, but then suddenly seems to believe that Elder is capable of killing anyone who disobeys him. You'd think after being Elder's friend for years he would have a good enough grasp of Elder's morals. And how does it work that the supposedly moral Elder defends Orion's murders by stating to Amy that Orion wasn't really that crazy, he had a logical reason to go on a killing spree? Huh?! Did I really just read that? All of the motivations and actions of the characters were so contradictory, I just didn't care about the story any more. It was also predictable. I knew Doc was up to no good from the start. Victria probably killed Luthor, although that seemed to be dropped altogether. And I thought the elaborate goose chase Amy was put on was also silly. So I guess that about sums up my review. There were weak, one-dimensional, changeable characters with a predictable and at times silly plotline. The only reason I MIGHT pick up Shades of Earth is because I am very curious about what "monsters" await. Beth Revis is very good at world building, so it could be interesting. As for Amy and Elder, I guess I'll take them as my narrators along the way.
A thrilling trilogy, especially considering it's actually a young adult fiction book.

Rating 3.5 Que bien se siente empezar el ano con un buen libro. Snow Like Ashes es una historia llena de accion, drama, suspenso, misterio y plot-twists. No dire que es la historia mas original del mundo pues a decir verdad no lo es. Trae premisas que ya hemos visto antes, no obstante, la historia es hipnotizante y atranyente, haciendote seguir leyendo para saber que mas vas a descubrir al voltear la siguiente pagina. Realmente me gustaron los personajes, Meira, Mather, Theron, Sir. Hubo momentos en que deseaba que Sir simplemente no apareciera mas en el libro, pero a medida que avanza la historia te vas dando cuenta de las verdaderas razones del personaje y vas cogiendole carino y pena al mismo tiempo. Creo que es uno de estos personajes tragicos que se dan a odiar muy a menudo en las series, y al final resultan uno de los mas nobles. Me gusto mucho el concepto en el que esta basado la historia. Una nacion divida en 8 reinos, las "Estaciones" y los "Ritmos", siendo las estaciones evidentemente Primavera, Verano, Otono e Invierno. Los protagonistas son parte del reino de Invierno, y la historia se desarrolla en ellos tratando de recuperar lo que alguna vez fue suyo antes de que el reino de Primavera los invadiera. Creo que lo que mas admiro de esta historia es la habilidad que tuvo la autora para crear un mundo magico tan diferente y al mismo tiempo tan parecido a cosas que ya conocemos y con las cuales nos podemos identificar. Me encanto su concepto. Creo que una de las cosas que no me cuadraron de la historia es que en ciertos puntos se pone demasiado lenta, es decir, la autora empieza a abundar en cosas que la verdad ni al caso. Creo que todo pudo haberse resuelto mejor en unas 80 o 60 paginas menos. Ademas, el desarrollo de los personajes y sus interacciones entre si tambien fue un poco lenta y es dificil conectarte con ellos y sus personalidades, asi como las relaciones que se suponia que debian mantener entre ellos, las cuales por momentos me parecian algo superficiales. La autora se enfoco mas en darnos a entender el trasfondo de la historia y por que las cosas eran de ese modo, y no se centro tanto en las relaciones de los personajes, que aunque esto no sea lo mas importante, si se nota a la hora interactuar y sientes que todo lo que hacen es repentino. Independientemente de esto, Snow Like Ashes fue una lectura entretenida, me gusto bastante, no deja un cliff hanger, y se que estare leyendo la secuela muy pronto.

When I first heard of this book, I immediately judged it and disliked it, which I suppose wasn't fair. This was before the big fan base had come in, however it had a large enough fan base that I came across an article on how more people were waiting for the 'Breaking Dawn' novel than the 'Deathly Hallows' novel. I believe the exact words used in the article were something like "The most awaited teenage boy this summer is not Harry but Edward." So as a Harry Potter fan, I instantly hated Twilight and vowed never to read it out of sheer loyalty to Harry. O.K. so maybe that was a little immature, but in my defense I was only 13 This was in 2007, four years ago. However that same summer, my close friend whom shared my love of Harry Potter told me that she actually read the Twilight books and they actually weren't bad. I trusted her opinion and so I decided I would read the books. I finished the first book in a matter of hours, same with the second novel, and the third, and the fourth. And no it wasn't a "so good I couldn't put it down" kind of quick read. It was a "this writing is meant for an eight year old." Because let's be honest with ourselves, the book is not by any stretch of the imagination deep. Nor is it meaningful. Nor is the writing anything but basic, and if I do say so myself exceedingly cheesy. The plot line if you can call it that was terribly unsatisfying, the characters were cardboard and the fact that it was quiet obviously based on Stephanie Meyer's fantasies was a little creepy, to be honest. I didn't HATE the book, but I certainly didn't like it and I was glad I had merely borrowed the books and not purchased them. Then, about four months later, the ridiculous fan base came flooding in. I'm talking about the "Team Edward" t-shirts and plastic vampire fans, crying, screaming girls, dolls for each character, etc etc. Now I know I can't really say much for the fan base because I know that a lot of the Harry Potter fans are the same. However Harry Potter is at least a good story, has a great plot, realistic characters and wonderful writing. To be honest, the media exposure around the Twilight turned it from merely a disappointing read into something I hated. And something tells me I'm not the only one.

If I Stay is a "nice" story about life after death. But in a book where death is such an important subject, "nice" is not enough. The story starts with Mia and her family going on a trip, but after a car accident, their plans and their lives change completely. After waking up and realize she is in a sort of "limbo" between life and death, Mia must face a difficult decision as to whether follow her family to the other side or to stay and fight for her life. If I Stay is a very light book. For me it was an intriguing concept that relied too much on YA genre stereotypes and ultimately failed to be anything else than a "feel-good" read. The story of Mia is very basic and the character is very transparent sometimes too transparent to be surprised by her choices. The problem is that when the climax of the book is her "choice" of living dying, you at least have to keep the readers wondering what is it going to be. But from the very first pages you realize it's going to be a happy ending and the story fails to be exciting or compelling while reading it. It does get you sad in some parts and you might cry, but if you want a more thoughtful story about death or life, as you want to see it this is probably not the book for you. On the other hand, if you want a nice teen love story, it will be right up to your alley. The writing is good and the characters are easy to like. It might not be the most original treatment on the subject, but If I Stay manages to be entertaining enough to "stay" until the last page.

I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. Thanks to The Fantastic Flying Book Club and the publisher Ever since Flashfall, the element cirium has been in high demand. Orion is a Subpar, someone with resistance to the radiation emitted by the flash curtain. She is an ore scout and her job is to find cirium in the tunnels of Outpost Five. Orion and her best friend Dram work in the caves together, fighting deadly animals while trying to obtain enough cirium to earn their freedom and passage through the cirium shield around Alara. New people arrive at Outpost Five and Orion learns that Congress may have been lying to the Subpars. Will Orion mine enough cirium to make it to Alara? Flashfall was an intriguing dystopian read. While I did see some similarities with The Hunger Games - mining and a Capital-like city - Flashfall did have unique aspects such as cirium and the flash curtain. Orion was a good protagonist but she could be very reckless. Given what Orion went through some crazy, horrible stuff goes down , I thought she coped very well. I liked lots of the characters but Dram was one of my favourites. There were a lot of characters in Flashfall and there were times when I got some of them confused. The romance wasn't over the top and I felt that it fit in well with the story. The plot was pretty much all action which made the book go very quickly. While the storyline held my attention, there were points where I felt that there could have been more description as I wasn't sure what I was supposed to be imagining visualising. Overall this was an enjoyable, unique read.

Reviewed by Sally Kruger aka "Readingjunky" for TeensReadToo.com I'll admit I picked this because of the title, GOING NOWHERE FASTER. Aren't there times when we all feel that way? Stan Smith has more problems than you can shake a stick at. One problem is his name - "Stan." Who names their kid Stan? But then his parents aren't exactly your normal, run-of-the-mill parents. They are another one of his problems. His dad is a crazy inventor and his mother is an over 6-foot-tall Amazon vegan who attempts to run an organic food market. Another sore spot in Stan's life is Prarash, his mother's smelly yoga and meditation partner, who practically lives with them. There's also Chopper, the family dog who produces more "gas" than the oil fields of Kuwait. The only normal one in the family is Stan's little sister, Olivia. She's the one bright spot in his existence. Stan should be thinking about college, but instead is working a dead-end job at Happy Video. It at least gives him the chance to watch endless videos in an attempt to prepare for what he hopes is a future in writing movie scripts. In the meantime, he is stuck riding his ten-speed, helping out in the family business, and hoping for a chance to date the girl of his dreams, Ellen. As if Stan doesn't have enough problems, he believes he has a stalker. The victim of high school taunting and bullying, he was threatened by Ellen's ex, Chad Chilton. Now the evidence is mounting and points to Chad as the probable driver of the speeding car that almost ran Stan off the road one dark night, as well as the twisted mind that left a mutilated Barbie doll on Stan's steps. These acts of terror, plus slashed bike tires and vandalism at the Happy Video store, are sending waves of fear through the frustrated Stan. Sean Beaudoin uses witty dialogue and hilarious descriptions to grab readers and get them cheering for poor Stan. The first person style helps readers understand Stan's above-average intelligence and his passion for movies and scriptwriting. This is definitely one I found difficult to put down once I started reading.

It's is a mediocre book that didn't really affect me that much. It is supposedly a touching story about life on an Indian reservation, dealing with poverty and coming of age. Those things make the book hard for me to relate to. I think that the book isn't necessarily well-written, but it isn't poorly written either. The writing perfectly reflects the book by being quite bland and neutral. I didn't really think about the writing, I mainly saw the book in my head. There aren't any complicated words, and it is generally quite an easy book to read. The book is filled with cartoons that the main character supposedly drew. They give the book a very childish feel, and the book generally looks as if it is thought to be for 7-10 year olds. The cartoons also give the book a feel of the Diary of a Wimpy Kid series. I was wondering if maybe one of the books copied the other? The first Diary of a Wimpy Kid book was published in January 2007, and this book was published in September 2007. Maybe this type of cartoons were a trend at the time? Another problem I had with the book was that there was too much death at the end. I felt that the deaths added nothing to the book. The last quarter of the book is unnecessarily sad and quite poorly written. One mans death happens and he is buried within one paragraph, and he is never brought up again in the rest of the book. This quarter is written so badly and so hurriedly, that I think that Alexie just needed a spacefiller a few hours before he sent of the book to the publishers, and in a state of panic and despair threw the last quarter together. Even though Sherman Alexie vividly describes the poverty and misery of life on an Indian reservation, I found that I was not very affected by it. I think that the subject was too distant from my life to relate to, and the subject didn't interest me that much. I feel guilty about this, and I feel that I should care and give money to charities to better the lives of Spokane Indians or something like that, but the book makes it seem to hard to believe that these kinds of things are actually happening. I give the book 1.5 out of 5 part-time Indians.

I was surprised to see that Daniel Handler had publish a book so recently and so far off my radar. Having loved A Series of Unfortunate Events, I was eager to see what he would have in store for an older young adult audience. Why We Broke Up is full of complex and interesting characters. Min, Ed, and Al were all quirky, multilayered, and lifelike in a way I have come to expect from Handler. Min was smart and over-the-top and entirely authentic. Ed was doomed by his good intentions, and even though I wanted to hate him, I couldn't. While there was the typical whimsy I would expect from Daniel Handler, I was surprised at the authentic realism of the book as well. Most notably, I really loved all the secrets that weren't entirely revealed. Min's respect for her own privacy and the privacy of the characters, even to the boy to whom she was writing, seemed so real to me. Her final rant seemed so genuine, and I could remember those same feelings of loss, regret, and foolishness. Overall, this was a quick and clever read for anyone who has ever had a broken heart.

I dragged my feet a little going in because I couldn't get wrapped up in The Windup Girl, but Bacigalupi has won me over with this one. The world he creates is, to me, perfectly balanced in terms of being awful but plausible, and the characters have the shrewdness and moral flexibility that fit into it. I could have read more about the world and the people, and will be pleased when he visits them again, but I'm glad it stood on its own, not waiting on a second volume. I am pleased with the Printz win, but will have to check my feelings on if it was my favorite when I finish the honor books.

I think that much of what makes Brian Robeson such a compelling figure is the way that his character reflects the life and philosophy of author Gary Paulsen. Brian is an intensely autobiographical creation, and the spirit of personal independence and craving for nothing more than to just be a part of the wilderness--a craving that had its origin in the first book of his adventures, Hatchet--is clearly the heartfelt desire of Gary Paulsen played out on the page, in a situation that he has imagined into being so that he can vicariously live out his own dreams of life in the wild through Brian's unique odyssey. From what I can tell, Brian's Return is a sequel to the storyline as it runs through The River, rather than through the alternate sequel, Brian's Winter. It's not easy to tell for sure, but references in Brian's Return indicate that Brian had returned once before to the wilderness spot where it had all started with his plane crash, rather than that he had spent the winter out there alone and had learned to survive the experience of the ungodly cold, as was the case in Brian's Winter. Then again, maybe there's a way to reconcile the story so that the reader can choose to go with either sequel as the basis for Brian's Return. Is it possible that the events recorded in Brian's Winter could have actually occurred before those of The River, so that the first sequel could be brought into accord with either original storyline? Readers who have gone through all of the books about Brian will wonder about these things, and there's a lot of information to pay attention to in order to be able to mentally set it all right. It's just not always easy to readjust to regular life after a shakeup like the one that hit Brian when the small plane he was in crashed and he became stranded on his own in the woods for so many weeks, with nothing to help him survive but a rudimentary hatchet and his own wits. Brian is back home, now, but though he has left the woods behind, the woods haven't returned the favor he has been changed by the harrowing trials of his ordeal into a different person, and trying to get along in the "real world" as if nothing essential has changed proves to be an impossibility. After crossing a line with a violent act albeit in self-defense against a high school peer, Brian goes to see a counselor to help him decide what his next move should be. Caleb, a tall man built like a linebacker but with the thoughtful consideration of a philosopher, coaxes Brian to speak about what it was like living by himself in the wilderness. Having gone blind due to a freak illness several years back, Caleb can imagine the glorious outdoor settings that Brian describes with a rich intensity that eludes most other people, and the incredible tales that Brian tells open a window through which Caleb can once again experience the visual majesty of the world around himself. Caleb soon realizes that there's nothing wrong with Brian he simply needs the wilderness, and there's nothing that can be done to take that desire out of him now that he's experienced its wonder and lived to want more of it. With the encouragement and support of Caleb, Brian convinces his mother to let him go back again to the place where he feels he first came to understand his own soul, and live there indefinitely. The trip is not an impromptu one this time around, though, and Brian plans and plots carefully to bring along the exact kinds of equipment that he will need to subsist in the wilderness for a long time. He is going back to where it all started, and of his own volition, but this time Brian will have the tools at his disposal to have a realistic shot at dealing with whatever surprises nature has in store for him. There is an adjustment period even for an experienced woodsman like Brian, but the real test of his ability to reassimilate to the dangerous outdoors will come when he's faced with a threat so raw and unpredictable that his response could never be tested ahead of time. Only if Brian can face down the greatest terrors of nature will he have proven his ability to become part of that nature and rise above its ever-present perils as a hunter, not becoming one of the unfortunate hunted. Will he be able to make it by himself in a world where eat or be eaten reigns as the supreme law of the land? I sort of found myself wishing that this book were longer, and covered more of what happened after Brian made his decision to return to the wilderness that had so claimed his heart and soul. Brian's Return is a very short book, and leaves off not far into Brian's latest adventure. The story ends before his time back in the wild really has progressed far at all, and I'm sure that it left readers with a strong desire for a fifth book, a desire that would eventually be satiated with the publication of Brian's Hunt. All in all, I think that Brian's Return is a good wilderness adventure story, with even more to offer from a nonfiction standpoint of describing survival techniques and tips than the previous three Brian Robeson novels, and I believe that anyone who enjoyed those first three will definitely want to read this one. I would give two and a half stars to Brian's Return.

Instagram Twitter Facebook Amazon Pinterest AMERICAN GIRLS was a quirky, interesting read. It's about a girl named Anna who has a massively dysfunctional family. Her mother had a midlife crisis after she came out as a lesbian, only to have yet another inseminated child. Her father is married to a woman half his age. And her sister, Delia, is off in LA somewhere, making a tenuous living as a bit actress. After a high school prank goes terribly wrong, Anna decides she can't take anymore and it's to LA she flees, to a sister who isn't all that pleased to see her and is busy wrestling with demons of her own. Anna is a flawed heroine in the best sense of the word - she's self-conscious, awkward, selfish, and yet, she really does try to be a good person. It just takes her a while. She's also morbid as hell, and has a dark sense of humor that made me cackle while also looking around guilty, like maybe I oughtn't to laugh. I noticed that the UK version is titled MY FAVOURITE MANSON GIRL and this title actually makes sense, because Manson is one of Anna's morbid interests and at one point during her stay in LA, a creepy indie producer actually hires her to do some research about Manson and his gang and give him her thoughts about the girls and the cult and everything. AMERICAN GIRLS, on the other hand, seems a bit vague, and its reference in the story isn't all that crucial, whereas Manson is. AMERICAN GIRLS actually reminds me of a book I used to love in high school. It was called BLISTER by Susan Richards Shreve, and it was also about a girl making her own way in the world after a traumatic family event. Both books deal with being a poseur, bullying, selfish parents, and travel, set against the backdrop of typical YA coming-of-age themes. Give it a read. If nothing else, it'll make you laugh inappropriately. Thanks for the free copy, Netgalley! 3 to 3.5 stars!

WTH is this? stereotip seniman? Nggak butuh waktu lama bagi saya untuk menyimpulkan bahwa Elang adalah seorang misogynist yang menganggap wanita hanya bersikap santun di luar tapi mesum di ranjang. Ketika Elang melihat seorang wanita, yang dipikirannya cuma "bisa diajak tidur nggak ya" dan tentu saja body yang hot. beli kompor sekalian Lang. Setelah itu, Elang adalah tokoh yang luar biasa kepo. Motifnya untuk ikut menyelidiki kasus bunuh diri penulis ini sangat tidak jelas. Cuma sekedar penasaran saja. Lalu dia pun dilibatkan dalam penyelidikan memangnya boleh Polisi melibatkan warga sipil untuk kegiatan kriminalitas? kacau banget dong . Lebih jauh lagi, Elang bahkan bersedia pergi ke Jakarta kasus sebelumnya ada di Pontianak dengan uangnya sendiri tanpa di-reimburse untuk membantu penyelidikan polisi. Baik banget lo Lang, abis berapa duit tuh buat sekedar kepo doang? Elang juga mau saja jadi mata-mata untuk selidik ini-itu yang malah dipake buat cari cewek. Iya, Elang disini digambarkan guanteng buanget sampe semua cewek yang dia goda picisan pula rayuannya mau diajak tidur walau baru sekali bertemu. Bener deh isi novel ini 40 nya dipake buat menggambarkan bagaimana wanita itu gampang dirayu, fisik bahenol baju ketat-ketat, dan manja ala kucing di ranjang. Sama sekali nggak diceritakan ada wanita pintar di buku ini. Bahkan seorang dokter wanita yang juga didekati Elang, digambarkan begitu berpikiran pendek sehingga mau saja dirayu si terduga untuk membunuh. Tapi eits, nggak lupa, telanjang dulu yuks.... facepalm Totally misogynist. Lanjut lagi, terbukalah misterinya........... yang bikin saya sinis juga. Peristiwa bunuh diri si gagak hitam juga pembunuhan si merpati putih yang disamarkan sebagai bunuh diri ternyata berkaitan dan dilakukan oleh orang dekat. Tapi motifnya, sungguh nggak masuk akal. Dan itu bikin semua peristiwa di buku nggak masuk logika. Ada pula peristiwa penyanderaan oleh si pelaku yang sangat dangkal banget, lagi-lagi menyeret Elang si warga sipil yang harusnya nggak ngerti prosedur penangkapan, juga ada Ronny, random guy yang ditemui Elang di warkop hanya 2 kali. Ngomong-ngomong, sama sekali nggak ada prosedur-prosedur ala Law Order disini. Kerja polisi sangat cepat dan nggak butuh surat-surat untuk penangkapan atau prosedur ijin dari atasan untuk penyergapan pelaku yang menyandera. Nggak perlu Brimob, nggak perlu kopassus. Cukup beberapa orang saja dengan 2 warga sipil. tepok-tangan canggih ya. Kesimpulan, buku ini cukup mengecewakan. Saya nggak suka cerita dangkal dan hanya asal tempel sana-sini. Katanya buku ini mau dijadiin trilogi? wuiiih, Semoga bisa lebih baik lagi.

Honestly, I just didn't appreciate this book. Too many cliches, ridiculous powers, stupid characters, etc. I'm probably just cynical about these sort of books because I've read too many like them. Jenny has always been afraid of trees ever since they snatched up her older brother seven years ago. But when she hears sounds of her brother in the forest, she has to go brave her fears and other faerie creatures to get him back. Blah. There are just too many things I hate. I hate Jenny for being stupid. She expects a complete stranger to help her and then make ridiculous demands. The only redeeming quality of her character is stubbornness, and that isn't even a redeeming quality in my book. Not to mention her stubbornness is more revealed by other characters calling her stubborn than her actually sticking to her decisions and being smart. In fact, she's usually just foolish as she jumps stupidly into danger and wanders around the forest on her own, or picks up potentially dangerous babies, or goes to a river and kisses potentially dangerous faerie creatures. And then out of the blue she's the May Queen with power! Oh whoop de doo. Go figure. This ridiculous character with no personality or intelligence gets to be queen. How surprising. I hate the lore in this book. Usually I am intrigued by this type of book and I love figuring out how the author will play on past legends or fairy tales, but not in this book. Here, there's a mishmash of strange legends that sort of rely on the reader to already know the references, but then changes it in strange and useless ways. For example, the mashup of Mab and Titania is just a strange thing to do. Especially since Mab is of ice and Titania is the summer queen. It doesn't really make sense and doesn't really make the story more interesting. Same with the use of Oberon. Obviously the reader has to know a little about Midsummer Night's Dream and Romeo and Juliet, and maybe a little bit of other faerie books and some Norse mythology for the name Loki... But then the changes to these characters in these books are not useful. What's the point? You might as well make up completely new characters. It's like she does these changes just because she wants to make something different just for the heck of it. I think the plot is kinda stupid too. For example, the woodsman and his wife feeding Jenny to the aired Caps is completely insane and unrealistic. They should know their vows would be broken to Nature and be destroyed. They're fairies for goodness sakes. So why do they make such a stupid choice? Dumb plot. Another example saving that baby and returning it to the mom in front of the dragon. Oh yeah, duh that proves she's the May Queen and not just an emotional girl who doesn't think things through. Another example the wager to find Jack. Why was it so easy? Why were the betrayals and the false promises so pointless at the end? I just can't. I don't really have any kind words for the book and that makes me a little sad. I guess the only thing I can say is that sometimes the syntax and phrasing or descriptions are quite nice. One star. I honestly didn't like the book. It's a bad version of a Tithe by Holly Black. Not recommended.

I honestly wish that I liked The Gardener more than I do. Bodeen's other novel, The Compound, is one of my favorite YA titles of recent years. I approached this one with high hopes, but left it fairly disappointed. The main problem is the book's length--it's just too short to do the story justice. Bodeen has a lot to say in The Gardener, but she just doesn't have the space to say it. The book has some depth, but the hurried pace never gives her--or us--the time to do anything more than skim the surface. As a result, the environmental theme comes across as preachy, the romance is inorganic, and the action is trite. However, I do appreciate the fact that Bodeen tells a unique and timely story in such a short space. And a stand-alone, at that! It gets tiring to keep up with overlong series of overlong books--short, exciting books like this one are great for both the reluctant teen reader and the busy adult. Yes, I wish this book delivered on its concept a little more. But it would be hard for anyone to follow up a book as good as The Compound without disappointing a little. S.A. Bodeen is still one of the most original, inventive, and teen-friendly authors writing today. I'm hoping that The Raft will be more indicative of her talents, but The Gardener is a decent book for anyone seeking a compact, imaginative thriller.

Spoiler Alert On to the plot line - Operation Popping the Cherry was an intervention Valentina Lena Bell's circle of closest friends put together when the seventeen year old girl was dumped by her boyfriend because she didn't want to have sex. Author, Aurelia B. Rowl, made it clear that Lena wasn't on board with this plan. Yet, she accepted to go along with it because to her, her friends made it seem it was losing them or her virginity. With Operation Popping the Cherry in full swing Lena finds herself in one disastrous situation after another. The one constant good thing, her beacon of light, turned out to be her best friend's older brother Jake. Inevitably, she falls more and more for this off-limits guy and when her secret operation blows up the internet and turns viral even her beacon fades. Facing summer vacation as a miserable and broken girl she desperately clings to the plan attaching herself to Zac a handsome lifeguard that saved her from drowning during one her over-the-top situation due to her crazy-no-longer secret operation. No matter how much she tries to give herself to this new relationship she just can't... her heart is with someone else. After yet another traumatic event occurs Lena finally... yes finally, grew a back bone and called an intervention of her own abandoning the silly operation and losing her best friend right along with Jake in the same process. Eventually her best friend returns bearing gift and apology. Tentatively, they mend their friendship. Even Jake reaches out to her, but she's not ready, willing to put her heart back on the line and ignores his overture. Jake is not so easily deterred and crashes her eighteen birthday with the perfect gift in tow. The couple reunited all is right in the world. With the exception of Lena's still intact virginity, after all seeing as the book is centered on Popping the Cherry it's only natural that Aurelia leads us there. It doesn't happen overnight. Which is great because that would have been too cliche. However, when the grand event does occur I find that the writing of it was rushed and didn't truly capture the essence of that pivotal moment making the entire book fall flat.

Read more of my reviews at Cornerfolds.com! Timekeeper is a book that I have heard a LOT of blogger friends talking about. Over the summer I finally read the blurb and then I realized what all the fuss was about. There aren't many good LGBT fantasies out there and this one sounded really intriguing! Alternative histories? Clocks with hours gone missing? Clock spirits? Steampunk is not a genre that I have a lot of experience with, so when I saw Timekeeper I knew I wanted to read it, but wasn't quite sure what exactly I was getting myself into. This book's protagonist is Danny, a young clock mechanic whose father is trapped in a Stopped town and who just wants him back. In fact, his entire life's work as a clock mechanic has been working towards getting on the crew of builders who will attempt to re-start the town, something that has never been tried before. Instead he is assigned to a clock that seems to be in constant disrepair and it's here that Danny meets Colton, the spirit of Enfield's clock. I loved these two characters so, so much! I'll admit I was a little skeptical of how Tara Sim could make a relationship between a human and a spirit work, but she did a fantastic job pulling it off! I feel like Colton in this situation could have easily come off as too naive or helpless, but instead he was adorable and certainly able to hold his own. Although Danny had his problems, I ended up loving him as well. His problems were easy to sympathize with, even if they weren't always easy to understand. I also really enjoyed Danny's relationship with his his best friend Cassie and thought she was a fantastic secondary character! I can't wait to see what role she plays in future books. While the characters are fantastic, the world building is where Timekeeper really shines. Like I said, I'm not incredibly familiar with steampunk alternate universes, but I really felt like I could see this one! The clocks and their mythology could have been really confusing and hard to imagine, but it's all so intricate that it seems almost like some forgotten piece of our own world mythology. This book has a little bit of everything - fantasy, romance, mystery, it's all here. There were times when I had no idea what was going on and I was surprised by more than one twist! This book had me on the edge of my seat! My one complaint is that the writing seemed a little bit too simplistic. I loved the whimsical nature the story had at times, but it is almost written as if it is aimed at a younger audience. As a result it seemed too cute, losing some of the urgency that I think was intended. This didn't necessarily take much away from my reading experience, but it's something to keep in mind. Timekeeper is an incredibly unique book in a sea of high fantasy, dystopia, and retellings not that I have a problem with any of those, of course . The world building and characters were amazingly well done and the story kept me guessing until the very end! It wasn't a perfect book, but it was a really great read that I'd definitely recommend for fans of alternate history and fantasy. I cannot wait to get my hands on book two!

Rating 2.5 stars. Blake is a basketball star and anyone would think his life is perfect, what anyone would dream of. But the truth is he feels his father is controlling and planning his every move, future included, and his mother lives in an ajoining litte dependance, drinking herself to sleep. Chloe has no freedom when it comes to her ultimate destination but she has only one plan to follow before she reaches it the Road. As soon as she graduates, she'll leave everything behind, her foster parents and siblings, and drive wherever the road takes her with no strings attached, not letting anyone get too close to her, for they'll only end up hurt. One night Blake and Chloe meet and all the facades will start crumbling down. Can you really choose who can and cannot love you? Or who you'll fall in love with? I loved this book to pieces. Jay McLean's writing style is fresh and smooth and captivating, I could read this book in one sitting without my eyes never growing tired or bored. However you must be aware of what you're getting into. Where the road takes me is a romantic book and I'm not referring to it being a romance, or studded with kisses and something more. Actually, I wouldn't even see it as a NA novel. I would say it was more of a transition from YA to NA, a story of self discovery and personal growth, where the characters were trying to figure out what their place is the world was, how to be that someone the person they loved need and face together whatever the road would bring them. But, going back to the romantic part, I must warn you. It is cheesy. Not in a negative way, of course, or I wouldn't have loved it as much as I did. The middle part of the book is filled with Blake and Chloe loving each other and proving how much the other meant, and while it was crucial for them to do so and it was all done for a purpose, not everyone may see it in the same way, so you must know what you're getting into. More than anything else, the message of this book was what really had me in tears no matter what life throws in your face, no matter if you can win any trouble or you succumb to it there's no pain or harm great enough to drive someone away from love because love is what makes us strong and if we are not alone, there's nothing that is too much to endure.

I really wanted to be blown away by this The Darkest Minds, but I was left disappointed. I'm not sure what exactly I was looking for, but I just wanted more. There were so many aspects I feel very neutral about. The concept and back story were interesting, but it's something we have all seen before. The plot was extremely slow paced. I found the ending to be very fast, but overall pretty predictable. The characters were believable, but I didn't find myself getting attached to them until the very end. The romance elements felt a little off. Overall, this book just left me feeling "meh." I have no strong feelings either way about it. I would categorize this book as more of a "survivalist" story than a dystopian. The world feels more post-apocalyptic than anything else, so fans of that kind of storyline will probably enjoy this. So, the last book I ever read that had pretty much anything to do with Egyptian mythology was Astarte s Wrath by Trisha Wolfe. Loved that book, thought I would give the genre ie. Egyptian Mythology another try. Its no secret that Im a mythology fan, and I always try to delve into as much as I can. Im pretty new to Egyptian though, so of course I read any book like this that I can. Daughter of Isis isn't one of those books where its romance or something and you just see bits and pieces of the mythology. Its like half mythology and the rest is romance, mystery, and horror. I was sucked into this book like there was no tomorrow. I would have finished it in a day if I had realized I only had like 10 pages to go, but I decided that I would leave some for the next day. Cant tell whether it was a good decision or not, but man Im mad at the ending! While it didn't leave me unsatisfied, it also made me very frustrated BECAUSE I WANT TO KNOW WHAT HAPPENS! But I think I will wait until the next book -sigh-. Im loving how each individual character is their own person. Even the secondary characters have spunk. Theirs Natti, our unwitting heroine, whos tough, sexy, and not afraid to say whats on her mind. Her mother s side comes from Egypt, so it makes the mythology bits a little better because she's not freaking clueless like most characters in other books are. Seth, omg, seth. And that's not a good OMG. While I get the reasons he acts the way he does, it still annoys the crap out of me. And Natti contemplating love with this guy? I wouldn't love someone who I walked in on TWICE and who sleeps through half the school. I will admit, I soften a bit towards him at the end, and I do look forward to seeing how he changes in the next book, but I enjoyed it every time Natti refused him and challenged him. Tough girls rule! Anywhoo, this book has about everything. Magic, mayhem, Cats, witty female leads, a sinister villain and a plot that will leave you on the edge of your seat! I thoroughly enjoyed this book and I look forward to more installments and more books from this author. I totally recommend it to anyone looking for a good read! A little warning though, its UPPER YA. Warned ya. I rated this book a 4 on Goodreads, but its more of a 4.5

Before Reading This gif is how I imagine Cass writing this book Oh god why? Why must I endure myself to such a pandering, trite, unoriginal, obvious cashgrab that makes it clear that Kiera Cass probably lacks a creative bone in her body? Because its fun to make fun of, that's why. Actually, it's just fun...period. As much as I hate these books on a technical level, at least they're entertaining, addictive fluff. Fluff that takes itself WAY too seriously, but I have to give Cass some credit. I still can't stop reading them as a guilty pleasure. Also, there's always the chance that Eadlyn will be a better protagonist than America, which would be cool. I also hope that the reality show elements of the Selection are enforced more now, since I thought that was a really wasted opportunity in the previous books. Less poorly-written dystopian rebellions, more "The Bachelor" please. After Reading Thanks Kiera Cass! You always know just how to suck the pleasure out of a guilty pleasure! That's quite the talent you've got there. I don't even know where to start with this. I'll put it briefly The Selection is like the How I Met Your Mother of YA novel series. That's the best comparison I have. Both The Selection and HIMYM took plots that could make decent standalone stories and dragged them on to the point of boredom for easy cash. Not only that, but both The Selection and HIMYM are thankless experiences that fans will pointlessly trek through to only be disappointed in the end. Or, at least, The Selection will end up that way, when Eadlyn inevitably picks Kile I'll eat my shoe if not and the readers realize that books 4-6 added absolutely nothing to books 1-3, in a similar way to how HIMYM fans felt after that horrible ending that devalues the experience of watching the rest of the series. Anyways, you can just feel Cass' disinterest in her own world as she numbingly drags Eadlyn, our new protagonist, through the a similar, yet more boring journey than the one Maxon went through in the first three books. The main difference is that Eadlyn is a faux "strong, female character" who actually is discrediting feminism. She talks all tough and independent yet her actions make her look like whiny putty. What's worse is that Cass drags down pre-existing characters with her new writing. I mean, I hated America as a protagonist in the other books, but at least she had a spirited personality. Here, she gets demoted to "supportive motherly queen" who only exists to sit in the woman's room and give advice. Worse of all, the ending twists the knife deep into America's character, using an unforeshadowed drama bomb to potentially throw her away. Yeah, I'm sure that will go well with fans. Plus, the Selection itself just wasn't fun. That's why I was excited for this book. Although I enjoyed the actual Selection bits from the first books, I hated how Cass bogged down the reality show element with the horribly written dystopian rebellion. Here, there is more of the dystopian rebellion, just for the opposite direction, which enforces the pointlessness of continuing this series remember those comparisons I made to How I Met Your Mother? Yeah... . However, I can deal with that. I did read the other books despite disliking them on a technical level. However, in The Heir, the Selection is a chore. It's a group date, then the Report, then Rinse, Dry, Repeat. There are a few one-on-one dates sprinkled around, but let's face it most of the guys are indistinguishable with very little lasting impression. By the time that book five rolls out, I'll completely forget everyone. Even the naming scheme is laughably trite. C'mon, naming two unrelated characters Baden and Kaden? One Eadlyn's brother, the other a Selection bachelor? Seriously? Positives? Okay then, Henri is a neat idea. I like the idea of having a YA romance between two people who can't understand each other without an interpreter. His interpreter Erik is also a pretty sweet guy, even if he is there to fill Aspen's outsider romantic interest role. Also, no laws to outlaw discrimination? That's stupid. This monarchy's stupid. I geniunely think that the people protesting against Eadlyn's family are right. It is unjust for a sole ruler to be forced on you who would make a horrible queen judging by how she acts in the book when your country is in such an awful state. Still, we've got to have forced conflict despite the fact that The Bachelorette should be enough conflict to satisfy Kiera Cass' fans.

Rating 2.5 stars Well that was disappointing. The plot is self-explanatory. It is a retelling of the Greek mythology story concerning Persephone and Hades with a modern spin. Nikki Becket is an average high school student until she ends up in Everneath which basically the Underworld. After six months in Everneath, Nikki returns to the real world temporarily. Nikki only has six months to say her proper goodbyes and tie up loose ends. This book would have been much better if not for the very selfish characters, especially the main character. Nikki was given a choice in the beginning of the book. She chose immortality or to see the boy she loved before got dragged into Everneath. Needless to say, she chose her former lover Jack. That doesn't sound so selfish, now does it? Well Jack went through hell when Nikki disappeared. He was devastated with her disappearance along with Nikki's father and brother, Tommy. But she still chose to return, just to see Jack and she'll disappear again after six months. What baffled me more is that Nikki acknowledges her selfish actions. She knows how selfish returning was to her family and friends. She repeats this throughout the book and she still keeps living out her lie. To top it off, Nikki didn't do much for the six months of her return. She went to high school, depressed and barely acknowledged Jack in the beginning. Nikki's character also annoyed me with her lack of personality. She was very bland and blah. Then there's the two love interests Jack and Cole. Jack just annoyed me and I didn't find him that interesting. Ironically Ashton painted Jack as your stereotypical heartbreaker hottie in his high school class but of course he has layers. His other layer is that he's only serious about Nikki. All the times he told other girls that he loved them was a complete lie and he only meant those words when he told them to Nikki. Honestly, I found it difficult to believe. I think Ashton painted Jack better as a stereotypical heartbreaker so well, that when Jack finally showed his soft and sensitive side for Nikki, the whole thing felt fake. Then there's Cole, the Everliving. He feeds of life essence and he wants to rule Everneath but he needs Nikki. Cole's just using Nikki because he's tired of taking orders from his ruler but he might also have real feelings for Nikki he's yet to discover. I think I understand the direction Ashton was going towards for this book. I love the idea of a modernized take on the Hades and Persephone mythology. I also like the idea of would have been complex characters like Cole who's supposedly evil and cold but slowly finding his own humanity. I also like the direction for Nikki's return to the world. I think her return was supposed to symbolize being able to say goodbyes properly and second chances. The ideas were definitely there but just not executed well. Overall, it was okay. I did not completely dislike it but it was not a good read either.

spoiler alert Ok, so I'm not going to lie. I started reading this book with the expectation that it was going to be horrendous. And, well... it was. And the fact that there are going to be TWO MORE of these atrocities makes me cringe. Tyra Banks. There are things that you are good at in life. Modelling, yes, writing books, no. This book is just America's Next Top Model in a book. First off, the preaching makes you want to kill yourself. I mean, watching Tyra preach in her show is one thing, because at least we have pretty pictures and ridiculous drama to compensate, but we don't get that in this book. So when we have scenes where girl's faces melt off and then they're lectured about the perils of sharing make-up which... really, who doesn't know that? I mean, if there is honestly any woman out there who didn't know that sharing make-up is bad news, I want you to comment on this post. Oh, and of course then there's the scene where we have the girl's introduced to the cafeteria and the four girls who are anorexic and this huge lecture about listening to your body and eating like it tells you to. But here is the thing. Since Tyra Banks can't write, she then contradicts herself. Because those four girls who are crazy anorexic become the butt of everyone's jokes throughout the novel. Over and over again, the four "heroes", who are supposed to be the compassionate understanding ones because OMG they're different so therefore ugly, are teasing and making fun of the girls who are having real weight troubles. Great message you're sending there, Miss Banks. Tyra also tries to send the message of independent woman in this novel but she takes it to the extreme, going on and on about how you don't need men and you don't need love and you just need yourself and to stand on your own two feet. She gets crazy ridiculous with it, and there is a certain amount of it that isn't supposed to be taken seriously. When the Belladonna comes in and says that you don't need ANY love in your life, I don't really think you're supposed to take that to heart. But Tyra is a terrible writer, so it's hard to tell. But see, the problem is, her main character, Tookie, gets gushy about a boy all through the novel. First about Theophilus no, I did not make that name up. In fact, I should warn you I did not make ANY of the names up. and then about Bravo who is, of course, the best looking guy in Modelland and did I mention completely modest and an amazing architect?. Tookie constantly seems to be defined by the boy she likes. Tyra is also trying to convey the message that beauty is unconventional. She's trying to convince us that Tookie and the other characters are not beautiful in the normal sense. But here's the problem with that. You have to DESCRIBE the characters for me to actually be able to tell if they're beautiful or not. Your four main characters in this book are Tookie, Dylan, Shiraz and Piper. I can tell you that Tookie has crazy hair, two different colored eyes green and brown? Green and Blue? I don't remember , is tall and has big feet. She may or may not be African-American. It wasn't clear. Dylan has large thighs. Piper is Albino and is smart though.. I guess that doesn't really have anything to do with her physical features. Shiraz is short. And that's all I can tell you about anyone in the book. Oh, and Ci L has auburn hair because one of the girl's in Modelland was obsessed with her and kept changing her hair color. Other than Tookie's mother has a very wrinkled face, I can't picture anyone else's physical features in my mind. No one. For a book that's supposed to be all about how people look, she failed pretty hard core on how they look. Writing 101. Your readers should have a fairly clear picture of what your characters look like. The story line was ridiculously insane and convoluted. The head of Modelland, who is the most cold hearted bitch you will ever meet in your life, actually knows Tookie's mother. In fact, they were friends in Modelland in their youth. And, low and behold, she's Ci-L's mother, the renegade model. And Ci-L's father... this random civilian that talked to Tookie sometime in the beginning of the book. Seriously. Plopped into the middle of the story with no context and was never talked about again until now. That, Miss Banks, is what we in the writing world call a plot device. And yours is REALLY OBVIOUS. But here's the real kicker. Creamy, Tookie's mother, has always treated her horrendously, and Belladonna, has always treated Ci-L horrendously. Yet by the end of the book, it's one big love fest, with maybe the exception of Creamy. Tookie just can't seem to live without her mother and seems to forgive her of everything terrible she's done. Belladonna is gushing over Ci-L despite being and A-1 bitch the whole book and hating Ci-L and Ci-L, who mocked Belladonna ceaselessly for the whole book, can't seem to love her mother enough. I mean, COME ON!!! Scars just don't disappear that easily! I know that my own childhood wasn't even NEARLY that bad and I barely speak to my mother! It would take more than finding out a woman is my mother for me to suddenly love her. I don't care what you say just because someone proclaims themselves my mother doesn't make their sins suddenly disappear. It doesn't make everything right. And what about Tookie? She knew all along that Creamy was her mother and still she was treated like this. If anything, that would make the scars worse, make Tookie less likely to forgive her mother, especially because by book's end, Creamy still was treating Tookie ill. Even if I could ignore the terrible characterization, the terrible plot points, the awful messages that Tyra Banks was putting in her books, I can't ignore the terrible writing. "Anytime you feel like you need a permanent breather, if the going makes you want to go on a go-see to go see your mommy and daddy, along this journey will be doors for the most delicate dames marked Home." "Myrracle wasn't the brightest tube of lipstick in the makeup caddy." "You begin your mornings staring at the fog, longing for the fateful evening when it will turn a golden yellow and then, finally, like a push-up brassiere, lift." These are just a few of the metaphors and similes that are in this book for your enjoyment. Not to mention Bravo the oh-so-perfect male that Tookie falls for telling Tookie that her "First time should be special." It's like reading bad fanfiction... only worse when you realized someone actually published this book. Basically, this book lived up to every expectation I had for it. I mean, let's face it, we don't read Tyra Banks for the good literature. We read it for the terrible slang because everyone in this book said, Gurl! . I just wish she had included pictures. I would have given it two stars. image error

Unlike in the first two books, I found myself confused most of the time. Some of this confusion had to do with the shifting points of view. I could not adjust to the shifts between Tris and Tobias because to me, both voices sounded the same. Halfway through a chapter, I 'd stop and ask myself, "wait a minute, who's talking now?" The changing POV's was only part of my problem. The other was that I could not follow the convoluted plot line. Whatever war they were fighting did not make sense to me and the title is totally misleading. Neither Tris nor Tobias were part of the Allegiant, one of the groups that they actually needed to stop in the end. Also, Tobias's descent into an insecure, sniveling weakling who first followed his mother blindly in Insurgent and then tagged after Nita in Allegiant was totally un appealing. Everything I loved about Tobias in Divergent shriveled away in book three. This powerful Dauntless instructor who was the epitome of strength and compassion nosedived into a pawn of three much stronger women Evelyn, Nita, and Tris . Who can get into that? I have always believed that good stories should end while they still have impact. Sequels are usually never as good as the original story, which the author probably worked on for many years. Forcing second and third books out within a year of each other does not allow the author the time to develop the story. While I understand that fans are waiting, I'd rather wait a little longer and be satisfied in the end. From an initial 5 star rating from me for Divergent to a 1 star for Allegiant, I'd safely say that much was lost in the hurry to churn out books two and three from what started as a fantastic series.

I was really excited to read a book about summer camp. But I'm just not sure that this one tickled my fancy camp slippers with matching pajamas, of course . With a camp story, you expect the grand arson of marshmellows at the end of woodland sticks, songs of kumbaya and jolly good fellows, spaghetti food fights, and zombie-apocalypse-survival-training Wait, that last one might have just been part of my delusions while I was at camp . But this was a lot of running around, talking, whining and complaining, and more not-so-intriguing things. I went into this book expecting something like the sisters version of Invincible Summer at camp, instead of the beach. But this was not nearly as entertaining as it could have been. Summer of Firsts and Lasts follows three sisters who are seemingly distinct in personality but not distinct enough in their voices. And guess what? Their names are THEMED! Yay! I love it when that happens. coughNOTcough Their names are Calla, Daisy, and Violet. Barf. Okay, again. They aren't bad names by any means but I just absolutely hate it when characters in books have "themed" names or similar names, because I can't frikkin keep them straight. And this time, there are three of them. I had a hard enough time with Harmony and Melody in Bumped. I would forget which sister was narrating and would only figure it out by the people she was with or the other sisters they mention. Like "Okay, so she just mentioned Daisy and Violet, so then Calla is talking." However, I'm notoriously book ADD, so maybe this was my own fault for not paying enough attention. The amount of nicknames was unbearable, considering the complete lack of consistency in which they were used. Each sister would use two or three different nicknames for each of the other sisters Violet is Vi and ViVi. Calla is Cal and Cow. Daisy is Daze, Dizzy, Zee and ZeeZee. And I think somebody is Bot or Shaz, or maybe Shaz was a stand-in for a cuss word. I can't really remember or, at the time, I couldn't tell. There seemed to be too much attention paid to the precise sequence of events and exactly what EVERYONE was doing ALL the time, as well as what everyone was wearing or talking about, or saying about the other minor characters. Sometimes when there are too many details in a book, it can seem not genuine. Not nearly enough character building, setting, or description was involved. None of the boys were swoon worthy. Even one of the main romances developed completely "off screen" and we never really experience it first hand. Mainly, what I really missed was the ambiance of camp. I wanted to feel the campfire's heat crackling against my forearm and smell the crisp sweet scent of roasting marshmallows. This book never quite did that for me. Personally, I didn't enjoy this very much, but if you miss the good ol' days of summer camp, give this book a shot. You might like it, anyway. ____________________________ In another way, reading this book was a completely surreal and somewhat nostalgic experience. I apologize in advance, because this part of the review may not be relevant to many of you. There were a lot of characters in this book with names that are the same as a lot of my Goodreads friends. I almost felt like I was at Goodreads camp... The sister named Daisy is besties with Flannery and this Flannery in the book loves playing twenty questions. Hmmmm, that doesn't sound familiar at all. But she puts a sadistic spin on it. Everytime you guess wrong you get dunked and held under the water in the lake. Are we sure this is fiction? Geez. Another favorite game of the book Flannery - Would You Rather. Apart from her, there is also a Jill, Olivia, Lucy, Jessica, April, Emily, Kelly and Joel. Then all of a sudden, other names that are similar to goodreads friends names started morphing into their names in my mind. Deena into Tina. Sally into Sandy. Steffie to Stef. Jordan to Morgan. It was so weird. Really, the only thing that kept me semi-involved in this book was the names coincidence. I kept thinking about how much fun we would all have together at camp or on vacation or some crazy crap like that. And wishing we all could have grown up around each other... Or at least that I could have grown up around people more like all of you. Do people even go camping or to summer camp anymore? The Great Outdoors? Never heard of it. Here's an attempt to get a Goodreader to go camping Thanks to S S for allowing me to read this as an ARC.

Nonnie, the famous grandmother, is dying and each family member is handling it in their own way. Ramona, the youngest grandchild, is flying off the rails. Very is reaching out to anyone who will love her. And their mom is sinking into drinking and depression. It makes for very dark, depressing read that is even more sad as you watch the inevitable descent they all make and the ultimate outcome. I can't say that I must enjoyed the ride of this story or the adventure for Very. I did not like her mom but I think that was the point and hated how everything panned out. Searching to free her captured kingdom, Aelin embraces her new Fae powers and prepares to fight. Fight for the prince, Dorian, her friend trapped in his own body with a creature known as a Valg Prince and her cousin, whose attempts to save her and her people has resulted in his capture. Not just that, but fight against the king who has caused so much pain for her people. Little does she know that other magic that of witches and wyvrens is brewing under the mountains... I wasn't able to physically be after getting struck by the emotions created by reading Sarah's book. Her writing style is exquisite, each word drawing you further in than the last. Aspiring authors should strive to be her and readers should strive to meet her. The created tension between Aelin and Rowan throughout the book leaves you begging for more and of course, Sarah supplies. Also, Aelin's fiery personality and temper help you discover hidden humor in her words. I recommend this book to anyone that likes a good read. The genre does matter Sarah makes it worthwhile.

The Nowhere Girls is phenomenal, it has such a strong and inspiring message, looking at misogyny and rape culture and how it can be challenged. What's wonderful about it though is that it feels like a conversation as opposed to a mandate, it explores different women's opinions in a way that makes it clear that those opinions are valid in the debate. That might not make sense unless you read, so go read it!! The characters were brilliant, whilst the reader gets to hear from a variety of people the three main characters and the founders of The Nowhere Girls are Grace, Rosina, and Erin. I loved all of them, I liked that they were the misfits to begin with and that through their actions they become part of this large and supportive group. The three of them have such different personalities but I liked how they gelled together. I love how Grace finds her strength in helping others and finds people that truly like her for who she is. Rosina puts up a good front but it was really nice to see her become vulnerable around Melissa and I loved the relationship between her and Erin. Erin was my favourite, how she manages to be herself and be unapologetic for it whilst dealing with a lot of situations she isn't used to. Getting glimpses into the other girl's lives and also the nameless thoughts gives the story another dimension, it provides a lot of different perspectives especially with regards to sex and I think is a brilliant way to highlight that there is not one size fits all when it comes to sex or sexuality. The Nowhere Girls really makes you think about what you can achieve if you put your mind to something and how we should all be more supportive of one another especially when going against societal norms. I don't really know what else to say except that I believe that this is a very important book, anything that can create conversation on sex, consent, and rape is. It's a book that I wish I had access to when I was younger so that maybe I wouldn't have felt so ashamed of my feelings towards sex and sexuality. I highly recommend it. I sped read this one for half a day and I'm sorry I spent so much time on it. At first I thought it was kind of awesomely terrible, in a pulp fiction kind of way, but then it just became completely awful. The story is a lurid one. It follows teenager Britt Pheiffer, who decides to go backpacking in the Grand Teton Mountains during her spring break. No matter that several young girls have gone missing in the area recently. Only, when she and her friend, Korbie, are driving up into the mountains, a vicious snow storm stalls their car on the road. They leave the car and hike until they find a cabin, but the occupants, two young men, take them hostage. !!! And. One or both of them could be a serial killer!!! Now, I'm not immune to such drama. I wanted to read this book precisely because the plot was so out-there. I think I would have enjoyed it too, if not for Becca Fitzpatrick's writing. I've never read a Becca Fitzpatrick book before, but I'm well aware that her series Hush, Hush is widely considered by respected reviewers to be a travesty of young adult fiction. The work of this author has received a lot of scorn. But, I guess I had to find out for myself. The results are in, and yikes. The immediate phrase that comes to mind is dumb girl. How can I have any respect for such an immature character? Girl, you've been stranded, held hostage at gunpoint, dead bodies are every-which-a-way and you're checking out your kidnapper's abs?! No, girl! Yes, yes, I know that Britt Pheiffer is a character -- a construction. I guess I should heap the incredulity and blame upon Fitzpatrick. What kind of example is she setting for young readers, romanticizing such shitty men? The romantic hero vacillates between wounded puppy and criminal asshole, as if the former makes up for the latter. And then there's the cheesiness of the prose and stereotypical characterizations... I think I officially gave up on the book as soon as I read a line that waxed over the "deep pain" in his eyes. Barf. The book would have been better with no romance at all, and this is coming from a reader who loves a good romantic element. As for the plot, for the most part it was solid. It was a creepy one, if predictable. The setting was ideal. The bitter cold, driving snow, and bleak isolation made for a great backdrop. This book was not without promise! Unfortunately, I think the issue with the book resides at the core of Fitzpatrick's writing style. I don't think I'll be checking out any more of her books, no matter how lurid the synopsis. One out of five north stars.

This book was a hard one for me to rate. I loved the story, but I think the execution really needed some work here. Some aspects of this book were really well done and some had me thinking a completely different person was suddenly writing the book. This book is an Aladdin retelling, where the Jinni is a female this time, and she manipulates the young thief into helping her obtain her freedom. Zahra has been trapped in her lamp for over 500 years, having been cast down into the long ago buried garden deep under the desert. Zahra had then committed the Jinni's highest crime she dared to love a human. Long ago a Queen had found her lamp, and the two bonded friendship and grew to be more like sisters. The ruler of all the Jinni commanded Zahra to strike down the Queen and then was exiled into the lamp never to be discovered again. Only 500 years later she is summoned from her lamp by the young thief, Aladdin, and she soon learns the reason why The Jinni rulers son has been captured by the humans and imprisoned in a bottle of his own. If Zahra can free him, she will win her hearts greatest wish her freedom. She then uses Aladdin to wish them into the palace so she can start her mission. She will stop at nothing, twist any wish around so it helps her obtain her goal. Only problem is that she is finding herself a slave to those human feelings that got her imprisoned in the first place. Eager not to repeat her past mistakes, but unable to ignore her heart, the story takes us on this crazy carpet ride of romance and betrayal. Okay, so the good bits There is girl power in full force in this book. Zahra is her own person, and she doesn't take shit from anyone, no matter who they are. She can be selfish and stubborn, but she totally owns it, and I love her all the more for it. I also love her back story with her fallen Queen, Roshana. She narrates her story as if she is talking to her old friend, and it was really endearing. In 500 years she still regrets and mourns for what happened to her greatest friend. The Princess and her Watchmaidens are so refreshing. They are all there to support and protect one another. There is no pettyness between them, no jealousy, just love and respect. They are all warriors, and in a world that believes men are the better rulers, these woman are fierce and unstoppable. I love the writing and world building in this book. It reads so lyrical and its full of magic and the land came alive in my mind really easily. No instalove in this book, hurrah! It was very slow burning and really natural how it developed, however I have some negatives for this point too, which I shall get to in a moment. What I didn't like Oh my goodness, but the dialogue in this book is atrocious. I was cringing and rolling my eyes the entire time. It mostly irritated me with Aladdin. I didn't really like his character all that much. He was portrayed as this charismatic, worry-free street rat, but I honestly found him extremely dramatic. I found he contradicted himself too much, and when he was trying to be suave it came out just the total opposite. I could hardly handle Zahra and Aladdin when they finally admitted their feelings for one another. Yes I was happy about the eventual romance, and I was looking forward to the romance, but Aladdin seemed to only speak in cliches, and Zahra all of a sudden turned from strong warrior Jinni to a total puddle of mush. Why couldn't she be both? Why does it always seem to be one or the other?? The back story with the Queen Roshana and Zahra was waaaaaaay more interesting, and I was disappointed we didn't get more of a developed story there. Prequel, anyone???? I liked the scenes we got that were essentially written snippets of history, but I wanted more. The story AND the dialogue in these were truly beautiful and lyrical. I was more interested in this story than what was currently happening in the book, which was unfortunate for me as it was only about 10 of the actual story. The story really wrapped up a little too neatly at the end. I was really irritated with Zahra's final battle with the Jinni in the end. Over and over the Jinni gave her opportunities to renounce her love for humans and come back to their side. Seriously, it was said about four times. And back at the Palace, suddenly Aladdin was able to create a riot of citizens to help the Princess defend her kingdom in about 15 minutes, even though Aladdin hadn't been seen in the city for weeks. Just a little to convenient for my liking. All in all, I enjoyed the book for the most part, but not enough that I felt it deserved more than an average rating. If I was on board with the romance, maybe it would have scored higher, but it just didn't do that much for me.

Que dramatic sighing, this review isn't what I wanted it to be. After reading glowing reviews praising this book and it's humour, I had my expectations set high. Especially since I read Libba Bray's other novel - the Diviners - and I found that one to be pos-it-tute-ly amazing, so I figured I would like this book all the same. I was wrong. Oh, so terribly wrong. Because not only did this book not meet my expectations but it was so bad I didn't even want to finish it. I had to force myself to finish this novel, for the pure purpose of me hoping it would get better. And it didn't. No, instead I got more of an unpredictable plotline mixed in with a slewful of randomness, and oh god those characters, just thinking about them gives me a headache. Now guys, I love you all but I cannot for the life of me find what you liked in this book. The humour which many have praised, I couldn't find funny. It seemed to me that Libba Bray tried too hard - with the "commercials", the endless footnotes, the stereotypical characters, I could not get into it. The whole book felt too fake and too, just, annoying to read. I couldn't stand reading about any of the characters. I wanted to hurt them all, especially the airheads. Reading about the girls - every single one of them - just angered me because they give a bad name to females. The supposed "smart one" isn't smart, she's just as annoying as the rest of them. The characters were the reason I had to stop reading and take an Advil because I was getting a headache. From reading their BS. I know, I know, that was probably the point. The characters stupidty is the purpose, the entertainment of the book. Well guess what? It wasn't entertaining or funny in the least bit. It was just stupid and there is only so much stupid I can read before getting frusturated - and this is coming from a 10th grader! And that's all this book was stupidty. I feel that Libba Bray wanted to make one of those perks-of-being-a-wallflower-esque type novels whereas she tries to shove all these issues into one book and call it inspiring. But unlike Perks of Being a Wallflower, it fell flat. You have your transgendered character, your lesbian, your disabled, your airhead, your control freak, your minorities, your I-don't-need-no-man girl ... basically you have this assortment of characters that may have worked if all their stories were developed beyond the cookie-cutter descriptions we were given. The "humour" actually overshadowed the characterization and made it unable for me to like anyone. Why? Because no character was developed properly. This book had the potential to work, if it was just taken a bit more seriously. And for christsakes, I felt like I was being talked down to when I read this book. I understand that Libba Bray was trying to make teenage girls feel better about themselves, and go all gung-ho for feminism-girlpower-we-can-do-it sorta attitudes but I mean c'mon. I'm in the target demographic, I'm 15-years-old, and I found this book to be exhausting to read. It was as if I had one of those teachers who thought they knew everything and I, the student, knew nothing at all. Talk about annoying. I am all for feminism and making girls feel empowered. I love making girls feel good about themselves and helping them be individuals and not a product of society. But using cliche and overused sayings does nothing for a book except make the reader yawn and roll her eyes. It's boring, we've been through this again and again. You want to make a difference? Don't tell us how we should be, show us through the story and the characters. Make the characters empowering. Make the story revolve around that and not a mixed-up, jumbled, everything plot. Perhaps that is what I hated the most, even beyond the characters. Although Libba Bray's characters were good with their words for the most part and said all those nice out-of-the-book phrases, they didn't show anything through their actions. The main character, Adina, frequently says that she doesn't need a man cough oldest and most cliched phrase ever cough and yet when the sexy pirates come along you read that right , she goes all gaga for them. Mhmm, and this is supposed to make me feel empowered how? I really feel bad about this review because I was so excited to read another Libba Bray and yet, this novel truly let me down. Sorry guys, I tried to love this but I just can't read this without feeling like I'm losing brain cells.
