After being caught shoplifting Sam Stonesong moved from Philadelphia to Lancaster. She's struggling to stay part of the popular crowd and hoping to find a boyfriend. When she meets a mysterious guy in a pizza parlor things start looking up. As Sam works to build a relationship her issues with her mom and her popular friends start to get worse, and Zach is definitely keeping secrets. Zach is Amish. Which is painfully obvious from the first time he's introduced because of the title. Amish Guys Don't Call makes it clear there's going to be an Amish guy somewhere in this book. If, for half a novel, the protagonist is going to struggle to work something out, then the reader shouldn't know. It makes the protagonist look dumb and makes the story feel slow because HE'S AMISH OF COURSE HE IS. The plot is all over the place with several subplots that are never really properly resolved. There are scenes that feel oddly out of place and sort of pointless Hell House wasn't really necessary for Zach to reveal he was religious, the Sunday work thing got that across . The book ramps up VERY slowly, climaxes...and then peters out without proper conclusions to any of the plots aside from the weird romance. Every character is keeping secrets and aside from Zach they're all pretty awful people. Their secrets are used to explain their actions but it's still hard to sympathize with awful parents, catty teens and worst of all Sam. Sam is awkward. A phrase which here means has the emotional intelligence of a rock. She makes "jokes" that are far and beyond cruel and is surprised when they fall flat. She's the irritating character archtype who's smart, unique and different ugh people who enjoy twilight are dumb etc, people who party are lesser. . Her love interest immediately knows she's "special". It's a character that's been done to death and it's not interesting. Zach is the gem of this book. Despite his secret being not so much a secret he's mildly interesting, a good human being and very likeable. His relationship with Sam is a bit boring, there's no real reason for them to be attracted to each other at first and the chemistry is weak at best. The teens also feel very fake. There is some knowledge of slang present but it reads more like "cool-mom trying to slang" than real teens. The "cyber-bullying" was an absolute joke where the worst insults were maybe at a 2nd grade level of savage. It was a book that tried to do too much. Deal with divorce, drug addition, leaving an oppressive community, dealing with shoplifting addiction, dealing with bullying, dealing with first love, dealing with religion etc. As a consequence it didn't do anything particularly well. The characters are two-dimensional and the plot is a bit of a mess. It wasn't a terrible read and had some funny relatable moments but it definitely doesn't elicit high praise from me.

The Stuttering Tattoo Steven Bishop rides a motorcycle he restored himself , is built like a star quarter backer and has a stutter. He lives in a town not the middle of nowhere and his dad works as a cop, is mom ditched them a while back and he's just waiting for the opportunity for fun to come kick the boredom out of his life, and that it does in the form of the mysterious Becky. And doesn't he wish that he'd stayed bored. When Becky comes to school she looks past the stutter and with her weird and unusual self is instantly lumped into the "Freak" category so when Steven gives her a ride home and a dead arm is found in her front yard mauled by her dog, things go from boring to Holy Moly! Armed with a Sudoku book a pen, a motorcycle and his ex hit man friend they battle Becky and her family. Part mystery, part thriller, part just plain quirky this book makes the "did that really happen? Is that even possible" believable, this story is weaved so well that it could happen to anyone. I found myself being drawn back into this book again and again. Logsted creates one boy who with the help of his Colombian cartel hit man turned cook construction worker takes his town from boring to center stage when he gets involved with the wrong people, the wrong people who kill, stalk, rob, steal and the wrong people are Becky's family. No longer behind the scene Steven Bishop is centre stage. With an array of supporting cast this book is quirky, scary, heart thumping-ly addictive. The stuttering Tattoo.

Crooked Kingdom is the epitome of a perfect book. This heart racing sequel to Six of Crows will have you you the edge of your seat. Praise is well deserved for this action packed adventure! The Plot In the aftermath of "the impossible heist" things continue to turn dangerous for Kaz and his crew. The deadly group of misfits must overcome more obstacles to re-unite and escape the world of hell that is raining down on them from all corners of the kingdom... Oh, the feels!! I never thought I would be calling a sequel my new favorite book, but...Crooked Kingdom is my new favorite book! Leigh Bardugo has delivered perfection. Yes, it is a sequel, but it honestly reads well enough that you don't necessarily have to read Six of Crows though I HIGHLY recommend reading it, as they are a pair and Six of Crows was fantastic . The author has done an incredible job with catching you up in the beginning of the story so, no matter how long its been since you finished book 1, you don't feel like you need to re-read it to be kept up to date. This story holds laughter, sadness, pity, admiration, fear, action, adventure, justice, revenge, and death. The book quickly jumps in to action, as there is never a dull moment. We learn more about the characters through flashbacks that are both relevant to the current story and a perfect length as to not digress too much in to the past but still help us learn exactly who they are. The characters are further developed with astounding backstory and we grow even closer to each one of them. There is so much emotion in the heartbreaking stories of each character that drives them to be the exceptional criminals that they are. The plot twists of the story are amazing. Bardugo does an exceptional job with keeping us guessing at every turn. Just when you think Kaz has been out-schemed, he pulls another scheme out of his sleeve! Each situation has a surprising, unexpected outcome that still fits and makes sense in hind sight. This duology has ensured the fact that I will read every book by Leigh Bardugo that I can get my hands on, no questions asked. Crooked Kingdom gets all the stars and moves to my number 1 read for 2017! Don't miss out on this amazing adventure!

Judul The Death Cure Penulis James Dashner Penerbit Mizan Fantasi Halaman 492 halaman Terbitan Februari 2012 Keadaan makin tak terkendali. Penculikan manusia kebal terjadi dimana-mana. WICKED menyebarkan foto Thomas sebagai buronan paling dicari dengan imbalan tinggi. Kejutan justru muncul di Denver, kota dengan pengamanan superketat terhadap penyebaran virus Flare. Seorang kawan lama muncul. Bagaimana mungkin? Bukankah dia sudah mati di tangan Thomas? Siapakah otak di balik penculikan itu? Mengapa mereka menculik manusia kebal? Sementara itu, WICKED mempunyai rencana baru yang tak kalah gila dan Thomaslah satu-satunya orang yang bisa menggagalkannya. Sanggupkah Thomas kembali ke neraka itu demi menghancurkan rencana yang mengancam kelangsungan hidup umat manusia? Review Ini akhir dari trilogi ini? Serius loh? Serius loh? Masalah terbesar saya dengan serial ini sejak awal adalah saya gak punya karakter yang saya suka. Si Teresa sebenarnya cukup potensial, tapi dia hilang begitu saja di buku ke-2 dan membuat saya tidak cukup peduli padanya. Hal ini membuat seri ini, bagi saya, bergantung sepenuhnya pada plot. Di buku pertama dan kedua, plot dan aksi yang ada cukup menutupi karakter-karakternya yang menyebalkan dan sangat emosian serta bikin saya yang baca jadi emosi dan pengin bilang, "Woles aja napa?" . Lalu datanglah buku ketiga... Karakter tetap tidak ada yang saya suka. Hal ini diperparah oleh plotnya yang membosankan. Kejadian-kejadian yang ada di buku ini juga cenderung tidak seru. Bikin ngantuk malah. Satu-satunya bagian plot yang saya taruh perhatian lebih adalah plotnya Newt. Itu pun saya masih heran dengan surat yang dia kasih ke Thomas dan dia suruh buka di waktu yang tepat. Kalau isi suratnya kayak gitu, kenapa dia gak langsung bilang aja sih? Pakai acara sok misterius segala. Akibatnya si Thomas kelewatan "waktu yang tepat" itu dan jadi ngegalau kan. Ya, secara keseluruhan, saya tidak bisa suka pada novel ini. Apalagi akhir ceritanya yang kayak gitu. Agak kurang jelas dan penuh pertanyaan gitu. Yah, kali kedua saya kasih 1 bintang di buku akhir sebuah trilogi. Para mi gran decepcion, Otono en Londres no ha sido para nada la novela que esperaba leer. He de aclarar que en si misma la novela me ha gustado, es muy entretenida y plantea unos personajes muy interesantes que le dan diferentes puntos de vista a la historia, pero no pasa de ahi. Las primeras 200 paginas consisten en presentar a los personajes, que claro, como son muchisimos pues lleva para rato. Y realmente algunos de ellos me han gustado mucho y creo que estan bien desarrollados y cobran vida por si solos, pero personalmente, hicieron que me costara introducirme en la trama. Algunos incluso me sobraron, y no entendi la importancia que se les dio para el final que tuvieron en la novela, pero bueno al ser la primera parte de una trilogia quiza jueguen un papel mas importante mas adelante. No hay demasiada accion y eso es lo que para mi gusto ha jugado en contra. Los grandes secretos por desvelar de algunos personajes, realmente me han parecido una chorrada, quiero decir que no me aportaron ningun giro sorprendente. La gran "accion" se comprime en las ultimas 100 paginas y se basa unicamente en malos entendidos, cosa que no me ha gustado nada. El gran giro final me parece cogido con pinzas, considero que no venia a cuento y que unicamente se ha utilizado para dar emocion a una historia realmente plana. Pero bueno, como he mencionado anteriormente, Otono en Londres es muy entretenida y la recomiendo si te gustan las historias de personajes. Las altas expectativas jugaron en mi contra...

I wanted to love this book so much but no matter how hard I tried in the end it just wasn't possible. Jackson Pearce has been an inspiration to me for many years and I was looking forward to finally reading one of her books. She just seems like an awesome person. Unfortunately this book didn't seem to have the same spark as her youtube videos. To start, the characters where difficult to get attached to. The only time I really cared for the characters was in the beginning and then as the story went on I got bored of them. I love the idea that the two sisters are so close that they believe they share a heart. My sister and I are incredibly close so in a lot of ways I understand that feeling but throughout the whole book they kept saying it but I never seemed to feel the connection. Both the sisters came across as very one dimensional. I really didn't care for Scarlett for most of the book. She seemed to only have two emotions, angry and more angry. I also found the fact that Rosie had to lie to her sister about wanting to take classes appalling. If Scarlett cared about Rosie's well being she'd be pushing for Rosie to have a normal life. Just because she knows there are monsters in the world doesn't mean your little sister doesn't need an education. Buffy slayed vampires and still managed to make it to school everyday why couldn't Rosie do both? All I have to say about the whole Silas Rosie thing is that he is an adult and should know better. Scarlett is also an adult and if my best friend had a crush on my baby sister and acted upon it I would have let the damn Fenris have him. Silas should have been the mature one not acted upon his feelings. If he liked her that much he should have just waited until she was damn well old enough that they weren't breaking the law but I guess killing feral werewolves puts them above the law. The Fenris never made since to me. Where did they come from? Why do they exist? Why do they lose their soul? What makes them lose all hope of redemption? How come the Fenris seemed to have more personality in the two sentences before they are killed than the main characters did the entire book? Why were the Fenris just a giant metaphor for pedophilia and why were highschool girls the only vitims? Why did the main characters never search for other hunters and why are there so damn many Fenris and no normal people have taken notice? I have a million more questions and I think that's exactly why this book didn't work for me. I feel like nothing was ever resolved at the end of this book. This book had the potential to be an entire universe of wonderful scary retellings but in the end I just felt very unhappy with the book and felt that most of it was wasted on the same repetition of events. I didn't like the way other females in the book where handled and potrayed. I really don't understand why Rosie and Scarlett seemed to think they were above the rest of the world because they knew of the darkness that lingered out there. Everyone is fighting a darkness whether it's internal or external shouldn't matter. I guess at the end my only real question is why are they hunting other peoples darkness when these characters couldn't seem to even accept their own?

I first read this book when I was in college. I immediately fell in love with Jessica Darling so much so that I bought each sequel on their respective release dates and read them immediately and I've even read the MG prequel and am excited to read that book's sequel as soon as I can . But let's start discussing Sloppy Firsts, shall we? This is the book that introduces us to Jessica Darling, her parents and sister wedding obsessed like the family in Sixteen Candles, one of Jessica's beloved "new classics" , her best friend Hope, her current "friends," who she has dubbed the "Clueless Crew" and possibly best of all Marcus Flutie. This book is technically marketed as adult fiction, probably because when it was released, there really wasn't a thriving YA market like there is today. Which is just as well when it was released, I wouldn't have read it if it were marketed as YA. I feel like there are two things people discuss with this book. The first, of course, is Jessica and Marcus Flutie. Oh God, it's highly possible that this is my literal favorite fictional relationship ever---more than Anna and Etienne, more than anything from Sarah Dessen, more than anything . But the second---and this is even better than Jess and Marcus---is Jessica herself. She's got this very unique, very funny, VERY sarcastic voice. Probably her closest comparison is to Olive from the movie Easy A and maybe a dash of Veronica from Heathers, but with a healthier love life. Bottom line, though---this book is perfect. If you've ever felt like you're in the wrong place or the wrong era, this book is for you. If you've ever felt even remotely like an outsider or misunderstood, this book is for you. So basically if you've ever been a teenage girl---or are one now---this book is for you. Highly, highly, highly recommended.

Title Eon Author Alison Goodman Genre Fiction, Fantasy, Young Adult Publisher Penguin Group Publication date 2008 Format Paperback Pages 531 Review This book is reminiscent of the literature I used to read when I was a "young adult." Books such as Blood and Chocolate, The Only Alien on the Planet... books that had a point and didn't assume teenagers were only concerned with three way love triangles, fickle emotions, incompetence in every form. Alison Goodman makes me believe that there are authors who still have faith in their audiences who don't think young adult means pointless and mindless. Eon is about a girl who is fighting for a future in a society so determined to oppress the female sex that it is engrained not only in the men of the culture, but the women are complicit in their own oppression, as well. This is a trait that is characteristic of Eon Eona as well, in fact, it is one of the main frustrations of the novel - a conundrum that keeps Eona confused for the duration of the book and yet it is so easily solved if she had faith in her own gender. It is one of the most revealing things about the book showing just how far this culture has fallen in regards to sexuality, but it is also one of the largest frustrations. A mystery that holds no mystery for the reader and it is why that as amazing as this text was, it will not be receiving a five star review. I read these books because I wanted a female lead who was worth cheering for and after reading an assortment of reviews for both texts on Goodreads, I thought this duology would present a heroine most likely to deliver - and I assure you, dear audience, I was not disappointed in any way. Eona is good, strong, and willing to die for the people she loves. Not the type of love presented in Twilight, but love that Aristotle would have endorsed. Eona's love for Chart, a crippled boy in her Master's household, her love for a Concierge and a warrior eunuch - it fills the pages. She's sensitive and delicate, and yet it does not make her a weak character - but rather it is a part of her strength. The character Eona is presented as unapologetically female - although in a culture that has no value for women - Eona herself is occasionally apologetic for her gender. I recommend this for any fans of young adult, feminine, Asian influenced cultures. This is what I believe authors have done if this is not the scenario then it is such a great tragedy that they actually take some of the shit they write seriously. Memorable Quote s "I wondered what would happen to a man robbed of his essence - would he become a woman, or would he become something else?" 31 "They are only women, but they are better than nothing," 43 "No wondered the nobles acted like gods they'd captured the very elements in their robes," 50 "There is no power in being a woman, and you are suffering for your choice," 244 "I could not move. A thousand lies were collapsing within me, the roar in my ears drowning out everything except two words which I shall not provide, naughty - naughty, go read the books! " 401 Now, there's much more of that... but if I keep going, I fear I won't stop, so that's all you get from me. Rating Four stars Title Eona Author Alison Goodman Genre Fiction, Fantasy, Young Adult Publisher Penguin Group Publication date 2011 Format Paperback Pages 637 Review I am happy to say that the sequel to Eon, Eona, does not have the same frustrating aspect that the first novel did. There is not one simple solution that is painfully obvious to the reader and yet Eona can't seem to figure it out for 400 pages. There's no easy solution to this novel and it is completely laced with tragedy, betrayal, and heartbreak. One of my favorite aspects of the novel is Eona's relationship with Lord Ido. I think it adds depth to both characters and I will say that if there is anything I didn't like about the book, I did not like the ending. Not to say that the ending wasn't fitting, just that I personally didn't like it. It's not that I wanted her to end up with Ido, it's not that at all - I just wanted something more. And yet, this is one of those novels where once you finish it, the characters follow you into the next book you pick up - because you're not ready to let them go and they're not ready to let you go, either. I recommend to anyone and everyone. Memorable Quote s "In war, truth is the first casualty," 1 "For almost five years I had lived as a boy, and even as a lowly candidate I'd had more freedom than this role as a woman," 52 "... the words of a woman who had tried to kill her empororer and sent her hatred across five centuries could not be trusted," 88 "...but as he recast me in the mold of woman, I had felt my body become a possibility to him, and my flesh the sum of what I was. At the time, it had shamed and infuriated me," 271 "And so I met the eyes of the man who wanted to kill everyone I loved and enslave me. And in their flat stare was a frown of recognition that chilled me to my very core," 290 "...the poet of a thousand sighs..." 347 "History does not care about the suffering of the individual. Only the outcome of their struggles," 462 "'This is not destiny,' I spat. 'This is ambition made from betrayal and murder. Do not dress your atrocities in the garb of the gods,'" 626 Rating Four stars I really just want to take a moment and say that the illustrator for these novels created visuals worthy of the text. In fact, upon beginning each of these novels I felt that Goodman had an obligation to write as beautifully as the cover artwork. Thank you, Tony Sahara, for the creations.

Meine Meinung Als ich die Prophezeiung der Hawkweed vom Verlag vorgestellt bekam, war ich sofort Feuer und Flamme fur diese Geschichte. Das Buch klang nach guter Fantasy, die durchaus auch jungere Madchen ansprechen kann und besonders das Hexenthema hat mich sehr angezogen. Als ich mit dem Buch begann, versank ich sofort in die Prophezeiung und war gespannt, welchen Einfluss diese wohl nehme wurde und wurde mit jeder Seite mehr von der Geschichte enttauscht. Poppy eine junge Hexe und Ember ein ganz normales Madchen wurden bei ihrer Geburt vertauscht und Leben nun im Leben der jeweils anderen. Das fuhrt dazu, dass Poppy viele komische Sachen passieren, wahrend Ember ein mangelndes Talent fur Hexendinge zeigt. Die Idee war zauberhaft aber die Umsetzung dazu hat mir leider nicht gefallen. Die beiden Madchen sind leider sehr stereotypisch und ich fragte mich, ob es nicht einen ahnlich tollen Effekt gehabt hatte, wenn man das nicht so uberzogen dargestellt hatte. Ich bin mir sehr sicher ja. Kurz nachdem sich die beiden sehr zufallig mitten im Wald getroffen haben, taucht dann Leo auf. Poppy verliebt sich in Leo, Ember verliebt sich in Leo und irgendwie verliebt sich auch Embers Cousine in Leo und das auch jeweils auf den ersten Blick, was ich schon sehr komisch fand. Im Verlauf der Story nimmt Leo doch dann auch eine sehr tragende Rolle ein, was sehr von der eigentlichen Thematik des Buches abgelenkt hat. Sie nimmt einen sehr starken EInfluss auf die Handlung und hat sie in eine Bahn gelenkt, die mir nicht gefallen hat. Daruber hinaus kam mir das Ganze sehr kindisch vor. Auch an vielen anderen Stellen war die Handlung kindisch und zu konstruiert. Daher hatte ich schon das Gefuhl, dass ich schlichtweg zu alt fur dieses Buch sei. Aber zahlreiche sehr brutale Stellen liessen mich das in Frage stellen. Sie waren sogar mir teilweise zu schlimm und ich mochte diese Buch eigentlich keinem Kind empfehlen. Neben der Enttauschung bezuglich Story und Charakteren, war der Schreibstil zwar nicht schlecht, aber dennoch nicht so gut, als dass er einiges hatte wettmachen konnen. Schade, denn die Idee hinter dem Buch versprach so viel. Fazit Ich habe mich sehr auf den ersten Teil von Poppy und Embers Geschichte gefreut und wurde dann enttauscht. Die Charaktere waren zu stereotypisch und blieben daher leblos und eine eher kindlich gestaltete Liebesgeschichte nahm einen grossen Teil der Handlung ein, die fur ein Kinderbuch jedoch definitiv zu brutal ist. Somit kann ich euch Die Prophzeiung der Hawkweed leider nicht empfehlen. Vielen lieben Dank an den Fischer Verlag fur die Bereitstellung des Rezensionsexemplars.

Aliens are coming! Not to save us or communicate with us, though. Oh, no. Aliens are coming to kill us. But that should be pretty obvious, right? Since when do aliens, or the ones we've seen in the movies, at least, ever come other than to cause trouble? In The 5th Wave, that's exactly what they came to do. The only problem is that no one knew what they looked like probably not like green sticks with bobble heads , which made it easier for the aliens to attack. They attacked in 5 waves, and Cassie, our protagonist, survived 4. The plot was unique. Not the alien part because when has that not been done? , but the waves. An EMP crashes all devices and electricity, tsunami's flood cities and countries, birds carry a deadly and contagious disease, and aliens pass as human beings only to kill real human beings. Let's just say the alien's enjoy mass-killing with a little bit of spice. Moral of the first 4 waves do not trust other human beings. They could be aliens for all you know. In the beginning, Cassie lived by that motto. Then she met Evan Walker, and what did she do? She immediately trusted him. Cue the eyeroll. Yes, there was instalove. Yes, his job was to kill her but for some unknown, unbelievable reason, he did the exact opposite because she's apparently special compared to the hundred other humans he's killed??? . Yes, it was ridiculous. But I liked Evan and there is no shame on my part. He could shoot and kill with little effort! It was soo cool!!!!!!!!! No, children, I don't condone killing. But when you gotta get through bad aliens to rescue your brother during the end of the world, a guy like Evan comes in handy. Okay, but on a sidetone, I won't ignore how easily Cassie trusted him. She knew better and yet she still kept fooling herself. Come on, YA, haven't we had enough of that???? I admired Yancey's writing style and his ability to handle four POV's. I was able to keep up with each one and it allowed an insight to different conflicts during the alien invasion. The only problem I had was with Sam's POV, a 5 year old boy who sounded like a young adult more than anything else... But he was a cutie pie, so who cares? My favorite character, however, was Ben. Benjamin Thomas Parish. Wow. So beautiful, I think I shed a tear. I smell a love triangle coming up soon, but hey, we'll see how it goes. It's a good book, but not great. The plot, the writing, and the characters were a joy to read about. Although there were minor set-backs, I was able to overlook them and enjoy the book as a whole. I'm so excited to read The Infinite Sea! Bring it on, Yancey!

"I love you," I say, because I really, really do. "I know," says Polly, because it's true. A retelling of The Winter's Tale. A smalltown where the cheerleaders are the true stars. It wasn't until I finished it I realized how much it has in common with Beartown, that I read earlier this year. Smalltown mentality, a sports team that is the hope and pride of the town, rape, slut-shaming, the unbreakable bonds between teenage girls, and of course - the BEAR theme. In Beartown it's the hockey team that are the bears but in this one it's the cheerleading team - the girls - which is more interesting I think. Although I think Beartown does other things better. I desperately wanted this to be a Sweet Vicious substitute since the show for cancelled, but it was just the dough to S V's fully baked batch of cookies. What I love about S V is that it doesn't kid itself into thinking what they are doing is excusable. It starts of movement, but the realistic kind. It shows consequences right away. Vigilante fails to portray the real insidious nature of sexual assault and rape is not that it can happen anywhere on the streets, but that it is most often committed by people we know and trust. Hadley's internal dialogue is matter-of-fact about her view and what's wrong and what's right that it's hard to believe in her character. I want more fem vigilante stories because even when they fail there is so much that is being said in the actions taken and the results and fears for these women. But Really, Netflix, please pick up Sweet Vicious. I want nothing else more. Maybe a million dollars and then I will produce it myself.

3.75 I really enjoyed this book and flew through it but I had a few problems with it. I think the main selling point for this book is that it's about a school shooting and I'd never read anything like that before so I was interested to see how it panned out. I gave this a shot because I've been hearing nothing but good things about it but it didn't fully meet my expectations. I found the writing to be very confusing at times and I had to reread scenes to find out what happened. That being said, it was also very fast paced which doesn't really make sense but there were some scenes where I couldn't turn the pages fast enough. I found the writing of the P.O.V.s to be confusing as well because I often couldn't tell who's perspective I was reading from. I liked the shortness of this book, but at the same time I felt like it prevented me from getting to know, understand, and connect with the characters. So while I enjoyed how unique it was that this book took place within such a short time frame 54 minutes , I also felt like it hindered a lot of the development of characters. I will say that I liked Ty's character. I thought he was written very well and was definitely a complex character. He was frustrating yet showed glimpses of humanity every so often. It's a haunting and heartbreaking read and definitely not for everyone. If it sounds like something you can stomach I suggest giving it a try but it's a tough book to read at times because of the events of the shooting. I can understand why this book is so popular and raved about since it talks about an important yet sensitive topic. Overall, I was impressed with this book but it didn't fully live up to my expectations. It's a really quick read but not for everyone. Give it a try if it sounds like something you'd be interested in. I enjoyed it and think it's unforgettable but it's not a new favourite. I'm definitely interested in reading more from this author in the future and it was excellent for a debut book.

Maybe 3.5 stars? Perhaps? I'm torn between giving a good rating in appreciation of her scope and skill and withholding stars as if it truly mattered because I was denied the things that I wanted. Repeatedly. Was this well-written? Absolutely, although at times it leaned so metaphysical that you struggled to follow the threads. I don't mind a dose of philosophy in my books -- I actually appreciate it -- but you had to juggle quite a bit of backstory, myth, and supernatural story threads in order to follow. Bit exhausting, really, and not what I thought I had signed up to read. Again, I don't mean to say it was poorly executed, but it did feel like a handful and I'm curious what her true young adult crowd thought. Even at 27 years old, I had had it by the end. "Stahp," I wanted to say. "Can we not? Can we not waste another chapter on characters I don't care about? Can we stop with the no-one-can-be-happy circle jerk? Can we stop with the Last Minute Upset kinkfest?" Can we? Can we? My goodness, if she didn't dangle happiness like water in the face of a dying man. Pages upon pages of denial. I often got the impression that the poor characters were just lions in a crumbling Colosseum and the author a conjurer with too many wicked inclinations, dreaming up things for them to fight, each battle more ridiculous and confusing than the last. What a terrible metaphor. Maybe you get my point. The point is that she loved prolonged suffering. I'm just honestly sick of that trope. Is it a trope? I'm not sure. But I'm sick of authors constantly withholding love or happiness across entire novels. Maybe the protagonist shares six paragraphs of joy in the entire series? Maybe? Not just referring to the hero and heroine although they're definitely included, as there wasn't nearly enough of them together -- much less together and happy -- to suit my tastes , but friends and family, as well. I very much understand the need for conflict in a novel. I do. When people are too happy for too long, there's no interest. But, jeezus. A bit more would be nice. I'd recommend this series, definitely. I don't know if people would stick it out to the end, but it's something that's worth starting. Her writing alone is worth it.

I started this book with excited anticipation. This was my last selection for the Canada Read list, and it was a Governor General Award winner. But now after reading it, I can't help but feel that this was a "token" awarding, as the subject matter is vital, but there is so much brutally lost potential to this book that I almost cried. There is creativity, critique, snark, word-play and vision, and like a bright light after long darkness, you are relieved and grateful to see a book that explodes sex and gender rigidity. Unfortunately, there is too much angry emptiness for the light to be even painfully enjoyed. Profound, incisive commentary fell at the feet of too-clever banter, crushing nihilism, and repetitive hyperbole. All the stereotypes of adolescence were there without true self-reflection, growth, or even literary elaboration, and I felt there was a hyper-pettiness and misogyny that completely drowned out the beautiful extended metaphor. Even the movie industry with all its fakery, cruelty, and corruption can occasionally have its moment of kindness e.g. The Princess Bride , sublimity or transcendence The Priest, 1994 . Nothing in this book transcends contempt, ranting, or bad judgment. The density of shock sex comments is so great, that one is bored by the sexual references by the 4th chapter. An absolutely crucial message is looses so much power by a kind of mechanization of human agency. The main character is written as entirely an one-dimensional derisive character such that the one redeeming quality possible compassionate feelings towards a younger sibling feels unbelievable. Whether a character is good or evil or even amoral, a one-dimensional character fails in literature and drama no matter how important the message. Brilliant lines such as that of page 30 "When we got to my grandma's house and she saw that Ray wasn't with us, she didn't seem surprised. She probably just thought he'd be in another meth lab explosion," are completely ruined by silly lines such as "Shame is so boring." Our protagonist, by constantly pointing it out and discussing it with the reader, must think it's interesting. If this is highlighting the hypocritical notions of the pre-teen teenager, then "Bravo." Narcissism, truly a factor in Hollywood entertainment, high school and life in general, is sadly all the character is, as he sums up so eloquently on page 137 "But think about how horrible it'll be to wake up every morning think about someone else before you think about yourself," which feels like a chance lost. In the rush to be edgy the message gets so overwhelmed by condescension, that the reader has a tough time connecting with narrative, the characters or subject matter a great squandering, indeed.

Alles im allem erscheint mir dieses Buch eher lustlos dahergeschrieben, weil der Verlag mit einem weiteren Scheck wedelte und ist ein eher klaglicher Versuch einer begrenzten Story eine Fortsetzung aufzuzwingen.

Paranormalmente sedicenne Paranormalmente e il primo romanzo di una trilogia che, in America, e stato pubblicato con il titolo Paranormalcy. Questo primo volume racconta la storia di Evie, una sedicenne apparentemente come tutte le altre ma che, invece, lavora per l'AICP, il Centro Internazionale del Contenimento del Paranormale. Evie, infatti, non e una ragazza qualunque, ma una paranormale puo vedere attraverso le sembianze umane assunte dagli esseri paranormali e quindi conoscerne la loro vera natura. L'idea di fondo del romanzo e, senza ombra di dubbio, molto interessante e per certi versi anche molto ben sviluppata. L'AICP, l'organo che si occupa di recuperare e controllare i paranormali nel mondo, e una trovata tutt'altro che banale che, lo ammetto, mi ha fatto un po' pensare Fringe, una delle mie serie tv preferite. Ad aumentare la curiosita che mi ha spinto ad acquistare il libro per fortuna scontanto! hanno contribuito le critiche di diverse autrici di Urban Fantasy, riportate in quarta di copertina, che si dicono entusiaste della storia. E' forse anche per questo motivo che mi aspettavo fosse un romanzo completamente diverso, dimenticando o, piuttosto, mettendo in secondo piano il fatto che si tratta, invece, di un Urban Fantasy rivolto ad un pubblico di lettrici molto giovani. Probabilmente, comunque, anche se avessi avuto dodici anni di meno non avrei espresso un'opinione tanto differente da questa, anzi, forse sarebbe stata ancor piu negativa. Evie, infatti, e quanto di piu lontano si possa immaginare quando si pensa ad una eroina in generale e ad una eroina per adolescenti in particolare. Io, che da adolescente mi sono innamorata di un'eroina come Jane Eyre, non avevo e ovviamente non ho proprio nulla in comune con Evie la quale, in una situazione critica, pensa all'ultima volta che ha passato il Silk epil alle gambe. Risulta poco credibile, infatti, che un organo importante come l'AICP piu o meno agli stessi livelli della CIA, per intenderci affidi delle missioni ad una ragazzina di sedici anni come lei, interessata piu all'abbigliamento maculato e al tacco di dodici centimetri che ad altro. Probabilmente le teenager di adesso troverebbero fantastici e spiritosi i suoi "bip" sostituiti alle parolacce e i numerosi sospiri dai significati piu svariati! di Raquel, cose che, invece, in un lettore che ha superato da un pezzo i tredici anni creano diversi "fastidi", come orticaria, nervosismo e qualche volta vera e propria irritazione. Per non parlare, in ultimo, della scelta del colore rosa! di ogni accessorio, compreso un taser e l'impugnatura di un coltello utilizzati come oggetti per difendersi dagli esseri paranormali e che costituiscono, quindi, l'arsenale di una "cacciatrice". Adesso, in tutta onesta chi ha paura di una cacciatrice di paranormali che utilizza Tesey il taser e un coltello rosa?! Ma non ci sono solo cose negative in questo libro anche se, devo ammetterlo, superano di gran lunga quelle positive. Tra gli elementi che si possono quindi considerare positivi ho trovato interessante l'idea di dotare i paranormali di "vere" sembianze, oltre a quelle "finte" che assumono in presenza di mortali, e di far loro possedere dei tratti di personalita particolari. Mi riferisco, nello specifico, alla figura delle fate le quali, negli altri Urban Fantasy, vengono sempre dipinte come esseri molto dolci e altruisti e che la White, invece, descrive come esseri spiccatamente intelligenti, molto astuti e tutt'altro che preoccupati per il prossimo. Nonostante le fate abbiano stuzzicato la mia curiosita, lo stesso non posso dire per gli altri esseri paranormali. I temuti vampiri, infatti, abbandonano l'aura sexy e diventano delle macchiette, piu simili agli stupidi zombie che ai vampiri veri e i licantropi si trasformano in teneri e dolci cucciolotti al servizio degli umani. Insomma per chi come me, appunto ha in mente il prototipo di eroina da Urban Fantasy in perfetto stile Anita Blake o Olivia Dunham, e per chi ha superato da un pezzo l'adolescenza questo libro e solo un'inutile perdita di tempo. Recensione presente anche sul mio blog Recensione Paranormalmente

This story focuses on three teens in "The Walled City," a city full of criminals, prostitutes, and a drug lord. It starts off with Jin Ling, a girl disguised as a boy, who meets Dai. Another boy with a mission to get into the drug lord's- Longwai- palace. They pair up to do drug runs for Longwai. Then another character is introduced. One of Longwai's prostitutes, Mei Yee. Mei Yee is actually Jin Ling's sister who was sold to Longwai when they were young. Jin Ling has made it her mission to save Mei Yee from Longwai. Dai then finds Mei Yee's window- not knowing she is Jin Ling's sister- and asks her to help him. Dai requests Mei Yee to find information on Longwai and the whereabouts of Longwai's ledger. You don't find out why Dai is doing this until halfway through the book. Dai is workng with some sort of government force to bring down Longwai. They need to find his ledger so they can have evidence for arresting him. They have until New Years to get this ledger, because that is when the government will raid Longwai's palace. ... I really really enjoyed this book. The writing is so poetic. It could have the worst plot ever- which it doesn't- and I would still love it because of the way it's written. I felt like the characters were well formed, but I didn't feel extremely close to them. I also think the reason why Dai was doing all this wasn't there much. It was only mentioned one time and I actually forgot why he needed the ledger when I was near the end of the book. I did love this book and I would recommend it. Four stars.

It seems that I like Bella The Vampire much much more than Bella The Human. Bella The Vampire could definitely kick some serious ass. The story started off with Bella and Edward's wedding, which was a bit weird actually. And right after the wedding which was marred by Jake's appearance who disappeared, heart-broken in Book 3 , Edward whisked Bella off to a private island for their honeymoon, which was kinda freaky. We were exposed to the love-making process between a vampire and a human... but not much really. And soon after, Bella was pregnant. Haven't they even heard about safe sex? Guess not. At this point, where Bella and Edward realized that she is carrying his not-so-normal baby, the story got really interesting. I was hooked from that moment on. And telling the story from Jake's perspective was great. At least I was grateful not to be in Bella's world where it only revolves around Edward. All in all, this book did not disappoint me much. This review was originally posted at Dual Reads Copy received via Netgalley for an honest review It's been a while since I've read a book that left me so breathless with anticipation! From the depravities and delights of the Gomorrah festival itself to the thoroughly lovable characters and tense plot I was thoroughly entranced. Sorina is one of my favourite lead characters. She is tough downright scarily ruthless at one point in the story but loving and trusting. The care she had for those she loved was so wonderful and made it lovely being inside her mind. Before starting the book I was unsure how I'd view her "illusions" - were they people in their own right or would they seem more like figments of her imagination. It was definitely the former. I loved reading about each and every one of her family and felt like I got to know them very well. There were some, like Nicoletta that had maybe a stronger presence than others - but they were all delightful to read about. And Luca was just an incredible love interest - the kind you can fall in love with as you read and not too perfect! The central mystery kept me on my toes the whole way through. Much like Sorina I would swing between options - thinking it was an outsider then thinking it had to be someone from the festival itself. And even there the number of possible guilty persons was starting to make me distrust everyone. It was so incredibly tense never knowing what would happen next and I was genuinely saddened by any death in the book I actually cried at one point . The world Amanda Foody has created here is maybe my favourite part of the whole book. It's not just the festival - although that felt so tangible I could almost taste the smoke - it was also the surrounding world. And I need more of it. Whilst this story is very self-contained and definitely doesn't feel unfinished - it is still a world I want to spend more and more time in. I am intrigued by the political side of the world for example and would definitely read a book with a different main character set in the same world. Whether it's this world or a new one though I am incredibly excited to read more of Amanda Foody's books. This was delightful. And the representation was excellent. There was a bisexual main character - the love interest was demisexual. And both were never a big issue. It was so lovely for me to read a bi main character just being. If you're at all interested in fantasy or festivals or illusions then I highly, highly recommend Daughter of the Burning City.

Since Mare surrendered herself to save members of the Scarlet Guard, she's been a prisoner of Maven. Her powers suppressed by Silent Stone, she watches and waits for some chance to escape. After a while, she begins to wonder if Maven might have changed since the death of his mother. How much of his sadistic nature was Elara in his mind? But the Scarlet Guard has plans, and it will be all out war to rescue Mare and prove their strength against the Silver forces. I have to say, this book seemed to drag until Mare finally escaped. First of all, the font was so tiny! Am I getting old or what?? And the narrative for the first half was shared between Mare and Cameron, and quite honestly, I barely remembered Cameron, except for her ability. I actually thought she was a he for quite some time until she mentions having her hair in two braids... . I wasn't sure why Cameron was used as the alternate POV, except that it seems the author wanted Cal's thoughts and plans to remain ambiguous to Mare and everyone else, who are hesitant to follow a Silver. And then, midway, Evangeline shows up as a POV, and drops a pretty big bomb in terms of her character motivations. I felt a bit like her being a lesbian or bisexual? it was not clearly spelled out was more of a plot twist. I'm not saying it was out of character, but three books in, I wasn't expecting everything I knew about Evangeline to change and for her to become a more sympathetic if not likable character. I like that Maven turns out to also be sympathetic if not likable. But yeah, the story really doesn't pick up until the second half, where there's a hell of a lot more action, only there are a ton of new characters introduced. I wanted more of the Lakelander princess, and more of the newbloods. It turns out that this series is not a trilogy, which means I'll probably be waiting around for the next book...

THE SECRET DIAMOND SISTERS is like a modern day version of the Luxe series fun, flirty, full of drama, and beautiful boys. What this series lacks compared to Luxe, however, is depth. It is an entertaining read, but not one to expect much from. This book revolves around three sisters who, all of the sudden, have to go live with their mysterious dad who turns out to be a billionaire hotel owner in Las Vegas, Nevada. If you've ever been there, you are in for a treat with this book because it captures the essence of the city of sin perfectly. It is one of my favorite places to visit and Madow has nailed the setting. "The casino played a song of its own--slot machines dinging, chips clacking as the dealer passed them out to the players at the tables, and the chatter of people throwing down money with the hope of hitting it big. It was like a carnival for adults. A person could get lost for days in a place like this." No, my qualms are not with the setting or writing, but with the actual characters and believability of the whole scenario. These girls lived their entire lives not knowing the identity of their father and then one day he insists they live with him and oh-he's a billionaire. Some can argue that this fact is what makes the book so fun, which is true, but a few readers will get hung up on the fact that the odds of any of this really happening are super, super slim. I can't say I didn't enjoy the idea, though. Characters in a Gif Adrian A.K.A Daddy Diamond THE SECRET DIAMOND SISTERS doesn't delve too much into the life or history of Daddy Diamond. So many questions arise about this dude, and only a few are answered. Is he really interested in being the father of these three girls? Are his motives really pure or does he have special intentions? Peyton A.K.A. the Grunge Sister Peyton is all over the place. Literally. She jumps into things and runs away from commitment. Peyton dresses down and wears as little as she can get away with, except makeup, which she loads on. I dare someone to tell her what she can and can't do. Peyton is a protective sister, but not great at looking out for herself. Her attitude and actions towards guys were really annoying at times, especially when basically threw herself at them. Courtney A.K.A. the Goody Two Shoes Sister Courtney is known for always following the rules down to every last word, staying inside instead of getting out, and focusing on being the best in school. Except, she doesn't. Once she's in Vegas, she pretty much does the opposite of everything we are told about her. Including breaking one of the biggest rules, ever. All three girls are way too perfect to be real, but Courtney takes the cake. Savannah A.K.A. the Naive Sister Savannah, obsessed with clothes and makeup, is so naive she is constantly being taken advantage of by boys and by the world simply because she doesn't know any better. Her two sisters need to look out for her better because she is only fifteen and already is doing things that a twenty year old would be doing-all the girls are. Still, the book is definitely a fun read, just not one with a lot of weight to it. There are some possibilities for twists in the books to come, which I am definitely curious about. I will be following this series.

What's the point in communication and understanding one another so there's the least amount of hurt feelings. Honestly, it's not like I have a problem that her first lurve was tru lurve. This review is also available on my blog, Read Till Dawn. This was a book I picked up for free at a book swap. The plot - about a medical and identity crisis rolled together - appealed to me, and I hoped it would be as good as it sounded. The short version of this review it was. Poor Rachel's life becomes a living hell when she suffers kidney failure and goes on dialysis. She quits ballet, the love of her life, and feels sluggish and snappy. She deals with her body's "betrayal" as she puts it very realistically, with tears and anger. She grows over the course of the book as she realizes that she must accept the fact that her life will never be the same. She also must come to grips with her birth mother's identity and reason for giving her up. This struggle also is extremely realistic, and I thought it was very well done. The only flaw I can find with the book is its pacing apparently it spans about a year of Rachel's life, starting with when her kidneys fail, but it doesn't feel like it. In fact, time seems to pass rather sporadically with detailed scenes intermingled with statements to the effect of "time passed." The passage of time is a recurring theme throughout the book, as the process of finding Rachel's birth mother takes a really long time. However, this didn't really work for me as sufficient proof from Rachel's character growth, you would think that only a few months at most have passed. I would highly recommend this book to anyone interested in what it's like to live after a kidney failure the food restrictions, the dialysis, the sluggishness, etc. It's also a great story about identity and the difference between biological and adoptive family. It's perfectly fine for younger readers, so you can be comfortable handing this book to anyone whose reading comprehension is up to it. I'm very glad I found this little treasure it gave me an up-close view of what it's like to suffer kidney failure. I just hope it's the closest look I'll ever get!

This book had a whole whack of things almost guaranteed to grab me a murder mystery, Southerners, the British, a paranormal aspect, and a connection to the Jack the Ripper murders. I really enjoyed it. When New Orleans native teenager Rory's parents come to England for a year's sabbatical in Bristol, she enrolls at a London boarding school to do her senior year and experience British life. Unfortunately, soon after she arrives, someone begins killing people on the same dates as the original Jack the Ripper killings, and the police have no leads. Then, the killer starts sending messages to Rory, and things get really weird. Without giving spoilers, I can talk too much about the plot, but I thought the author wrote a really great story, with interesting, realistic characters, who are thrown into bizarre situations and have to figure out what to do. The plot is a really clever approach combining real-world detecting with paranormal components and the result is a terrific thriller that had me on the edge of my seat waiting to see how it would all come out. Particularly the end is very nail-biting. Although this is about a teen, it doesn't really read like young adult, but is simply a well-written entertaining thriller murder mystery. Even the paranormal aspect is only a part of the overall story, so if you aren't into paranormal, you could still enjoy the rest of the plot. Definitely recommended as a great read!

Click for the full review contains spoilers! ... THE FULL REVEW Overall, I don't think the series is well-written. But that means more than what it appears at face value. I don't mean the writing itself was poor - the grammar, the spelling, the paragraphs, the chapter endings, et cetera. On the whole, the book is 'written' just fine. The problem is more with the story, the characters, the plot, the action, the pacing, the tension, the character arc, and so on. To me, Hunger Games was written by someone who worked hard to learn all the 'rules' of writing and all the techniques of writing a great novel, but... it just doesn't work. It's like she looked in a cookbook, saw all the ingredients to make a fine dish, and threw them all in with no regard for taste. It just comes out bland. Without flavor. It doesn't bang. It doesn't pop. The result is it just feels forced to me. It feels like a novel that was designed to successfully appeal to a commercial audience, while the product itself just isn't up to snuff. Everything begins and ends, I suppose, with the protagonist. And I just thought Katniss was bland. From the start of Hunger Games through Mockingjay. At the very beginning, I saw no reason for her to be the protagonist. Why is she the protagonist, over any other tribute? She volunteers as tribute to save her sister, which is supposed to be noble, but every other tribute has family and a reason to fight. So again, why is Katniss the protagonist? Why should I root for her over any of the other tributes, who have families of their own? As the book progressed, Katniss was just unlikeable. She didn't have any personality. Then, when the Games began, she just had a boring role in it. All she did the whole time was walk, run, eat, sleep, nap, nurse wounds, and hide. When she is finally joined with Peeta, all her feelings for him are faked, and poorly so. She doesn't care at all about him, she just views him as a tool for her survival, and lets him go on being in love with her and pretending she cares the same for him, when she doesn't. In that book, Gale is nothing more than a hunting buddy. Throughout the book, I wondered how it would end, would Peeta try to kill her, would she have to kill him? In the end, they are spared from having to make that decision. It is decided both of them could live if they're the final two competitors. So the biggest choice Katniss would've had to make in the book is removed from her by someone else she is rescued from having to make the big moral decision that the entire book has been building up to. In Catching Fire, she is suddenly wishing she could spend her life with Gale, and views Peeta as a sort of punishment. She is punished by the Capitol with having to spend a lifetime with Peeta. Again, he loves her, and she doesn't care anything for him more than as a friend and a one-time ally in the arena. As she is taken around the country on the Victory Tour, she is responsible for inciting rebellion, but even this, she is doing accidentally. She is again thrown into the Games, and this time, she seems determined to make sure Peeta survives and she dies. This point is repeated so often, however, it becomes tedious. We know Katniss is going to live. The only reason she wants Peeta to survive, I think, is because the author had to make her more noble. But just by repeating it so often, that she wants Peeta to live and for her to die, it just destroys any actual meaning for that. She's never tested, really, to fulfill her pledge. In the end, she is rescued, and spared from having to make the decision to lay down her life for him. Again, as with the first book, that big moral question she's been battling, whether she'll die for Peeta, is answered for her. She doesn't have to kill anyone, because she's rescued. In Mockingjay, again, her persona as hero is created by others. She's really nothing more than a green-screen actor, being made to play hero as filmed battle sequences play behind her. Everything about her is a lie. Would she still be the Mockingjay if she told everyone, then, that the whole romance with Peeta was fake? That they lied about the baby? That so many of the film promos with her were staged? So overall, Katniss is just bland. She lacks empathy. Her whole love triangle is forced and fake. Her whole persona as the Mockingjay is an act and a lie. Everything she's famous for was forced on her by others. Her volunteering herself as tribute is pointed out by Caesar. He makes her look good. Her being the Girl on Fire is made up by Cinna. Her being the star-crossed lover is made up by Peeta, Haymitch and Caesar. Her inciting rebellion in the districts is accidental. Her being the Mockingjay is propaganda by District 13. Peeta, I think, could've made a much more interesting protagonist. His feelings were genuine. He was the better speaker. I don't get why Katniss was the Mockingjay, why it was always Katniss, Katniss, Katniss, when Peeta was there all the same. He was also the Boy on Fire, was he not? He was the one who professed love for her. He's the one who saved her from the trackerjacks and saved her from the career tributes. He's the one who volunteered in place of Haymitch. Why, then, is Peeta never seen as a sympathetic character by the viewers? Why isn't he the Mockingjay? In Catching Fire, everyone says how much better for the rebellion Peeta would be than Katniss. Katniss is sniff and unlikable, and bad at acting. Peeta is smooth, likeable, and genuine. Anyway, I've said about enough. The series is way over-rated. Katniss is bland. The story is bland. So much of it is just about eating and sleeping and faking emotions and faking battle scenes and hiding from the real action and just waiting for everyone else to kill each other. So overall, Hunger Games, three stars, Catching Fire, two and a half-stars rounded up, Mockingjay, one star. The series overall, I'd give two stars. So I'm going to just give Mockingjay two stars and call it quits.

The attempt to create a plot twist in the end - Audrey being taken hostage by a false dead senator - totally felt forced and thus became a pet peeve for me. I haven't begun ranting about the characters yet. Audrey was poor. Scarlett wasn't. Audrey kept up a good a grade to compensate for her being impoverished and all. Scarlett's the total opposite. Negative attracts positive. How predictable! And don't get me started on their love hormones spreading fast through their veins like wildfire! If you're wondering what those 2 stars are for, they're given for a reason. Personally, the overall theme of the story was likable. There's nothing but love and acceptance from her family. No nasty serious sit-down confrontations about her gender preferences and who she dates. To be fair, one thing unique about this book is that it highlighted characters with scanty means. Whereas most YA books talk about characters bleeding cash from their parents' pockets. Well some would touch this topic though just as an accessory. Audrey was poor and she struggled to keep up with the affluent lifestyle in her school. The writing style was actually pretty fine so readers won't have a hard time. I'll recommend this to those who are fans of LGBT romances but with great patience to static plots.

Review also available from on my blog. For the handicapped, the universe is restrictive. They're tied to one planet rather than being able to portal to others. I imagine this feels like being confined to your hometown for your entire life. To make things worse, most were given up by their birth families, and all are constantly mocked by offworld "norms". Enter Jarra, the main character of Earth Girl. She's handicapped, and understandably bitter about that fact. However, a love of history and a desire to escape lead her to enroll in an off-world history course - one she can attend for the first year only, as it takes place on Earth. I thought Jarra was an excellent character. Her bitterness at being handicapped felt very real to me, but it never overshadowed her drive to succeed or her love of history, other core aspects of her personality. Other reviews have called her a Mary Sue, but I disagree. It's true she initially outshines the others on her course, but this is understandable thanks to her disability, she's had amateur experience at Earth dig-sites, and is a history-nerd to boot. My only complaint was the reason why Jarra kept her identify secret for so long. I won't spoil the book, but I feel like the ending glossed over the ramifications of this choice. Hopefully it'll be better addressed in the sequel. Jarra's classmates were an entertaining bunch. They're a diverse group hailing from every sector in the galaxy, providing steady subplots of gossip, friendship and romance. I thought the sexual Betans were particularly well-drawn. Karth, a foil for Jarra rather than a person in himself, was the only character I found frustrating. He was described as suspicious of the military thanks to his left-wing conspiracy theorist of a father . Ok, fair enough. But he was also most bigoted norm of the course again courtesy of his "left-wing" father . How does that make sense? I think it would have been better to split the character into two, and give each more complexity. Despite that, I really enjoyed this book. It's a clever YA novel that pairs a bitter and capable teenage protagonist with excellent worldbuilding, and absolutely deserves all the hype it's been getting.

I adore books about high school queen bees, and about the trials and tribulations of teen popularity, so I thought that The Betrayal of Natalie Hargrove would be right up my alley. Unfortunately, it seemed to miss the mark, and I am struggling to articulate why it didn't quite work for me, because there were so many elements that should have made me love it. There is a thoughtful exploration of life and character that lies beneath the glitz and drama of Lauren Kate's plot. The true nature of Natalie's deprived and depressing past is gradually revealed as the book unfolds, and there are thought-provoking contrasts between the two very separate elements of society that can be found in the town and in Natalie's own history. Kate presents a picture of people with no prospects and little hope, against which Natalie's social climbing and ruthlessness become more easy to understand. While the two socio-economic groups detailed in The Betrayal of Natalie Hargrove seem worlds apart in some ways, Kate also shows that they're a lot more similar than her characters might consider. Indeed, the reader is forced to ask whether Natalie was really any safer once she had "made it" than when she still lived in a trailer. On both sides of the tracks, sex, drugs and alcohol rule. Natalie tries so hard to put behind the world in which a girl like her is only useful for sex, but yet her relationship with her boyfriend - overtly described as loving - is shown to be largely based around sex. It is the main way that Natalie and Mike know how to relate to each other and, once sex and physicality are removed, they flounder. It is also sex, and her mother's willingness to use it as currency, that got Natalie out of the trailer park in the first place. On an intellectual level, therefore, I have a good amount of respect for this book. Lauren Kate says rather a lot beneath the facade of a fairly fluffy story. My trouble with The Betrayal of Natalie Hargrove is that this facade just doesn't work for me. The reader is presented with a cast of unlikeble characters. Natalie herself is self-focussed beyond the point where it is easy to excuse her behaviour through knowledge of her past, Mike is almost entirely bereft of personality and the supporting characters are either caricatures or similarly unlikeable. J.B was, by far, the most interesting character to me and he isn't in the book much at all. I found that the writing style also distanced me from the novel. The choice of first person seemed odd, given the book's ending, and both the prologue and the epilogue felt over-written. More importantly, however, the world of The Betrayal of Natalie Hargrove doesn't feel real. It read to me like a fantasy of what it is to be popular and daring and to be dating a fabulous boy. While, on the whole, The Betrayal of Natalie Hargrove didn't quite work for me, it certainly wouldn't deter me from picking up Fallen. I saw a lot of promise in the ideas behind Kate's writing, even though the style and characters of this work were not as strong as I would have liked.

I am not going to lie, I had pretty high expectations coming into this one, especially after being repeatedly told that this really was a must read and something that I would absolutely love. I think maybe having those high expectations wasn't necessarily a good thing, because, it took me awhile to get into this, longer than I thought it would. I think I was expecting to be able to jump right into it and be instantly in love and that just didn't happen for me and I had to make myself push through the first few chapters and telling myself that I just knew it was going to get better and to hang in there. It didn't have anything to do with the writing per se just the fact that this book has a darker feel to it than most I have been reading lately. It definitely isn't a light read. It deals with some very hard subject matters right off the bat, suicide, depression, abuse both physical and sexual , drug addiction, so yeah, pretty heavy stuff, not to mention The Gates and Shadowlands. They are most definitely not a sunshine and rainbows type of place but instead stuff that nightmares are made of. A place so dark and desolate and so haunting that it is in fact referred to as hell itself. A place that only the lost and desperate go to after they die. A place no one really wants to visit and certainly does not want to spend the rest of eternity. Although the Shadowlands are in fact beautifully dark, Fine did manage to bring the place to life with her rick attention to detail and to the citizens that lived there. You could picture the bleakness, smell the rancid scent of desolation and despair that hung in the air. You could feel the hopelessness surrounding the city and the only bright spot, the only saving grace in a world so miserable, was Ana and Malachi. Two bright stars in an otherwise nightmarish place. Malachi was truly good, selfless and honorable and everything a great hero should be. I have to say, I loved him from the moment we meet him. Lela too was a good person. Selfless, kind and caring and incredibly strong and brave, especially considering all that had happened to her over the course of her life. I loved watching her grow and open up even when it didn't seem like she ever would. It was nice and added a really sweet element to the story that it wouldn't of had otherwise. She and Malachi made a great team and I was happy to see them working together and growing together as much as they did. Fine does not shirk away from some really tough topics and somehow even though some of them are really sensitive and might not even be things that you believe in or think are possible, she makes it all work and come together beautifully. I have to say, I may have had a hard time getting into this from the beginning but that certainly didn't last. Before I knew it I was completely engrossed in the story and just couldn't get enough. I know now why everyone is raving about this read, about this series, because it truly is a stand out series. It truly is something everyone should try because they are going to love it, just as much as I did.

If you've read Wither or The Selection then you've obviously already read this book. Where Wither or The Selection went wrong, this book goes even worse because it includes the most ridiculous amount of insta-love that not only emphasizes the shaky world building and annoying protagonist, but it also includes a cliffhanger that felt added for shock value than anything else. Violet Lasting is the protagonist of this book. She is a special snowflake. Her eyes are a beautiful color, she's a beautiful specimen, her cello playing is beautiful, her body is beautiful, and she is all around beautiful. Beautiful, beautiful, beautiful. Despite all the beauty and praise she constantly receives from pretty much everyone, Violet's life is horrible. She lives in a horrible mansion where she has her own room, her own lady in waiting, marvelous food brought to her whenever she pleases, a huge library that she can visit whenever she wants, and gardens so vast that she can walk around. Not to mention the fact that she attends balls, goes to parties, intoxicates herself with champagne, plays the cello, gets primped and pampered constantly, and is protected from the "horrors" of The Jewel. Violet's life is absolutely tragic, don't you think? Despite reading 358 pages where I'm being told how horrible being auctioned off in the surrogacy auction is, I really couldn't believe it. Violet's life is absolutely privileged and she, more than anyone knows it. Never once in all those pages does she ever stop and think, "Wow, this place is horrible. I need to leave here immediately". Hell, I'd volunteer for that life, since I am never shown any legitimate reason to feel fear whatsoever. My main issue with Violet is the fact that she is so compliant. She never stands up for herself, never acts rebellious, and never tries to escape her household situation. She was sold in an auction. She is treated as no more than a uterus to bear a child. And yet she does absolutely nothing. Katniss she is not. Never once does she ever make a decision for herself. Everything that happens is because someone else decides it for her or because she's told that it's the best decision she can make. She was more preoccupied in admiring the mansion or walking through the gardens than about her own life. Was she even a little bit distraught because she was going to have to bear someone else's child? Absolutely not. The world-building is very poor. We get some small details here and there from info dumps conveniently placed within the story, but other than that we know little to nothing about the setting. How did the world come to be like this? Since when has it been like this? Is this even set in America? We're expected just to take this as it is because Violet's story is apparently much more important than actually building a believable setting. The surrogacy theme is by far the most unbelievable part of the book, and this has to do with the fact that the world building was so flimsy. We are never given a legitimate and believable reason as to why girls from poor cities must be used as surrogates to give birth to Royalty. There's also a small paranormal aspect that is used as a way to try to explain this, but it was also completely vague and basically looked over until it was necessary to keep the plot moving along again. Then to add icing to the cake, as if the annoying protagonist and flimsy world building were not enough, we have a case of insta-love that'll make you question Violet's sanity if you weren't already . One, very short, conversation between Violet and Ash about music begins this love story. Violet's every thought is consumed with Ash just because he totally understands her. His beautiful eyes can see right through her. Violet becomes possessive and jealous from one little conversation about cellists. She's jealous when he does his damn job of accompanying the Duchess's niece she becomes possessive when he doesn't glance at her when she knows that they can't have a romance because it is forbidden. BECAUSE THEY CAN BE KILLED IF ANYONE FINDS OUT. "He doesn't look at me. His eyes seem to skip over me, as if I'm not even there. Like I'm invisible. The pain of this is a sharp, physical thing." It doesn't matter if later on in the story we can actually see why they love each other and "cannot live without" the other, because by that point I was already annoyed with the couple who can go from "my favorite cellist is..." to "I think I love you" based on one conversation. The story in itself was very simplistic. There were many repetitive descriptions and similar situations. The dialogue seemed contrived and forced when Violet wasn't the one speaking, and it really felt more tell than show. Nothing much happens other than Violet angsting over Ash and going to parties and getting makeovers. There are actually a lot of descriptions of dresses and makeup and hairstyles. At one point I really believed that this book was going to be amazing. And I'm pretty sure I would've forgiven most of its flaws if it weren't for the ending. We reach the 300-page mark, and suddenly everything is going at break-neck speed, there is plot twist after plot twist after plot twist and revelation after revelation after revelation until all of a sudden, it ends. I felt like everything was still left out in the open and like pages were missing from the book. Absolutely done with this book I honestly cannot recommend this because I couldn't find anything about it that I could like or that I could say I had never seen before. If you've read Wither or The Selection, then you're not missing out on this one..

Things that really bothered me about this book -All the characters seemed dull and shallow, but none more so than Harmony. I just couldn't deal with her chapters. She was a complete idiot. Harmony was raised on a religious compound that reminded me of the Amish communities. She enters the story with the goal of converting people to her faith, but then just throws everything out the window for a hot stranger. It's utterly ridiculous and makes a mockery of actual people of faith. -The religious aspect of this book in general felt comical, but it wasn't supposed to be. I just couldn't enjoy it that way. Either be serious, or be funny on purpose. If this WAS funny on purpose, it lacked a good delivery. -Inconsistency. Harmony especially, see the first point. Her faith wavers back and forth at the flip of a page. But what annoyed me most was just that she was so dumb she couldn't remember conversations from the previous page. One minute she as narrator is saying something like "I know he doesn't believe me, so I quit trying to convince him." And the very next chapter we get this gem, "OH my grace, he never believed me? But I told him the truth, why didn't he believe me?!" What the heck is that?! I also felt inconsistency in Melody who flips her feelings for her sister on and off. She goes from being mad to super best sister ever with no warning that left me as a reader wondering if I had skipped a chapter explaining her change of heart. I could possibly say that the whole idea of glorified teen pregnancy annoyed me too, but I think that in the world of this book it actually makes sense. I did enjoy learning the ins and outs of the baby business, even if I was creeped out by it. This was a cute premise, especially with how popular dystopian books are right now, but unfortunately it left me detached, didn't make me care at all about the characters or their outcomes, and just didn't live up to what it could have been. I read the book all the way through despite figuring out by the second chapter that I wouldn't enjoy it. I will say that in the book's favor, it has short chapters that move it along very quickly so this wasn't a huge waste of time. Am I glad I finished it? Not really. Now that I know the full story, I could have easily skipped this book and not missed anything. But I am glad I started the book because I had been curious about it forever. It wasn't a terrible book, just not for me. I'm mildly curious about the sequel, so I'm going to put it on my to-read shelf, but I'm in no hurry to pick it up.

I read this book because someone told me it was a lot like The Hunger Games only better. Well, they got one thing right. It was almost identical to The Hunger Games. However, it was just as bad if not worse than Suzanne Collins's festering turd of a series. This book is a mixture of The Hunger Games, Twilight, and a fish flopping around on a dock gasping for air. I thought there might be a small link to Harry Potter as well, but the only connection there is the dynamic between Tris, Christina, and...Will, I think his name is. That's where the similarities stop with that wonderful, wonderful series. Anyway, we're in a futuristic dystopian society real original and the city of Chicago has been separated into factions. Each faction prizes a certain attribute of its members. Truth, Bravery, Intelligence, Kindness, Selflessness and maybe one more but I can't remember. When the kids turn 16, they take an aptitude test to see which trait they most inhabit and which faction they should choose. Then they can choose which ever they want in a Choosing Ceremony. The whole storyline was ridiculously and aggravatingly predictable. I knew almost every major reveal pages, sometimes chapters, before it happened. If you are shocked by anything in this book, you are absolutely terrible at reading context clues and should stop reading books forever. The main character, Tris, is wholly unlikeable and unrelatable to any reader other than the ones that are her age and gender. Even Katniss Everdeen had some redeeming qualities. Four is boring and Cullen-like to the point where you'd rather seem him take a bullet to the brain than keep going through the story. The whole thing was like a wounded zombie that's too stupid to know that it's missing a leg and both arms but just keeps trucking along because it sees a big, juicy brain it can sink it's teeth into. The brain in this scenario being teenagers and their parents' wallets. Thought I'd explain that for those of you shocked by the dramatic "turns" in this book since you're clearly bad at deciphering basic language devices. Divergent was so bad that I went on Wikipedia and read a plot synopsis for the second book to see if it was worth wasting any additional time on. I can say with certainty that it is not. I don't give 1 star ratings lightly. Most books have something redeeming about them somewhere along the line that will garner a 2 star at the very least. I've read Oprah Book Club books that were vastly superior to Divergent that I'd read daily for the rest of my life before reading this waste of paper just one single time more. If you prefer to spend your time and effort on good books with genuine, loveable characters and an interesting storyline that keeps you engaged, you'd do well to stay far, far away from Divergent. In fact, maybe don't even step into a bookstore that has more than one copy on the shelf just in case it rubs its crappy crap off on you.
