I was so excited to read Gone and can not be more disappointed. The only reason it is not shelved on the Disappointing shelf is because I think I hyped it up too much for myself. I love dystopian and end of the world stories whether its Hunger Games to Revolution, I can't get enough! When I read the synopsis, I immediately fell in love with Gone. A world where adults disappear and teens are left to roam AND its a series of 500 page books....it sounded like Lord of the Flies on crack! Somewhere in my excitement I lost the part about mysterious powers and growing darkness. That is the start of my disappointment. But before I begin, let me back it up. For those reading the review, but haven't read the novel, enjoy this very brief synopsis. Those who have read it can skip to the next paragraph. While sitting in class, attempting to listen to his teacher lecture, fourteen year old Sam and his classmates witness the unimaginable everyone over the age of 15 vanishes. Babies are left crying in their cribs, cars careen out of control, and chaos reigns. Sam finds a group of friends and tries to salvage what they have. In the mean time, a group of students from a prep school joins them. The bullies from both schools soon take control. As can be expected, sides are taken and feuding begins. Throughout all of this, different groups are attempting to understand what is happening and various students are developing X-men like powers. Also a dome like barrier is found erected around the city and a big evil essence is found in a cave. Still with me? Great, because I am lost. There is way too much going on in this novel and unfortunately too much going wrong. For one, you cannot introduce three sets of seemingly unconnected plots in the same novel and not provide some resolution or cohesion. It leaves the reader unsatisfied and uninterested in the sequels I was the fool who bought books 1 and 2 in anticipation of loving it . Next, I find the story to be difficult to believe. Don't get me wrong, I am capable of suspending disbelief and immersing myself in the fantasy world. However, when things don't make sense, even by the standards set forth by the fantasy world, then I can't commit to a novel. I found too many events to happen "just because." My examples? Squid arms and secret brothers Don't know what I'm talking about? Read the book! ... or just message me . It was like the author had a handful of scenes he liked and keyboard smashed until he had a book. My final critique, though I feel like I can go on, is that the characters were not realistic. For one, there wasn't enough characterization to make me care about them and there were far too many characters to keep track of. Most were walking stereotypes, which is offensive to readers who expect more out of their authors. To top it all off, in no way could I believe they were all 14 and under. Granted extreme circumstances will bring out the best worst in people, but I find it hard to believe that someone 14 or under could do the things these kids did. Maybe I haven't been 14 in a while why did I say maybe? , but I still can't suspend my disbelief. Now here is where I start to be confusing, my exact reason for disliking the book, is why it got 3 stars. Young characters doing extraordinary things, from running a McDonalds to shooting firebombs from their hands, is addicting to young adults. Every review from a young teen on this website loves this series. Not just this first book, the whole series! These books are huge and there are more than three No more trilogies! . This series is getting teens, especially tweens, reading. To me, that is the most important thing about a book and the reason this book series isn't drowning in a low rating right now. I can't say that I will fangirl about these books with any future patrons, but I am not afraid to recommend and promote them.

Originally posted on acrossthebookiverse.blogspot.com Nick's in a great mood. There's no one out to kill him, no one is dying, and it seems like a perfect normal day where he can pose as a perfectly normal human having a perfectly normal life. For an hour maybe. That is, until an omen of death that only Nick can see goes flying through his school hallway. All of a sudden, Caleb falls ill, which is impossible for demons. Everything comes crashing down at once. Nick's mother disappears and he begins to realize that the people he held closest to him are lying to him almost constantly. He doesn't know who to trust or who will betray him. And with his new Malachai powers barely under control, will Nick be able to save everyone with his best friend out of commission and his slippery grip on sanity? I didn't think this was a particularly spectacular book. I absolutely adore the Chronicles of Nick books, I think they're interesting and full of interesting lore, but this one didn't catch my attention as much. Best part of this book by far - Malachai Nick. The fact that he can lose control any second and completely destroy the world is awesome, but when he uses his power to save his mother and his friends, I love it. Nick almost dies about twice and it had me freaking out both times. The first time was a little sudden and was never really explained, but the second time...phew! Overall, though, I still think this is a great book, full of action and everything I love in a book, but not as outstanding as the others. Here's to hoping for more Malachai Nick!

I dislike giving bad reviews when I know the author worked hard to craft the story and the fact is so many others have liked this book--it makes me feel like I'm not getting something but I hated this book and will not be reading any more of this series. Zoey is the main character who has been blessed by Nyx. Being the protagnist she is set up as a sort of role-model and overall has good traits like loyalty to friends, not liking to swear etc.. However, when you set this girl up and have her date 3 guys at the same time, and the only reason and justification is her hormones, I'm sorry if there was a "dislike" button it would be hit repeatedly. If we were watching a movie, and a guy tried to play the same stunt he would be the villian, not the hero. Some of the supporting characters have no depth. They repeat the same type of things over and over. Though the thought of being a vampire and having gifts is new and unique it is not worth having to suffer all the trouble that Zoey ultimately gets into and how as long as she has her circle, she can fix without any thought but by just calling on the elements like a person calls on their genie to solve their problems.
Really boring and cheesy.....the story seemed to drag a lot. I really wanted to finish this book but I got to page 72 and had to stop because it was soooo boring.
Not quite what I was expecting, and I'm still a little confused about the ending. Still, will probably read the sequel.

I give it about a 2.5 stars. I couldn't really get into the writing. The long paragraphs that took up two or three pages pulled me out of the story and I ended up skim reading them. I never understood why the two started going out in the first place. Even though I've been out of high school for almost ten years, it really reminded me of just those couples that are only together a few months then with someone else. I did enjoy the art though.

spoiler alert "'Do you think your drinking is a problem? Do you get drunk when you don't mean to?' I always mean to." This is comedian Shappi Khorsandi's first novel. Let's get her writing more of these, please. Seventeen-year-old Nina drinks too much. She sort-of knows this and sort-of doesn't. It's just that things were easier before her longterm boyfriend Jamie met the love of his life on a plane and broke her heart. And things were definitely easier before that night she can't entirely remember - the night she got kicked out of a nightclub for publicly giving a blow job to a random guy and ended up in a taxi some time later clutching her knickers in her hands. As you might guess, this is not quite for younger teens, but I do hope that older teens as well as adults will pick up this coming-of-age novel. Nina goes through a lot she feels "upside down, inside out and back to front. I was myself, just the worst 'version' of myself." After the drinking gets out of hand and she does something utterly mortifying, destabilising the family she's staying with while her stepfather, mother and half-sister are abroad, she ends up in rehab, where she notes "...feeling rejected is how most of us got to be in this place. No one says in a meeting "I've always felt like I belong! Now if I could just sort out this silly drinking habit I could skip back off to my perfect life!" AA is not for those people." This is a terrific exploration of sexuality, from the ways in which alcohol gets tangled up in decision-making and in Nina's and many girls' cases, also leads them to blame themselves for the actions of predatory creeps to what it means to be attracted to both men and women. I also loved Nina's friend Beth, who has many feminist rants throughout the novel and points out some of the double standards that Nina can't quite accept, blaming herself for an assault. It's absolutely heart-breaking in places, and feels incredibly real I loved it.

Review originally published at Love Literature Art and Reason Darkness Before Dawn was mediocre. It had a great premise and the potential to be good, but it lacked any real depth. The characters lacked personalities and everyone basically did what was expected of them at all times. Even when the main character started to care about a vampire, which was against the norm, it was obvious that it was about to happen. Dawn was not a very interesting character at all, despite having the potential to be. She was boring. She was so boring that if you compared her to Bella Swan, YA fiction's most notorious dull character, Bella would be considered a wild party animal. The book wasn't necessarily bad, but yet it was bad because it was just so bland. I felt no emotion reading it and I didn't care at all for any of the characters. I still have no idea what made Dawn such a special character, despite the fact that it was hinted at in the prologue and there were plenty of times when any special characteristics could be revealed. But I'm not even upset that I don't know because I don't really care. Honestly, I don't recommend reading it. If you are looking for a decent post apocalyptic vampire fiction, The Immortal Rules by Julie Kagawa is really where it's at in YA fiction. This was just a waste of effort, really. I'm sure the author s could have crafted a wonderful story if they would have put some more defining characteristics and emotions in it. I think this book came out during the pretty girls in dresses on covers craze. Like so many of the books that released during that time, the best thing about the book is it's cover.

It was AMAZING !!! if you like the Pretties series you will like this. Love a disease, think of it? the book captured me from the very first page, i could not put it down. this is a really recommended book.

Nowhere Land is definitely not my favorite of the series. It was way more corny and childish than the other books. The strangeness is multiplied and the characters' growth is magnified in this book. I have no idea where this is going. What is going on?! Who are these people? What's happening to everyone. It's like "Lost" with kids.

Isobel is one of the most sought after portrait artists in Whimsy, a city between the human and fae lands. She lives there with her aunt Emma and her sister March and May, twin girls who used to be goats before the fair folk changed their lives. Isobel supports her family with her Craft and is paid in enchantments. Her patron Gadfly, a delightful and frivolous fae, warns her of the arrival of Rook, the prince of the Autumn Court. She becomes infatuated with him during the course of painting his infuriating portrait that always has something off around the eyes. Finally figuring out the detail, she sends along the painting only to find later that she depicted a deep, human sorrow in his eyes. He abducts her from her house and plans to take her to his realm to stand trial for the transgression, only to be taken way off course by fairy beasts, creeping rot, the Wild Hunt, and other assorted chaos. Will Isobel ever make it back home to her family? Will Rook ever gain back his people's respect? An Enchantment of Ravens is my favorite read of this year. The writing is poetic, the worldbuilding dazzles, plus the characters and romance are well developed. Right from the beginning of the novel. I was sucked into the story right from the beginning because of Margaret Rogerson's unique world. Her take on the fair folk and the rules of her world are like nothing I've ever seen. Humans create Crafts like cooking, art, and music that the fair folk covet above all things. Fairies will die if they attempt to create anything of the sort, but surround themselves with these things anyway. The age of the Craft doesn't matter as fairies can glamour it to look as it did when it was new. The fae pay humans in enchantments that need to be carefully worded or they could ruin lives with their trickster ways. On the other hand, enchantments can provide food, protection, and other necessities for human life. Humans need to be cautious living in Whimsy because of fairy whims and all carry iron somewhere on them for protection. The fair folk live for centuries and have no concept of time, but feel very little emotion. Human emotion is frowned upon and seen as weakness, opening up opportunites for other fae to take what they have. Despite this, the veneer of manners and composure are paramount to their kind. They have to respond to niceties like bowing, responding in kind to thank yous, and so on. The fair folk are beautiful, but alien, selfish, and cruel underneath their glamour. Each fae has one flaw in their glamour that sets them apart from humans whether it's fingers that are too long, emaciation, or height. The Spring Court is the only fairy court we see and it seems beautiful and fantastic at first until the horrific, cruel elements are revealed over time. The power of true names works both ways in this world where knowing it gives the person absolute power over another no matter if they are human or fey. Rogerson takes well known rules of fairies, gives them a twist, and adds her own unique ones to create a singular, detailed fantastical world. The characters and their relationships are incredibly well drawn. Isobel is a practical, serious person forced to grow up early in life. She has been making portraits for the fair folk most of her life, so she has a healthy caution about them. Every time one comes in for a portrait, she's careful to be polite and as inoffensive as possible. The enchantments she earns are carefully worded because she knows their mischief could be disastrous to her and her family. Although her sisters are magicked goats, she loves them all the same and cares for them unconditionally. Over the course of the story, she demonstrates cleverness, ingenuity, and compassion. I love a heroine with a strong will, realistic familial connections, and good sense. All of her decisions are not always the best, but she has a good head on her shoulders that serves her well throughout the novel. Her romance with Rook starts as a sudden infatuation based on his carefully crafted facade. When he shows who he truly is, Isobel understandably hates him because he's petty, vain, and inhuman. Over the course of their journey, they both reveal what's under their respective protective shells while fighting to protect each other and navigating fae lands infected with rot, fae society, and numerous enemies. Love kind of sneaks up on them when they weren't looking. Their declarations aren't poetic or idealistic and they disagree and see things they don't like in each other, but they grow to love by getting to know each other. I haven't read such a good romance in a while. The Good Law condemns fae and human lovers to death and one solution to this problem is the Green Well, which has the power to turn a human into a fairy. Isobel soundly rejects this because of all she would lose, namely her art. It's not just a interesting detail to flesh her out or be forgotten it's an intrinsic part of her character that she isn't willing to compromise on, even in the face of the death. Her art is also used I could write so much more about An Enchantment of Ravens because I loved every bit of it. I wanted to read it super fast to see what happened, but also wanted to savor the world slowly. I've been reading a lot lately and this one amazed me. I had to be left alone to read the last 100 pages so I could find out what happened with tears streaming down my face. I'm disappointed to see it's a stand alone novel, but I hope other stories will take place in that world. Margaret Rogerson has made me a lifelong fan with this one book and I can't recommend it highly enough.

Cuando vi este libro pense hermosa portada, cultura china, YA, mitologia y Richelle Mead, y me dije Bitch, esta es la mia! Pero hasta ahi quede, porque no fue lo que esperaba. La novela es bastante simple en el sentido que no hay gran descripcion del universo donde se lleva a cabo la historia, detalles de la cultura en la que se vive, ni muestran una gran cantidad de personajes. La historia comienza rapido al mostrar a la protagonista Fei tomando decisiones para proteger a su hermana e intentando comprender por que su sentido de la audicion vuelve una noche despues de un sueno. Eso es algo que me dejo "marcando ocupado", porque aunque el libro se llame soundless, si no es porque Fei dice que se comunican por lenguaje de senas ni cuanta me hubiera dado. Lo que no me gusto del libro fue la lentitud con la que se desarrolla la historia. Recien pasadas las 120 paginas, se dejan de lado las grandes descripciones de personas, lugares y del porque de las cosas para dar paso a lo importante de la trama. Es una novela disfrutable, fuera de lo comun de las tipicas del genero YA, incluso madura. No hay triangulos amorosos que compliquen la trama, ni personajes "atascados" en dudas que hagan enojar al lector. Al pan, pan y al vino, vino. FIN Hay que darle una oportunidad, porque la historia en si es interesante.

An inteteresting steampunk dystopian Peter Pan retelling. Some confusing parts where it was hard to picture where the characters were in the setting. That seemed to be the biggest issues I had with the story. It was like the author just wanted her characters to be here or there for a specific action but no thought to how they got there or how long it would take to cover the distance. Overall it was entertaining and I love steampunk so I'd try the next one.

Forever... is written as a pretty realistic accound of first love between high school seniors Katherine and Michael. They spend countless hours and nights together and promise each other that they will be together forever. Katherine quickly falls in love and seeks out birth control at a Planned Parenthood in New York city. The summer after they graduate, Katherine and Michael are forced to be apart because of jobs. Their love will be tested in the weeks that they spend apart. This book might be of interest to students in 9th grade and up.
I enjoyed it, and it's very different to normal fantasy books. Enjoyable!

I'm sorry but this book is so bad omg it's the worst book I've read this year. It was badly structured, it lacked dept, it lacked character development, I don't like Eadlyn Schreave and her bratty attitude and big head at all. This book really disappointed me
I had trouble rating this one. It's like somewhere between a 3 and 4

First of all, I bought this for Kindle on sale for less than 3 and even at that price, I consider it a waste. The writer seems so unabashedly obsessed with trying to describe the way a scream sounds and feels that I got the sense of it being the only writing she's really capable of. She can spend three pages describing a scream, on three separate occasions with nearly identical, therefore redundant, descriptions within the first few pages of a book but an entire week in the hospital is filled with little more description than one might expect from a comic book. Her attempt at illustrating panic and despair is so over-the-top that she makes, what could be, an intriguing story of supernatural concession into a tired and boring melodrama. I was really into this book within the first few pages and became yawningly bored in just a few more. The panic attacks don't happen often yet she has two in one day and another just a few days later. While I grant that fantasy paranormal science fiction is not necessarily intended to be realistic, I am a firm believer that it should still be believable which this book most certainly was not. If you want to see how many times someone can describe a scream apparently the most epic scream on the planet, unmatched by any of the professional screamers employed by Hollywood's finest then this book is for you. If you're looking for an actual plot and maybe some sustenance and entertainment, try Kim Harrison instead. My dislike for this book actually crosses the line from simply being a book I strongly don't care for, to causing mild anger that something this redundant, dry, and flat could have been published.

Sigh I don't know why Divergent is as popular as it is. I didn't finish this book because I reached a point where I simply could not continue. It was a slog. The writing was horrendous, the pacing was slow, the world building was abysmal. Descriptions? LOL what descriptions? The whole time I was reading this I imagined the characters floating around and interacting in a blank white space because the author didn't bother to describe anything. The prose boiled down to "They went there. They did that. They talked to this person. Then they went somewhere else." What did all these places look like? Heck if I know. I just could not handle this book, it made me too mad. It was very very very very very very bad. And that's me being generous. I hated reading this book so much that it is no longer worth it to continue, even if it counts towards the reading challenge. Just, no. I refuse. In short I absolutely loathed this novel.
I received this novel as a free ebook through NetGalley. Review to be posted closer to release date.

I had read Go Ask Alice a couple years ago and decided to try out another book from the other "Anonymous" author collection. I am so glad I did. Like Go Ask Alice, this is the main character's journal, which started off as a food feeling journal. It is interesting to see what she wrote, her weight changes, and the evolution of her disorder. Also, interesting, because it was a journal, we never know her name - really who writes their name in their journal entries?? But for the remainder of the review I'll just call her Ana - for simplicity. This book gave me so many different feelings - I just wasn't expecting it. I find eating disorder books very interesting and very relatable since I had an eating problem when I was a teenager not a full-out eating disorder but I believe it was borderline . I found that the topic was handled very well and covered all the ups and downs of the disorder - how it starts, the actual issue, and all the ugly. All the characters were written very realistically. I believed everything that was going on and how each individual reacted to Ana and her behaviour. I completely felt for Jack! It must be hard standing there watching people you love hurt themselves. I could relate to Ana and her entire situation although I have not experienced it all . Unlike what the back of the book describes, she did not start out by wanting to lose weight, but her sport forced the girls to track all the food and exercise they did. This was actually one of the parts of the books that completely irritated me! Why was it only the girls, yes it is predominantly girls who have eating disorders but why just focus on them? If you're worried about eating disorders and are going to force people to track what they are doing which I believe would just cause disorders instead of stopping them then make the entire team do it not just the girls! Also, the coach's reaction to Ana cutting her calories and losing weight just irritated me - if that's how you are going to react the whole exercise was for nothing! I was completely surprised by the ending and didn't fully no how to react. I wasn't expecting it - although I should have. Do not go into this expecting anything or having a certain mindset. It will throw you for a loop! I would recommend this if you're interested in eating disorders, Go Ask Alice style, journal writing, or realistic fiction.

spoiler alert 2.75 Slow start. Fast ending. This book would've done better with an Isabel POV. Also maybe every single woman in this book didn't have to be terrible? And maybe every single girl didn't have to be sick or dead?

1.5 stars I received an ARC from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review . Bella...I mean, Clary, no wait...Luce...no? Oh right, Samantha. Samantha is a teenager with a crush on an older boy and finds herself finally being kissed by him. This kiss changes her, literally. Odd things start to happen, yada yada. She meets a boy...yay! That is the last thing I remember before falling into a coma until I finished DARK KISS. I am supposed to review the second book, WICKED KISS but for the sake of my mind I will pass.

I read this book for the second time, hoping that it wouldn't be quite as dry as the first time that I read it. Unfortunately, this book does drag a little bit for the first part. Once you push through the first 10 or so chapters, it does start to pick up and draw you in more with each chapter. That said, the concept of a world where the adults vanish, leaving the kids to fend for themselves is interesting. I have unanswered questions about how the kids have come into this situation, and wonder why many of them have newfound powers. The last couple of chapters had me wanting to know what would happen next in this new world. This series has a lot of potential. My hope is that book 2 will start off right in the middle of the action, allowing for a faster and more fun read.

Ladies and gentlemen, we have another knockout novel from Amanda Hocking. I'm actually pretty convinced this woman can't write a bad book. Anyone who can make trolls and mermaids cool is definitely someone worth keeping an eye on. Lullaby has all the goodness of Wake, but with the dark undertones swimming farther to the surface. This is a great beach read with a dark side, and I was happy to let it take me out of my cold house and to the warm tourist-y town of Capri again. When I read Wake, something I wanted more of when it was over was more of Harper's side of the story. Lullaby certainly provided that, and I think I may actually like Harper more as a character than Gemma. They are both interesting characters, but to me the romance between Harper and Daniel is made all the more romantic by Harper's struggles to get over her own anxieties and fears of commitment. Plus, Daniel's got the whole bad-boy-gone-good thing going on, which makes him super sexy. Since Lullaby was even better than Wake, I can't even imagine how good Tidal is going to be. Let's hope that she can keep raising the bar!

Begrudgingly moving up from a 1 star, which doesn't really feel fair for a epic 629-page saga that I finished in two days. In some ways, I'm a bit impressed that the question is really presented that Bella might pick Jacob, someone who she actually has a reason to like besides being DRAWN to his AMAZING BEAUTY AND SELFLESSNESS. In other ways, I'm so frustrated with sweet Jacob not realizing how dark it is to force a kiss on someone when she has no ability to push back your brute strength. UGH I can't believe I'm rhapsodizing about this book. Stupid book not realizing I'm hate-reading it.

The first half or so of the book was pretty good, but the rest just went downhill for me I couldn't quite connect with the character, make sense of some of her decisions and thinking, and thought the romance took up too much of the plot. This IS a book that romance fans may enjoy though. Longer review to come! 2.5 5

Speak has a lot of heart, but it's not really fleshed out. This very short young adult novel follows Melinda as she attempts to navigate high school after a trauma of which she dares not speak. Melinda's narration paints one of the most genuine portraits of depression I have seen I young adult literature. Her world is stark and desolate, without much relief. It is not romanticized or made trivialized into quirkiness. It sucks, and that is the plain truth of it. The rest of the novel just falls apart, though. I personally like novels with light plotting like this, instead focusing on character. But most of the vignettes this novel strings together can feel a bit pointless. There are many points where I asked myself "what's the point of this?" other than to just cover the bases of various aspects of adolescence. Generally, there is not one. But what irked me most was just how artificial everything else felt. I get that Melinda does not have a supportive environment at home or at school. But in attempting to depict this, each character falls into cardboard cutout cliches. High schoolers are not this overtly cruel all of the time. Parents are not this flat and pointless. Teachers are not demons there to just antagonize students. Nothing about Melinda's environment rang true. And in a novel with such intelligence with her struggle, I find this hard to swallow. There is a lot of value to be found in this novel. But while it may have been groundbreaking at the time of its publication, it has certainly been done better since.

I was intrigued by the premise of this story - a Twilight-style romance with robots - but I found myself disappointed on almost every level. It's not the ideas behind this story that are problematic but it's entirely the execution. The entire novel just feels like a first draft. Issues ranged from continuity errors Robotatouille was sometimes a French chef and sometimes Italian , to repetition Snow describes the hair and eye colour of every character to just generally confused writing. It's a really hard novel for me to analyse, just because I'm really not sure what happened. What little plot it had completely broke down at the point Vienna was captured by the Government. I'm not even sure why they were hunting her, let alone what was to be gained by her "torture" and abrupt release. Was she even human? At times, I wondered if the implication was that she was also "half robot" but I've no idea if that's what Snow was going for. The characterisation was also all over the place. We're frequently told what attributes characters are supposed to possess i.e. people frequently tell Vienna how great she is but the characters don't really show any personality themselves. Case in point is Vienna's mother. Until she and Vienna had their argument which was sparked by next to nothing , I didn't get the impression that she was an uncaring mother. Yet Vienna tells the reader over and over that her mother found her to be a disappointment and didn't care for her. Vienna herself is also really dislikable. She spent half of the book being really prejudiced towards robots for no good reason. Why didn't she trust them? Why did she just assume that the government was lying about them? I couldn't see anything in the text that explained this, it's like she just plucked her suspicion out of thin air. Her relationship with Alec was also lacking. It was very insta-love. The two didn't really have much chemistry but became a couple because of an electron imbalance? It was a lot like the imprinting werewolves of Twilight, only it made even less sense. All in all, it was a really disappointing novel. It's very confusing and it's not one that I'd recommend purchasing. It is really in need of a good edit to get it to anything close to professional quality.
I really enjoyed this book. It is so thought provoking, real and powerful. It is a page turner. I found it difficult to put this book down. It is without a doubt my favourite book I read this year.

Sorry guys, but this one just wasn't for me. I felt like the beginning was very strong. Strong character voice, strong writing, plot that makes you want to keep going, but it all went downhill from there. Every few pages I would find something new that I didn't enjoy. It didn't hate this book, but it was very worthy of a few eye rolls and confused looks here and there. The world building started out really sketchy. I was like 'huh?' the first time the author tried to incorporate it, and from there I only got more and more confused until I literally no idea what was going on in this world. I could see that Nyx had a very complicated family dynamic. I know some people would like how honest she was, but all that felt like to me was whining, and I couldn't stand it. There's a difference between a brutally honest character and an overdramatic, whiny brat. Not trying to be mean, intentions with Nyx were good, but I honestly didn't like her at all. I should mention, this is supposed to be a Beauty and The Beast retelling told in a Greek setting. To me, I felt like this was very similar to the story of Rumplestiltskin and Belle from OUAT, at least at first. Anyone else watch that show? It's a favorite of mine. Once we got to the castle of Ignifex, our beast, things got pretty bad. I mean, love triangle, instalove, annoying characters, creepy characters... I will admit, I did like that everything was pretty easy to visualize. The romance really killed this book for me. Nyx falls madly in love with Shade like as soon as she meets him, and I didn't buy it for a second. Both romances were so overdone and dramatic and instalovey that I actually put the book down several times. I don't know bout y'all, but I couldn't stand Nyx and Ignifex's relationship. Nyx is there to kill Ignifex, but I never for one second believed she could do it. Every time she's around him she starts talking about how attractive he is and how muscled and perfect he looks, and I'm like, 'oh yeah, that's exactly how an assassin thinks about their target. Quit staring at his muscles and do your fucking job, Nyx!' I might be the only one who felt this way, but Ignifex creeped me out. I really like bad boys usually, but in this case, I thought Ignifex was a real creep with his sexual type jokes. This made it really hard for me to root for him as a love interest. Pardon my language but, what the fuck was that ending? Like literally, what happened? Someone explain it to me, because I have no clue. I couldn't figure it out while I was reading it, and I have too many books waiting to me read to waste my time rereading this ending trying to figure what just happened. There was time travel? And amnesia? And soul splitting? So, I can see why a lot of people liked this book. The premise is great, the writing was enjoyable, but there were quite a few aspects of this book that made it hard for me to enjoy.

I'm not going to be exaggerating when I tell you I have about a million quotes from this book written down on random scraps of paper. When something makes you laugh as much as this made me, it's criminal not to write it down. Now I can't even tell you guys how amazing this book was. It's so many kinds of awesome it's untrue. If you haven't read this series yet, I'm gonna do the book review equivalent of begging on my knees. I... am going to say please, IN CAPITOL LETTERS! PLEASE, PLEASE, PLEASE read the Drake Chronicles and discover the awesomeness for yourself. It's so utterly and all-round amazing you'll love it forever. And you'll love every single one of the Drake brothers too. 'Cause they're yummy. Very, very yummy... "Solange was gone. "I wasn't sure who was standing in front of me. She might have Solange's ethereal beauty and her ballerina grace, but she wasn't Solange..." Solange Drake changed when she became a vampire. Now she's struggling to hold onto her humanity, to keep the feral side of herself at bay. Her brothers have been raised to protect Sol, knowing they must keep her safe no matter what. But with the vampire tribes gathering for the Blood Moon ceremony, bringing with it a mysterious stranger who is putting them all in terror danger, can Nicholas keep Solange safe? Especially when he's forced between Lucy, the girl he loves, and Solange, his baby sister... This series... Oh, how I love it. It's shot way up my fave series list no matter how many books I read, it never gets even the tiniest bit dull. I could actually read about it all forever and ever. And then a little more. If you haven't read this series, please, please do! All the books are amazing, addictive, almost drug-like in the addictiveness. Whenever I put Blood Moon down, I was instantly desperate it pick it right back up and read and read and read. And yes, it really was that good! I love all the characters in this series, even the smaller one. But Lucy is just my favourite character ever. She totally kills me, with her loathing of taking orders and that insane vampire rights activist side, what with her hatred of "rampant vampire racism"! God, she's awesome. People could learn from the way she handled bullies. Well, y'know, the ones she doesn't punch in the nose or pepper-egg... Nicholas Drake, how I love you! How can you not when he says things like "I knew damn well if Lucy broke up with me I'd still love her until I turned to dust." He's so brave, strong, wonderful, and just perfect. But please, oh please let that last bit not be true!! Solange was just... whoa. Terrifying. I wanted to jump into the book and slap the stupid outta her. I am so insanely glad there's a reason for the freakiness, but man! She was scary! And I loved seeing some of my old favourites, like Chloe, a Helios Ra student and Lucy and Hunter's friend. And I almost forgot how kickbutt awesome Hunter is! I also really liked newcomer Jenna - the snarky retort scenes between her and Lucy had me cracking up! I also love Kieran, especially as we learn more about his past. But Constantine grr! He reminded me of Spike from Buffy, but without the yumminess. I trusted the guy about as far as I could throw him not far at all, given my lack of upper body strength . I just couldn't get a read on the blasted guy ergo, grr-ing. Mirror, mirror on the wall, who's my favourite Drake of them all? God, I love the Drake family - the brothers in particular. They kill me! I love the banter and jokes and how they'd do anything for one another. They're all so loyal, protective and yummy. And their parents totally rock too! But why must you make me fall head over heels in love with this family, Alyx, and then terrify me about their safety? Why, why WHY?! sniffles Nicky... I adore the writing in this series. I love the split POV, how we get into everyone's heads, how all the voices sound unique. And, oh, how awesome it was to finally have Nicholas as a narrator! While I loved the Sol chapters though they were mega creepy , Lucy and Nick just stole the show! They're both so funny and my two favourite characters - and my favourite couple ever! And, man, I love the plots in these books. Action-packed, suspenseful, twisty and addictive - double dollop of each with a nice spoonful of romance too. But after I finished Blood Moon... Damn it, Alyxandra Harvey another worst freaking cliff-hanger EVER! You're gonna drive me insane - my sanity already pretty sketchy is at stake here! See what I did, with the joke 'bout the stake? Heehee, I thought it was funny anyhoo... But it could just be me going crazy already... With more suspense, twists, mystery and the WORST EVER CLIFFHANGER, Blood Moon quite literally rocked my world. I could not put it down. At all. Ever. It was so addictive, so amazing, so... wow! I can't put into words how all round awesome it was. So I'll just say this if you only read one vampire series ever, please, please, PLEASE make it this one! It's my favourite vamp series... Plus, the Drake boys are all so totally yummy! Extra Mini Review of Lost Girls by Alyxandra Harvey The short story at the end of my book, Lost Girls, was more than awesome. I love Helena - she's the coolest mom ever - and it was awesome getting to see why she's so kickbutt! It made me love her even more! And Liam Drake has always been 'Dad', but in this... he's actually kinda hot. Maybe it should be weird, fancying Nick's dad, but really it's just another Drake boy for me to love. It's so easy to just think of them as parents, but after this they're so much more! I love them even more and totally get them now too. And the story line of Lost Girls totally rocked! It was just such an awesome little novella! I loved it to pieces! I always knew Helena was kickbutt, but I never knew how kickbutt! As for Cass, Lucy's mum? Man, can I see the mother-daughter resemblance! P.S. This is a reference to the inspiration of the story Snow White and the Seven Dwarves get it, Sol is Snow and her brothers are the dwarves! Ha!

This book was not what I expected at all. I had read a lot of reviews about it on some blogs I followed and it sounded so interesting but I was totally caught off guard, in a good way. Hanna's father passed away and she has been living with an aunt. After a big blow out with her aunt, Hanna hitchhikes to Portero, Texas where Rosalee, the mother who abandonned her lives. When Hanna arrives in Portero she finds a hostile town riddled with monster where outsiders are unwelcome. Hanna strikes a bargain with Rosalee, if she can fit in, she can stay. This book is exactly the kind of character driven work I like Hanna is an interesting protagonist to say the least. She's diagnosed as a manic depressive and she does have some bouts of depression in the book, I found myself wondering if her hallucinations were really hallucinations or a manifestation of her relation to Rosalee and the town of Portero. Especially since these hallucinations allowed her to do things many of the locals couldn't even do. I also loved that Hanna was half white, half black and she owned it. It wasn't a major issue but it was acknowledged and refered to when appropriate. She was also dating a hispanic local, and while Hanna was not loved by his family, her race had nothing to do with it. The town of Portero was a character into and of itself. It was ominous and hostile and sometimes it was just plain weird. A lot of the time it felt like the town was it's own entity. The whole book is strange and weird. It's also very violent and graphic, so if that kind of thing bothers you it's best to steer clear. Normally this isn't the kind of thing I comment on but with all the other strangeness in the book it just felt like it was worth mentioning.

Yet another fictional account of 9 11! I suppose it makes sense given we are coming up on the fifteenth anniversary of that tragic Tuesday. This time the novel is aimed at a young adult audience and is told through the eyes of two sixteen-year-old girls. The story flashes back and forth between 2001 and 2016. Alia, a talented artist, lives in Brooklyn and has decided to inaugurate her hijab on the morning of September 11th. Fifteen years later Jesse, although only two years old at the time of the attacks, is still affected by a day she cannot even remember. Her older brother, Travis, perished in the North Tower and her family remains broken, unable to move past their grief. Travis and Alia are trapped together, struggling to make their way down many, many flights of stairs. Jesse has never heard much about her brother's death and sets out on a mission to learn the details of his final hours. The back cover leads the reader to believe Alia also died in the Trade Center but because she is one of the narrators it is pretty obvious that's not the case. The story is well told and emotion evoking. I would think even today's teens who were either very young or not yet born will still feel the depth of the horror. Of course, a young adult book would not be complete without a forbidden love story so you can bet you won't be disappointed in the romance department. Though the novel plods a bit in some places it is overall an engaging, worthwhile read. I remember how, as a child, I desperately wanted to read a book where the narrator dies so I could know what dying felt like. After reading the dreadful,The Lovely Bones , my desire quickly disappeared.

This review will be fairly short, because, well, as my rating suggests by my own rating scale I couldn't finish the book! Before starting The Mephisto Covenant, I read another review saying to stick with the story until about Chapter 4. I did. It didn't help. I was really excited about the potential of The Mephisto Covenant. The mythology underlying the story is interesting, and new to me. It builds on the Adam Eve story in the Bible, explaining that Eve actually had a daughter before "the fall", and said daughter was untainted by sin. Consequently, those coming from her line are untainted as well. Sasha is one of these wonderfully good people. Jax is of Mephisto, the right hand man to Lucifer. He and his brothers have been tasked with keeping a certain entity from taking over Hell. My telling of the mythology is essentially what we're told in the first chapter. Here begins my problems with the story. It's ALL tell and no show. Nothing seems to really evolve. It's just info-dump from the third or fourth page. Instead of keeping some mystery as to what is happening and why, the reader is completely aware. Sasha, however, is not until aware, for some unexplained and maybe if I'd kept reading it would have been reason she suddenly remembers all sorts of things that have happened to her. All the while, Jax tries to woo Sasha as a human. When she finds out what he is and then what she is, she just goes with it. No problem whatsoever. She's just soooooo drawn to him. Puke I didn't realize from the beginning that this was the first in a book series that essentially mirrors the idea of the Black Dagger Brotherhood among others. Fair enough. But the writing is nowhere near as good. I certainly would not recommend this book to anyone. It pains me to see more and more books like this, with seemingly terrible writing get through to publication. I'm normally not this direct, but I was just angered by lost potential in the story.

I was pretty much in love with this story until the very end. The fairy tale, Abel said, doesn't have a happy ending. It sure doesn't. And I didn't expect one - not after I figured out who was the murderer. It was beautiful and bleak and terrifying there's nothing that can make you colder than reading about pedophilia explained in Antoine de Saint-Exupery's simplistic, lyrical language and I couldn't wait for Anna to figure it all out. Then, finally, she did, and her reaction ruined the whole story. What Anna wouldn't have forgiven Abel doesn't seem to exist. She forgave rape. She forgave coldness. She forgave lies. And, finally, she forgave murder. Sure, love might be irrational and blind but there needs to be a limit to how much you can forgive a total stranger until your one true love leaves the lands of the romantic madness and crosses the borders of psychopathy. Rationality is not highly valued by the characters in this story, from Abel who would murder and prostitute to escape the terrible probability of losing his sister for just a few months, to Bertil who stalks Anna from start to finish and calls it love, to Gitta, of all people, who thinks the laws of friendship require her to keep quiet about the fact that her best friend's new boyfriend is a prostitute. Linda and Magnus seem to be the only sane people in this story - a saneness that is derisively described by Anna as blue light and that she desperately wants to get away from. By the way, this is the first modern German novel I've read and I must note that its world is much more relatable than the worlds of American fiction novels.

This is a funny mystery story with an overweight deaf young man as the main character--someone who doesn't see either of those things as handicaps. "Some people just like to eat--get over it, world!" Will Halpin has just started school at the main public school, because he was tired of attending the deaf school and wants to prove he can make it just fine in the hearing world. He struggles with bullying and with the lack of accommodations for him--no interpreters--but his excellent lip-reading skills serve him well. And he soon makes a friend in nerdy Devon, who is willing to fingerspell and sign and even text with Will so that they can chat as fluently as anyone else. When a popular student dies while on a field trip to the local coal mine museum, Will and Devon become convinced they can investigate and solve the crime a la The Hardy Boys Devon is comically obsessed with the crime-fighting literary brothers . I really enjoyed the characters, the humor, and learning about the deaf community. Will is likeable and funny, and the slapstick nature of the sleuthing scenes is really cute. Great book for anyone, but especially boys and anyone who's interested in reading about a deaf character who is confident for the most part he still has typical teen boy hangups and insecurities .

The Twilight series continues with this next installment, New Moon. Bella and Edward are together but a freak accident leaves Edward wondering whether his presence in Bella's life is simply too harmful. He and the Cullens leave and in his absence, Bella is shattered. She befriends Jacob from the nearby Indian reservation and they become close friends. Close enough for them to eventually share some secrets of their own. I am a firm believer in SM's storytelling capabilities. I have to hand it to her, I blew through the 400-odd pages in just a few days. However, there were just too many moments where I was reminded of the fact that this book is meant for teens tweens, whatever. I never ONCE got that sense when reading through the 3,000 or so pages of the Harry Potter series. SM's characters are all very one-dimensional and predictable. There's no subtlety, no nuance, no layers to her entire plot. And jesus, Bella is the worst. She's right when she says she has nothing to offer! She's sniveling, whining and selfish. The only reason she hangs out with Jacob is because it alleviates her pain from being without Edward...I mean, seriously. What kind of lesson does that teach the young girls who are voraciously reading through these series?

The underlying message seems to be something about not overanalyzing things, just taking emotional situations for what they are in the moment, which I think is kind of a cop-out it promotes a general idea of "oh, it's ok if you hurt my feelings and don't take responsibility for your actions, I should just lighten up." I guess that's a pragmatic message for teens because their peers AREN'T going to take responsibility for their own actions, but it seems like someone who internalized that message would get into some pretty terrible situations. The parts of this story are more than the whole. Where this book shines is in the details. Nic's internal monologue is clever and rings true, especially when it comes to her ambivalence about labeling her sexuality and the levelheaded and sarcastic undercutting of her own drama at key emotional moments. While I've never been to a summer geek camp myself, I know people who have and their stories seem to jibe pretty well with this it's also rather like the beginning of college . And there are some cool possible references to the book's predecessors Nic's occasionally Harriet the Spy-esque notebook entries, even if they are printed in a stupid handwriting font and at one point, Nic and Battle lapse into medieval ladies-in-waiting pretending, very much like Annie On My Mind . The minor characters are pretty good, especially the outrageous Katrina, and the often legitimately funny geeky one-liners come fast and furious. There's also a zing from a computer scientist on botanists which I would swear was a Stargate Atlantis reference if the timelines worked out. I may just have to like any book which features a teenaged lesbian dressed as Prince Valiant, a boy in eyeliner, and a zing on botanists. Read the original review at http shelversanon.blogspot.com 2013... I don't know if I've said this before, but I have a thing for invisible protagonists. I don't know why. Maybe because it's one of the rare superhuman abilities authors choose, or maybe it's just because I feel like there is more opportunity for sneakytimes with an invisible main character. I do love sneakytimes. As the daughter of the head of a feared crime syndicate, Fiona has experienced her share of sneakytimes. In this alternate history of the world, scientists in the '50s created a pill called Radiasure to combat radiation poisoning from the inevitable nuclear fallout from the Cold War. The nuclear holocaust never occurred, but Radiasure created its own set of problems. The chemical compounds present caused mutations first in the generation directly exposed and then in their children and their children's children. Each generation became progressively more mutated or superpowered, so that while the first generation might have oddly pigmented hair, by the time Fiona's generation came to be, abilities like super-strength and flight were popping up around the nation. Fiona's invisibility makes her the perfect tool for her Leck-like father. Daddy dearest controls the Radiasure market in the United States, which became a desired and highly illegal commodity after the mutations became more severe. Able to control any woman around him with a whiff of his intoxicating scent, Fiona's father keeps his territory under tight rein with the help of his super-powered women, including Fiona's mother, an incredibly talented telekinetic, and Fiona herself. Of course, there always has to be that one order that the faithful lackey can't follow, and when Fiona receives her, she and her mother run away to a tiny desert town. I blame myself for not paying more attention to the synopsis. I expected a gritty and tense story about an invisible girl that focused on her Mafia-esque ties. I guess I expected more of an inner-city story, if that makes sense. It was my own fault for glossing over the part about the small town. I had so many issues with this book. What's really bad is that they weren't major issues. With major issues, I feel like I can work myself up into a justifiable rage and bang out a sparking review. But, for me, Transparent's issues weren't major. They were just there and in such a quantity that they hindered my enjoyment of the story. For instance, I had the hardest time connecting with any of the characters. I don't know how to explain it. It's like the psychology behind their motives were off. They didn't feel internally consistent. I wish I could give specific examples, but it's more one of those things that I can feel rather than explain. I know, bad reviewer! While I allowed myself to be mostly charmed by the characters who were supposed to charm me like The Pack , I can't say that I felt any particular emotion when any of them were put in danger. Even the two boys Fiona found herself interested in failed to really grab me. One was so nice as to be suspicious, so I never let myself trust him. The other one I think was going for a Mr. Darcy-type chemistry with his "misunderstood" attitude, but I just found him to be abrasive and jerky. Look, buddy, if you think a girl has a learning disability, ask her nicely. Asking her if she was dropped on her head as an infant and then trying to excuse yourself by saying you really meant your question is not okay. NOT OKAY. Also, I expect some quality world-building in my books, so I was sadly disappointed by Transparent. Again, it wasn't that the world-building was bad. It just... wasn't there. Outside of the bare bones structure concerning Radiasure, I had no clue what Fiona's world was like. We're kept in her tiny desert bubble. I have no idea how what the social or class structure is like, how mutant abilities have changed the day-to-day goings on of life in America or anything. Speaking of the mutant abilities, is it too much to ask that they make sense? I mean, not scientifically. Not having a detailed description of how the mutations work didn't bother me even though a genetic mutation that lets someone know all known languages is impossible . What bothered me is the work-arounds that weren't accounted for. Take, for instance, Fiona's dad. As far as I can tell, his powers come from his pheromone-y scent. So couldn't you just plug your nose? And what about Fiona? She makes a big deal out of how she can't run from her dad or brother, but HELLO! YOU'RE INVISIBLE, WOMAN! Their reach only stretches so far. You and your mom didn't even leave the stinkin' state. Ugh. Do you all understand why I'm grumpy? I don't think relatable characters, a small dose of world-building, some logic, and some internal consistency would be too much to ask for. I do think other readers will like this book. It's fun in its own way, and I don't think the things that bother me will bother everyone else. However, for me, this book was fun, lightweight, and ultimately forgettable. Points Added For The Pack as a whole, an interesting premise, superpowers, Miles. Points Subtracted For Paper-thin plot, a jerk of a love interest, scant world-building, plot holes. Good For Fans Of Superpowers, silliness. Notes For Parents Language, some kissing, some nudity but she's invisible, so... Note I received a digital ARC of this title from the publisher for review.

This is a review for the third and final novel in the series about Twelve Dancing Princesses, but what I say here about Princess of the Silver Woods holds true for all of the books. I so wanted to love these - I had heard great things and excitedly requested this as an ARC, even without reading the first two. Sadly, I was confused, bored, uninvolved from the very start, so I DNF'd 50 pages in. A week or so later, the first two went on sale for ebooks for less than 2 each. I thought I would give it another try - this time with the benefit of reading the series in order. I read the first two... and it wasn't pretty. They aren't the worst books I've ever read, but I am hard-pressed to remember a series as lackluster and unengaging as this was for me. Each novel tackles a different fairytale, and occasionally Day George would create a new twist or idea that worked well for her books. I liked the spin on Red Riding Hood meets Robin Hood, but it's hard to recall a lot about these novels. What didn't work well, ever, were her characters. Galen, Rose, Poppy, Christian, and here in book three, Petunia and Oliver all come across as wooden and flat for the duration. Their actions are contrived, their dialogue laughable or vague, their magic and abilities too convenient or too unexplained.I wanted to like them, but their trials, tribulations and eventual coupledom were all too expected and very predictable. Also working against the books is the worldbuilding. Or rather, the lack of any substantial effort to create a real, vibrant setting for these characters to operate upon. The thinly veiled countries that represent a more magical Europe Breton Britain, Spania Spain, Russaka Russia, so on and so forth left a lot to be desired in terms of backdrop. It's all too simple and easy across the board - the relationships, the magic, the world itself. I wanted more from Jessica Day George, and what is provided leaves a lot to be desired.At several points in each novel, I would think that these books and characters came across as much more MG than YA in tone and characterization. This series is too simple and predictable to be memorable. I read all three in a four day span, and I doubt I will remember anything about any of them in a week's time. All in all third verse, same as the first. Too simple, too easy, too predictable, too short to pack a punch. The magic is too vague, or too silly the whole knitting aspect just makes me laugh, every time , and once again, none of the characters really stood out as remarkable, or even really three-dimensional. This series is just not for me, though I can see why others are drawn to it and enjoy it.

I just thought it was a little lame that Tris survives the death serum only to be shot to death a few minutes later. I also felt that the story didn't need either of them to die. I know I'm in the minority when I say this, but I did not like The Dream Thieves. At all. Die-hard fans, you may want to look away. I'll confess, part of it was due to my dumb decision to read this book without having read the first in the series, a huge mistake I wouldn't recommend. Glendower? Cabeswater? Greywaren? Ley lines? I didn't have a clue what these things were. Most of the time, I can jump into a series thanks to that quick background refresher that usually happens at the beginning of books, but The Dream Thieves dove right in without any explanations. I was left in limbo until things cleared up after about a third of the book, but I never became engrossed into the story. I didn't care much for the four Aglionby boys. Instead, my favorite characters were the secondary characters - Blue's psychic family and the Gray Man. Blue was pretty awesome too but, like all the good elements in the book, there wasn't enough of her. Gansey and Ronan were the stars of the book, and unfortunately for me, we didn't really get along. Gansey, Ronan, Adam and Noah all fell flat as characters. Maybe this was because I didn't have the first book to get to know them properly, but you'd think that after 400 pages of The Dream Thieves we would have gotten acquainted enough. But no. Adam was whiny and annoying, Noah was practically nonexistent, Gansey seemed boring and unreal, and Ronan, well, he was just such a jerk that I could care less whether he died in his dreams or not. To make things worse, the plot was soooo slow and uneventful. The story The ley line breaks thanks to Greywarens stealing things from their dreams. Adam fixes it. The end. So what was in those 400 pages? Nothing but useless scenes and descriptions that contributed nothing to the plot. I kept waiting for that familiar anxiety to know what happens next to creep in, but it never came. Even at the climax, I was able to turn off my kindle when I got off the subway rather than trying to maneuver the crowds and stairs with my eyes glued to the screen. The only other Maggie Stiefvater book I've read is The Scorpio Races, which she wrote beautifully. But in The Dream Thieves, I felt like she was trying too hard. She had some nice metaphors here and there but she went completely overboard with them. Every page had so many unnecessary descriptions that I lost track of what was going on in the plot. Getting through the book felt like a chore. It reminded me of reading The Scarlet Letter for 10th grade English. I'm all for pretty writing but the story is king and when it gets overshadowed by fluff, that's when I check out.

First off, let me start this review by saying this I get it. I get why everyone is so in love with St. Clair Anna, and swoons over him and thinks she's the most adorable cupcake thing to happen to contemporary YA ever. A lot of readers were probably hardcore shipping them and just wanting them to be together and kiss already, dammit. Now, that being said, I was not as in love with this book as everyone else to put it mildly . This was a well-written book, absolutely. And an original one too. I applaud Stephanie Perkins for making us want the bad guys to win, in a way. Because let's face it Anna St. Clair are being bad guys. They're condoning cheating. Again though, I plowed through this book, had to know where things were going, and I enjoyed all the secondary characters i.e. Meredith, Josh, Rashmi, Mark, and even Bridgette . And after having really thought this through and taken a day to mull the book over before writing the review, I have to say "You got me, Stephanie Perkins." Because I didn't like Anna as a character. She was an idiot. She thought the French watched mimes all day in their free time, and she DIDN'T EVEN KNOW FRANCE WAS FAMOUS FOR FILM despite waiting to be an effing film critic professionally. BUT. Despite not liking Anna, it made her character development more drastic. She was a dramatic, self-centered person, and terrible at being a friend. She never talked to people, and just assumed things all the time. This, understandably, led to many misunderstandings, fights, hurt feelings, and solitude. So I get that the lesson is supposed to be to open your mind to new experiences, new education, and to your friends. Because you just don't know what they're going through or how they feel until you talk to them and they tell you. This is a great message, and Anna was a great character to tell it through because of all her traits. But she's just so effing stupid sometimes it's annoying, I'm sorry. But again, I get it. I get why the author chose to do that. And it was well done. Also, this is a book about cheating. Yes, St. Clair is in fact cheating. After Anna and St. Clair sleep ONLY sleep together, she says, "Wait, if I can't tell anyone about it, does that mean it was wrong?" YES. YES IT DOES. And holding hands, and grinding on each other at the club, and how often he calls her beautiful and all of the presents he gives her, and the fact that at one point he actually says that he was thinking of Anna whenever he was with Ellie and that "in his mind he was cheated on her every day" ...that's a problem. And Ellie being stuck up or slutty or bitchy DOES NOT MEAN we should want her to get cheated on. Nobody deserves that. It is the worst. But I bet many readers hated Ellie and were happy to see that happen. Ugh. Again, a problem. BUT. I can appreciate the singularity of the situation story. Because real life is messy. And in real life the bad guys win and can repeatedly make mistakes and get away with it. And things aren't as clean in life, and don't have a nice ribbon with the "right" ending. And this book reflects that. And that makes this book a brave one. SO. I'll try not to put my bias about the bad character story or morality into this, and leave out my feelings. Because this was a solid book. 3 out of 5 2 feels too mean and low, but 4 is definitely way too high stars.

I don't know why people say that this book is in the same league as Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins, in all honesty, The Maze Runner is way BETTER. James Dashner opens the book with protagonist Thomas, rising in a box lift for about a half hour, before the box stops, and is opened by a group of boys. Like the other boys, Thomas has no memories of his past life. Only his first name remains in his mind. The boys call themselves "Gladers" and live in a make shift society in the center of what Thomas soon finds out is a gigantic maze. The maze consists of huge walls, so high the tops are dark. At night, the gates that connect the boys "glade" to the maze close, the maze walls shift around and heinous half mechanical -half creatures known as Greivers swarm the maze's paths. When a person gets too close to a griever, they either face death by its many metallic weapons, or an injection with a deadly venom that can only be cured by making it back to the glade for a serum and undergoing the painful three days of "the changing" a curing process that can possibly open up past images and change its subjects whole personality and sanity. Right away Thomas finds he is different. He has a strange sense that he has been in the artificial world before, people who have undergone the changing dislike him, and he has a high calling to become a "Runner" one who runs the maze during the day to map it out. When the glade's first girl ! shows up in the box, an abnormal day right after Thomas, and shares she is the last one before entering a coma, events are triggered that lead to the necessity of solving the maze fast. There are many specific things that I really like in the book. First of all, this book is never boring. Lots of action and inquisitiveness- inspiring plot. In the boys' society a believable mini government is created to keep order. Specific jobs are assigned to each boy for living purposes and only runners enter the maze for the safety of all the Gladers. Each boy has a specific and believable personality. Some authors have a hard time dealing with so many characters and being able to consistently make them individual. When the reader meets Thomas, Newt, Minho, Alby, Chuck, Teresa, Frypan, Gally ..etc they can think specifically, "wow, that is totally something Minho would do" or feel as confused as Thomas feels. In the Hunger Games I don't feel too much deep thought about any of the Characters, including Katniss. It took me a bit to get used to... but I thought it was ingenious to add the glader lingo in the beginning so, without swearing in a YA book, there is still the dramatic seriousness and realistic-ness that swearing adds. Yes, if you were stuck in a torturous maze with a bunch of boys I imagine there would be curses- instead there is klunk, slinthead and Shuck. I also like the non curse words that appear in glader culture- shank, beetleblade, changing, runner, Keeper, blood houser, med-jack, gathering, slammer etc I am pumped for the sequel. And once again I hope this book varies from Hunger games in that it doesn't repeat the same exact plot in its second book.

This book wasn't bad, but it just wasn't good either. There was nothing in it that felt fresh and exciting to get me invested in the characters. There were a number of reasons why 1. The Firebloods vs Frostbloods felt too much like other books, particularly Red Queen. In Red Queen, the Silvers are in a place of power and have magical abilities, while the Reds do not. The few Reds that do have powers are hiding from persecution. In this book, The Frostbloods are in a place of power and have magical abilities. There are not very many Firebloods left because they've been killed. Those that live are hiding among the regular folk from persecution. To add more similarity, this book even has a fighting arena very similar to Red Queen. 2. Ruby, the main character, is one of the last Firebloods. But wait, there's more! It's not enough for her to just be one of the last of her kind, no. She also might be special, a "chosen one" you might say. Because that's never happened before... 3. Ruby's time spent at the abbey training for half of the book was very dull. Again, there was nothing exciting going on. Usually there's a good story going on behind the scenes of a training section at least, but this one was rather flat. The training wasn't even exciting. 4. The racism and animosity between the two main characters Ruby, fireblood and Arcus, frostblood is just annoying. Even after spending plenty of time with each other, they both keep stereotyping the other. All firebloods have a lack of self control and will burn the place down. All frostbloods are cold hearted and don't feel anything. It's bad enough to get it from a multitude of other characters throughout the book, but it's especially irritating coming from the two main characters who should know better a lot sooner than they do. It seemed way too past-minded to believe that such an exorbitant stereotype was so widely believed to be carried by all people of that type. 5. Ruby's "revenge" felt so false. The book never shows the girl to have a vengeful thought, other than "I want revenge." If the book didn't tell me she wanted revenge, I never would've guessed she did. Now, giving credit where it's due, the book does get better in the last 100 pages or so. The story starts to become interesting, and the climax becomes intriguing. It's enough that I will probably read the second book eventually. I just won't be rushing for it on release day. While it felt a little more original, it still reminded me of a lot of other books I've read in the last few years. Rating I'd give this book a 3 out of 5. While it wasn't a bad read, it wasn't really anything special. This is going to be one of those books that some people love and some people don't. If I was new to YA fantasy, maybe I might have enjoyed this one more. I'll be interested to see how the reviews go on the second book, and from there will decide whether I will be continuing the series or not.

Comparing these books to the Hunger games is like comparing a gun to a knife. One is a sophisticated piece of equipment, while the other is a sharp instrument made for many tasks, but both are weapons. The Hunger Games series is nuanced and full of symbolism, and Divergent series isn't. The Divergent is simplistic almost to point of being painful, but the themes of these books are much more compelling than the Hunger Games. The Hunger Games focus on man's ability to be cruel vicious. They ask you what makes people kill one another. But Divergent asks what makes us human in the first place. Is it our virtues, our motivations, or our choices that make us good or evil. Is it human nature to be selfish self-indulgent, ignorant, disagreeable, and cowardly. And if it our nature to be these things in what circumstances do they become truly evil actions instead of negative impulses. Insurgent is a stripped down allegory, but it is a beautiful one.

This review was originally posted at http francesandlynne.wordpress.com ... "Harry Potter is about confronting fears, finding inner strength, and doing what is right in the face of adversity. Twilight is about how important it is to have a boyfriend." Stephen King Twilight, by Stephanie Meyer, tells the story of Isabella Bella Swan. Bella moves to Forks to live with her dad at the start of the book. She starts a new school and is all the town is talking about. One person at the school stands out Edward Cullen. Edward is handsome, but aloof, and seems pretty disgusted by Bella at first. They are both drawn to each other though, and Bella begins to notice odd things about Edward. Finally, she figures out his secret he's a vampire. That's not the biggest problem. You see Bella's blood is extra special to Edward. It's his crack cocaine. Will Edward resist eating Bella? Will their relationship survive the odds stacked against them? I actually cringed writing that summary. Sigh. Let me start at the beginning. I first read Twilight in the summer of 2010. I'd been given the book to read by my boyfriend he'd read them after watching the movie . I really enjoyed the book and lost a whole day as I raced through the pages, eager to find out what happened at the end. A few months later, I decided to re-read the book. It was like reading a completely different story one that lacked plot, and one that was badly written. I quickly became irritated by a number of things. First, the plot was severely lacking. Three quarters of the book literally go like this Bella watches Edward, Edward watches Bella, Edward tells Bella to stay away from him, Bella ignores Edward, Bella does incredibly stupid things and Edward saves Bella. That's it! Finally, Bella learns what the reader already knows Edward is a vampire. Shock horror! When the pace picks up a little, as James a hunter vampire sets his sight on Bella, Bella blacks out when the action starts and the reader misses it. What was Meyer thinking? Honestly! Second, the relationship between Edward and Bella is creepy and young adults should not use this as a reference in their own relationships. For example, Edward sneaks into Bella's room to watch her sleep at night. What the hell? If someone did this to me, I would call the cops and report a stalker. What does Bella do? She likes him more for it. Third, although Edward is supposedly a Vampire, he is pretty lame. He lacks all of the characteristics that make a Vampire. While Meyer says that Edward has a lust for blood, if she didn't tell the reader, you wouldn't know. He's too in control. I get that some vampires might drink animal blood, but they should still be dangerous. Jasper was a better take on a Vampire who drinks animal blood, but still feels the blood lust. Edward is just too good. Plus, Edward doesn't have fangs, which is weird. Instead, he just has sharp normal teeth. He isn't affected by crosses or stakes, and he can go out in the sunlight i.e., he doesn't burn . Instead, he sparkles. What is that?! Why would an author do that?! Fourth, Bella actually offends me as a woman. She is a terrible role model for young, impressionable adults. Bella is so weak. She's entirely dependent on Edward. When he goes away to hunt, she has no life. She does nothing. Oh wait, she obsesses about Edward. She's also so consumed by Edward that she passes out when he kisses her. When he says it would be best if he left, she almost dies! It is disgusting to read about a female character who is that dependant on a man. It frustrates me to no end. Fifth, why would any writer talk about how god-like Edward is repeatedly? Meyer talks about Edward's chiselled marble skin, and his amber eyes, and his Adonis looks WAY TO MUCH. Seriously! I got it after the tenth time! Jeez! Sixth, what is Edward's obsession with making Bella eat food? There are too many times in the book where Bella describes the food she is cooking to eat because Edward told her to. My theory is that Twilight is a good read if you're not really thinking. If you just race through, without paying much attention and without using your brain, it's enjoyable. Once you engage in the story, it falls flat, really flat. There just isn't enough of a plot to make it interesting. It's literally about two teenagers falling in love. Okay, so one of those is a vampire, laughs although he's not really. Don't even get me started on the movie. I didn't think it could possibly be worse, but oh how wrong I was. If you take a crappy book and take actors that can't act, well, that's Twilight for you. Final Verdict Don't waste your time. Frances
