She is suddenly snapped back into reality when it becomes apparent that it's up to her to protect the children of the camp from a surprise vampire attack. From then on, she makes it her mission to be more than just a hassle to the rebels and actually help out with the rebellion, even if it risks her life. This story is definitely heavier on the romance than it is on the action, but the plot is still well-developed. I noticed a few things that seemed inconsistent to me - like, it's mentioned that there are really only two ways to kill a vampire drowning what? why? or beheading , but later in the book they 'kill' a few by shooting them through the brain and heart while apparently still leaving their heads intact. There's some repetition too, as Jane "flushes" every time she catches Will or Thane checking her out. While we're on the topic, can we all just agree right now that we're team Thane? Yes? Good. Also, the final showdown was just WAY too easy. I'm expecting something bigger to finish out the next book but this one just seemed rushed. Jane's not the perfect heroine but she doesn't crumble at the first sign of adversity either. She seems pretty dumb to me but she HAS been locked up in a compound her entire life, and catches on pretty quick considering. I'm looking forward to reading the conclusion to this story in The Forsaken Ones to round out this story. P.S. Team Thane

"Under the Mesquite" by Guadalupe Garcia McCall is a coming-of-age story. The main character, Lupita, immigrated to Texas from Mexico when she was a young girl. When her mother is diagnosed with cancer during Lupita's freshman year of high school, Lupita is forced to take on an extraordinary amount of responsibility for her seven younger siblings. Not only does she have to put on a brave, strong front for her younger brothers and sisters, but she must also try to be support for her parents as well. Meanwhile, she struggles with who she is, who she wants to be, and how others perceive her. I've never been very fond of poetry, so at first I was leery about reading a book written in verse. But once I got into the story, I thought the format was effective. The chapters flowed well from one moment to the next, and I think it was the right format to delve into Lupita's complex thoughts and feelings. I felt an immediate connection to Lupita because her relationship with her family is similar to my own. But more than that, I felt like I could relate to her because of her love of words. From the moment her father teaches her to write, words are an important part of her life. Not only are they the key to her future, but as Lupita watches her mother fight cancer, she finds comfort in the plays she practices and the poems she writes under the mesquite tree in her mother's rose garden. Words give her a welcome escape. Throughout the story, the image of the mesquite tree reappears and we're reminded of its innate sense of survival. It isn't difficult to make a connection between Lupita and the tree. Her roots are strong and deep as she grows skyward, and despite life's attempt to cut her down, she flourishes. "Under the Mesquite" is a lovely book, and I enjoyed it very much. It deals with heavy issues, but the overall message is hopeful. No matter what life throws at Lupita, she handles it with unimaginable strength for a girl her age.

I enjoyed the political drama, and all the backstabbing that goes on, and I'm glad that the author showed this side of court life. On to the characters. First is Breck. She is Nym's lady-in-waiting for lack of a better word to call her . I really don't want to say that she is Nym's slave, because Nym too is a slave, just a different kind of one. Anyway, I liked that Breck didn't instantly become Nym's BFF. I wouldn't even call her a friend. She is really just there to make sure Nym does what she is supposed to do. However, she does play a central part to the ending of the book. Colin is Breck's twin, and he is also somewhat of an elemental. He trains with Nym. I must say that he annoyed me most of the book because he wa so arrogant most of the time, and I thought that there was going to be a love triangle thankfully not! . Eogan is the love interest in the book. He is dark, moody, and mysterious. You just know he has one hell of a secret that he is hiding. And although his relationship with Nym is rocky at best, you know that they'd both care for each other. Adora is the one who bought Nym to train her to be a weapon in the war. She's crazy at best, and extremely dangerous. And then there is Nym. I must say that at times, her whinning and self loathing got on my nerves. I wanted to just shake her and tell her to suck it up. Nym has awesome powers, and most of the book she is too scared to use them. There is a growth in the character throughout the book, and I hope in the next book she is not so depressing. I definitely can't wait to read her next book!

At the end of school year, Amy and her best friend Julia attend a party, but only one of them makes it home alive after a deadly car accident. Blaming herself and recovering from alcohol abuse, now sixteen-year-old Amy checks out of rehab in time to start school without her friend. She feels out of place and flounders, refusing to reach out to the existing cliques. The only people who talk to her are English partners Mel and Caro, whom she used to call Corn Syrup. Caro and Mel might have their own problems, but it's silent Patrick who Amy feels drawn to. But does Amy deserve to be happy after what she did? I was reminded of Wintergirls by Laurie Halse Anderson when reading this book, and there are quite a few similarities. Girl feels responsible for and must come to terms with best friend's death due to their self-destructive behaviors. Anderson's narrative has much more immediacy then Scott's though, grabbing your attention from the first page. It's the quote cited above that really grabbed my attention in this book. You don't find out exactly how Julia dies until about half way through, and by that time budding romances and friendships keep you invested through the rest of your wavering attention span. Scott's narration is slow build up, followed by some emotional and tense scenes where Amy has ephiphanies about her past and open up to her parents and therapist. Some readers might be slowed down by her letters to Julia, in which she mostly rehashes the events and feelings that readers are privy to already. Her parents are actually portrayed with depth in the few scenes they appear in, trying to determine what's best for their daughter while pulling strength from eachother. I was able to sympathize with them almost immediately as they struggled to relate to their daughter and come to terms with what little they know about what has happened. I'm not sure how I feel about the characters. The book has some strong characters, and while I liked aspects of each, I never really fell in love with any of them. Amy is opinionated and strong-willed, which helps her maintain her self-reliance during school and home, but her dependance on Julia and her second-guessing nature impede her development and growth. She sees a relationship possibility between other characters, but doesn't realize Patrick's interest in her until it's completely spelled out, even though they have a history and similarities that allow them to relate to eachother. Her sessions with her therapist probably give the most insight into her character. Caro is weak-willed when it comes to her friends and the school's social pecking order, but she grants herself more self-worth in her love life, at the end of the story saying "He picked her, and even though he changed his mind, I want a guy who will pick me first. ... I deserve better." 275 I never got a full grasp on Patrick, who seems insightful beyond his years and which might contribute to his silence in social settings. I had high hopes for Mel, who was the first to interact with Amy at school, but I ended up being disappointed by his association with queen-bee Beth at the school. All in all, no one and nothing that I really loved or really hated.

I have to admit that I am a niche reader. If there's something in the Dystopian Genre, there's a good chance it's on my to read list. The Testing has been on my list for a while now, and while I attempted to read it back in October of last year, I've only now had a chance to grab my own copy and read this lovely book. Cia Vale's dream is to go into the University, but nobody from Five Lakes community has been chosen in almost ten years. Still, a girl can dream, and Cia does though it seems her dreams will all be in vane as she graduates without incident and no officials from the capital colony of their United Commonwealth are present. That changes the day after graduation however. Summoned to the Mayor's office, Cia finds herself with three other students from Five Lakes who have been selected for The Testing. The Testing is what one has to go through to get into the University, a test to determine only the best for the future leaders of the Commonwealth. Suddenly Cia's world is shifting, and she's starting to learn things she didn't know and possibly didn't want to know. Informed by her father that she'll likely never see them again and to 'trust no one', Cia heads off for testing though she finds it hard not to trust Tomas. Tomas, a fellow student from Five Lakes, has been Cia's crush for as long as she can remember, and with the world seeming to close in around them, she finds to trust Tomas means having one thing from home to latch onto and not let go. Still, she doesn't take the warning lightly, and it saves her life when her roommate offers her what she's certain are poisoned corn cakes. Things only spiral out of control from there as the first death in the book show is the death of her roommate by suicide. From there, it's apparent that if you don't pass a test, whether by your own mistakes or by accepting their 'medical' help, you will die. While it's never explicitly said in the books that accepting medical help lands you in a coffin, it can be assumed since it's highly unlikely that they've been sent back to their colonies or sent out to another colony. Slowly, the 108 participants in the testing are whittled down to 29 surviving students from the last, and most dangerous, part of the test. Given the realization her memories will be repressed or erased after the testing, Cia makes a valiant effort to retain them by recording them on a device she'd borrowed from her brother before leaving for the test. While Charbonneau's ideas are interesting, I found that the idea of the test seemed a bit underdeveloped and brutal. While, I understand that was the writer's intent, I find it unfeasible that a nation or commonwealth would be willing to kill off more than seventy of supposedly the brightest upcoming minds of their range. It also seemed unlikely that while being remote, Five Lakes might not have reported all of their students who would have qualified for a decade before Cia. Not unheard of, but unlikely. I was reminded of the Silence in Doctor Who from the adults who govern the tests, silent guides and influences on the students and largely unseen though always watching and listening. Still, this story is an interesting enough one, perhaps a bit close to the idea of the Hunger Games, but a must read for any Dystopian fan.

I really wanted to love this book. The blurb made it sound amazing, and sci-fi's been a pretty reliable genre for me recently. And it was good, but it wasn't the brilliant I'd been hoping for. It started well, lots of action and betrayal, characters I could root for. Rhee Princess Rhiannon was likeable and confident, bordering on arrogant, and the expected rude awakening shocked her into realising how little she actually knew. But she didn't really change over the course of the book. She stayed blinkered and rash, and her selfishness and stubbornness became irritating after a while. However, it's the first book in a duology and there were signs at the end of the book that she was beginning to learn from her mistakes. Alyosha, on the other hand, was dynamic, engaging and adorable. Not that he didn't make mistakes, but he had more depth and his decisions were more believable, plus he had a reasonable amount of character development, and tried not to make the same mistakes again. At times, I found myself rushing through Rhee's chapters to get back to Aly's. Most of the side characters, unfortunately, were little more than ciphers, although I did like the way the alien-ness of some of the races were portrayed. The main villain had potential, with a nice line in propaganda and mind games, but got a little pantomime-y when action actually closed in on him at the end of the book. The sci-fi elements were well handled, the tech and its possibilities were intriguing and there was some real depth to the worldbuilding I'm always a sucker for decent worldbuilding! Plot. Aly's plot worked. Even when it was going badly, he was making things happen rather than happening to him, and generally he was responsible for getting himself out again, with help coming where he'd earned it. Rhee's, on the other hand, ought to have worked but fell a bit flat - she seemed to be buffeted about between one event and the next, despite being a lot of talk about what she wanted to do. Too often she was rescued by other people, in ways that sometimes seemed a little too convenient. I also got a little fed up the longer it went without the two storylines joining up, which I expected to happen early on from the blurb but still hadn't by the end of the book , and there were a few incidents where something major happened off-page, and we were told about it afterwards, which felt like missed opportunities. Vin's death? Shouldn't we have seen Aly react to that? And he was a good character, it would have had a lot more impact on the readers as well. Also, a couple of the main plot twists? Saw them coming a mile off. The romance was unnecessary, had hints of insta-love and inappropriate priorities the unfortunate tendency of YA protagonists to be unable to think of anything but the fact the love interest just touched them, no matter what is going down around them and developed far too quickly for my liking. Overall, it was a fast paced, fun read and I'm going to continue the series, but it failed to quite live up to its potential.

When I was in my final year of high school I went through a phase where I wrote stories that asked the big what if's. What if an element of reality was suspended, twisted, or momentarily substituted with something fantastical? What would be the consequences? How would one weave a tale from an imagined scenario? These were questions that I loved exploring when I was younger, and for me, Never Never was nostalgic of that exploration. In Never Never, Colleen Hoover and Tarryn Fisher ask what if you and someone you loved suddenly had no recollection of your family, your friends, your life, and of each other? Phew, this book was a page-turner. It has such an addictive quality, and packs quite a punch despite its length. So if there's anything I can appreciate about Never Never is it doesn't stagger around its purpose. It is to the point, and is therefore gripping. The accumulation of mysteries throughout the novel are intriguing, dark, and kept me very curious. What has befallen the two main characters how did it happen, why did it happen? I need to know! I think I should read more mystery I think I would really enjoy them. With regards to its characters, I think it is difficult to pass judgement for now because there's still so much the reader does not know there are many questions left unanswered, and the characters are further from the answers than the beginning. Furthemore, the cynical and dark depiction of teenagehood was intriguing and an element of the book's narrative that kept me hooked. Never Never unashamedly presents very flawed characters the most interesting part is that the characters themselves - having no memories - steadily discover that they are very flawed people. The revelations that follow are an interesting exploration of the self and who or what the self is. Never Never is a quick read, and easily digestible in one sitting I read this across two days during my commute to and from work, and the last few chapters at home . Unfortunately this book is the first of three parts -- why the three parts could not be amalgamated into one book is beyond me. Nonetheless, as it is a short book, I could argue that it's worthwhile giving Never Never a go. Regardless, whatever qualms you may have about the book's length, Never Never is enjoyable, mysterious, and thrilling. Given its cliffhanger, it is very likely I will pick up Part Two! Rating 2 5 - Review can also be found on my book blog, Read, Think, Ponder!

While I am enjoying the story and am really curious to know what is going to happen in the end is that not the whole point behind reading fiction at the end of the day? , I also can't stop myself from feeling slightly disappointed with narrative technique. First person stories are fine. I have read loads of them. But to write a story in the first person from more than one perspective is a bit jarring. I never seem to find that I can lose myself in the story because I am constantly having to look at the font to see who is talking next. Now if the voices of the different narrators were noticeably different which they should be, considering their very different upbringings on earth it could still work. But, I don't know. I feel that he they could have done a lot more. I also get a bit 'sea sick' from all the jumping from one character to another. It is like watching a three way tennis game. I just get interested in one, and then the story's focus changes. And then I sit with another character who I am initially not interested in because I want to know what is going on with the previous one and then ... wash rinse repeat. Yes, overall, it works brilliantly. But it always takes me a while to get into these books after finding them extremely annoying. Although this sounds horribly negative, it is not really my intention. As I said at the beginning, isn't the story the real reason we read?

What a massive, crushing disappointment. And I say this having had pretty low expectations going into Allegiant. But it failed to meet even that low bar. I cannot believe that I gave the first book in this series four stars. I cannot believe the series tanked this hard, this fast. Where do I even begin? Remember my review of Insurgent? The one where I basically trashed Roth for making a mopey crybaby out of Tris for no apparent reason? The good news is, Tris was not a mopey crybaby in Allegiant. The bad news is, Tobias was an even mopier crybaby! She ripped the poor guy's character to shreds! He was weak, simpering, terror-stricken, and insecure. He let Tris order him around, blame him, and yell at him for the treacherous crime of disagreeing with her "because I'm always right and you know it! How dare you not trust me!" WHAT?! . Then he apologizes for all of it. Just ridiculous. And while I'm on the subject of Tris Tobias, weird and totally forced sexual tension much? Every three chapters or so, we'd just cut to this weird suggestive dialogue and they'd grope each other a little bit, and allude to a makeout session or something, and then abruptly wrench back into the main plot like nothing ever happened. The random bursts of lust might've been intended to make the readers think that this relationship had a bright future, because hey, at least they're starting to express themselves a little, but it felt completely canned and didn't mesh at all with the rest of the book. In fact, the entire book just felt forced. Like Roth sprinted to churn out 500 pages, glanced at them once, and then got them bound and put on the shelves ASAP. The writing was clunky and weird, the plot rough around the edges at best, the themes felt slapped-on, and it was just...bad. I mean, I'm sorry. It was just bad. It's very rare that a book gets so bad that I ache, I mean ache to throw in the towel and just stop reading. But that's how I felt when, yet AGAIN, a young adult series centers around a insert huge string of expletives here FREAKING GOVERNMENT CONSPIRACY! That's part of why I liked the series in the first place, because finally there was a YA series that wasn't centered around an evil government. I cannot express my rage when Roth turned over that particular card. I mean, there are no words to describe how angry I was. I'm going to rage at specific plot points for a while now, so let's just pre-emptively hide the whole thing for spoilers To me, the"this is all happened because government is inherently bad" revelation undid ALL the other work that Roth however clumsily tried to do to avoid other cliches of the genre. Otherwise, I might have really respected the honest effort to make the series end on a somewhat realistic note. In fact, that final message that Roth leaves us with is a beautifully painful truth. Life sucks sometimes, and people you care about die, and you've just got to figure out how to deal with that. But of course, like other reviewers, I do not understand why in the WORLD Tris actually needed to die. Now I'm not one of those who feel that Caleb should've done it, because I still fail to see what the hell Caleb did that was so bad in the first place. Here's the thing--I am ALL for killing the main character, if the circumstances or the message are right. But they weren't. Like the rest of the book, the "necessity" of Tris's sacrifice felt forced. Maybe Roth thought that if she said often and insistently enough that "someone had to die", I'd just buy it. But a lot rested on the readers following that leap from "the evil government must be stopped...we must stop it...this is the only way to stop it...and it means that someone must die..." and I did NOT follow that leap. And it's not even that I'm against killing a character because death is senseless. The futility of war, the senselessness of death, can be very effective reasons to pick off a character. But Roth chose her message, that message was "when your back's against the wall, sacrificing your life is the ultimate gift of love", and I'm not on board. Roth also lost major points with me for the way she wrapped Peter's storyline. I'm so over this idea that all bad characters must feel remorse about being bad people, and must want to change. Sometimes mean people are just mean people, you know? Was this Peter thing some stab at redeeming him? Or are we painting him "coward" like we did to Al? Who knows. It was poorly handled and, deja vu, forced. Geez, what else? I've covered the bad plot, the bad character development, the bad theming...I mean, why rub your face in it any more than I already have? Either you loved the book and think everything I'm saying is wrong, or you hated the book too and know exactly what I'm talking about, or you haven't read the book yet. I can't very well say "Don't finish this trilogy that you're already two books into because it's a horrid ending", but once you're through and sharing in my post-trilogy letdown, don't say I didn't warn you.
So - we are at book 6. B is back, and finds herself in a situation whereby she is being forced into gladiatorial combat at the whims of some upper crust humans. Quick, and decent read.

Michelle Hodkin really manged to make Mara Unbecoming. Throughout the book we find Mara as PTSD addled, guilt ridden, socially removed, Supernaturally Powered and completely paranoid. Mara is struggling to keep her shit together although it hit the roof, many times. How unbecoming of her!! I really liked Daniel right away and adored Joseph. Jamie is one tough nut to crack, I still don't understand him. Mom and Dad were their usual selves, fretting and cautious. Now, Noah Shaw, is still a big mystery. Oh, come to think of it, so is Mara. One amazing book by John Green. The spirit of Holden Caulfield lives on. This is about the story of Pudge Nickname who used to lead an uneventful life until he embarked on a journey at boarding school, made some new friends including the incredible Alaska Young. This book is simply as amazing as catcher in the rye. I would recommend it to anyone.

This is the forth novel of John Green's that I've read, and I'm not reading them in the chronological order in which they were published. I felt like the protagonist, Colin, was pretty much the same person as Miles in "Looking For Alaska." Maybe that's because they are both very smart, teenage boys who are a bit on the nerdy side. But, I felt like Miles was more interesting since he was searching for an adventure, a more exciting life, whereas Colin is just moping over a girl. I did think it was a nice little twist that Kathrine 1 and Katherine 19 were the same girl. Green also described small town life very accurately, coming from someone who grew up in a small town that relied on a paper mill for jobs. Hollis was one of the most interesting characters in the book. And I like how each of Green's protagonists have a little quirk that teaches me about random things like anagrams, famous last words, paper towns, etc.

This book was basically a combination of Maze Runner, Divergent, Hunger Games, and Lord of Flies. The premise was very promising at first but turned out to be mediocre to how it could have been. It was a quick and entertaining read, though I'm not sure if I'll read the rest of the series yet.

Actual rating 3 1 2 Well, at least I tried. I originally picked up Peaches because it's by Jodi Lynn Anderson, who wrote one of my favorite books of all time, Tiger Lily which I recommend to everyone reading this review . This book was written before that, so at least we know she's getting better with her writing, because Tiger Lily is honestly like poetry. This one, being a pretty light-hearted contemporary, so not so much. Peaches tells the story of three girls from very different backgrounds who come together and discover themselves. Birdie, the token fat character that is constantly shamed, is the daughter of Walter who is the owner of the Darlington peach orchid. She loves her job and her two dogs that follow her everywhere, but she doesn't like to go out of her comfort zone ever, leaving her friendless and boyfriend-less. Leeda is the flawless and rich girl who has a boyfriend who she doesn't exactly love, but she's so beautiful, she has to have a boyfriend duh . She's cousins with Birdie, so she comes to help keep the orchid afloat. Murphy is the "slutty" cringe friend whose mother is also a "slut." Huh, I didn't realize that it ran in the family now? Anyway, she doesn't have much about her character other than that. She's sarcastic and a troublemaker, which is how she ends up working at the peach orchid. The characters aren't exactly well developed. They have good dynamics when they're together, and they're definitely easy to discern because of how different their main traits are, but they definitely are all very stereotypical and I didn't like how they were defined by one trait throughout the whole book. Birdie was chubby, Leeda was a bitch, and Murphy was a floozy. I just wish they were more three dimensional. Other than than, I did enjoy a lot of things that this book had to offer. In some ways, the plot was not really like anything I've read before. The characters all had good development and I admired their commitment to the farm, Birdie from the beginning and the others by the end. The romance was eh. Enrico and Birdie were pretty cute, but Rex seems like a guy that all of the girls should stay away from. I might read the rest of the series just to see what goes down with everyone after this. The ending was a little overly optimistic, but sometimes it's nice to have a happy ending.

I've always had an affinity for the bad guys and boy did I love the Darkling in this book. He was by far the best developed character in this book, not only because I didn't see him as the bad guy for a long time!

People with that blood type can lose their control and kill. So four of the teens go to get Josie away from the terrible place she's in. That Dean, one of our two POV characters, is in looove with Astrid, who also loves Jake, was an element of these novels I didn't love. Dean didn't know what she saw in Jake and neither did I. I stayed up waaay too late reading this book last night and was nearly late to work this morning, because I was determined to find out what was going to happen. I'm very glad I read this. The copy I read came from interlibrary loan.

Inhalt Die 17-jahrige Sky ist starken Gefuhlen bisher aus dem Weg gegangen. Wenn sie einem Jungen begegnet, verspurt sie normalerweise keinerlei Anziehung, kein Kribbeln im Bauch. Im Gegenteil. Sie fuhlt sich taub. Bis sie auf Dean Holder trifft, der ihre Hormone tanzen lasst. Es knistert heftig zwischen den beiden und der Beginn einer grossen Liebe deutet sich an. Doch dann tun sich Abgrunde aus der Vergangenheit auf, die tiefer und dunkler sind, als Sky sich vorstellen kann. Meine Meinung Und damit ware dann auch ,,Hope Forever" von meinem SuB verschwunden. Zum Gluck! Ich kam mir namlich langsam so vor, als wurde ich einen drittklassigen dramatischen Bollywoodfilm sehen. So viel kunstlich aufgebauschtes Drama und grottenschlechte, schmalzige Dialoge habe ich ja zuletzt bei GZSZ erlebt. Ganz ruhig, Wuuuuusa, fangen wir doch einfach am Anfang dieses Fetzens an ... Das Buch fangt schonmal richtig scheisse an, namlich mittendrin. Also wortwortlich. Der Prolog besteht aus denselben anderthalb Seiten die irgendwann im letzten Drittel des Buches nochmal vorkommen und zwar Wort fur Wort. Wir erfahren in diesem Prolog auch, dass die Protagonisten Sky und Holder heissen. Und uns wird auch gleich auf dem Silbertablett serviert, dass die Beiden ein Paar sind - dadurch ist die erste Halfte dieses Kloppers also schonmal uberflussig. Und dann geht die eigentliche Geschichte los. Wir lernen Sky kennen und wenn sie eines kann, dann jammern. Ohja, dass kann sie wie eine Meisterin. Wenn es einen Preis furs hemmungslose Jammern gabe wurde Sky haushoch gewinnen. Das gesamte erste Kapitel kriegen wir ihre ganze jammerliche Geschichte bezuglich ihres Liebeslebens serviert. Klatsch, Klatsch, Klatsch. Ein Fakt nach dem anderen, immer mitten in die Fresse rein. Wen das interessiert? Ja, keine Ahnung, mich jedenfalls nicht! Sky lasst Kerle nachts durch ihr Fenster steigen, leckt und sabbert ein bisschen mit denen rum und schickt sie dann nach Hause. Funf Meter weiter, im Nachbarhaus, macht ihre beste Freundin Six genau das gleiche. Mit dem einzigen Unterschied, dass Six auch den Horizontaltango mit den Burschen betreibt, Sky bleibt beim Vorspiel. Weil sie ja naturlich noch Jungfrau ist. Die gesamte erste Halfte des Buches handelt von Sky, ihrem Gejammere und dass ihre ABFFL bald nach Italien geht. Die heisst ubrigens burgerlich Seven Marie, will aber Six genannt werden. Herzlich willkommen zum 1x1 der laufigen Hundinnen, kann ich da nur sagen. Und naturlich geht es um Holder. Dean Holder ja komm versau' mir doch meine Lieblingsserie, Colleen Hoover . Holder ist naturlich Gottes Geschenk an die Frauenwelt. Und weil er so absolut perfekt und fehlerfrei aussieht, spielt es fur Sky auch keine Rolle, dass er sie beim ersten Treffen wie der letzte Padophile anstarrt und ihr auf den Supermarktparkplatz folgt, seine Kasemauke zwischen Tur und Rahmen schiebt und sie fragt wie sie heisst. Stellen wir uns diesen sexy hexy Dean Holder mal dreissig Jahre spater, funfzig Kilo schwerer, mit einer Brille und einem Bart vor. Richtig! Er ist all das wovor deine Eltern dich gewarnt haben! Ein Psycho, ein Irrer, der Grund schreiend wegzulaufen. Aber hey ... er ist voll heiss und ich schwimme schon in meinem Schlupper, also sage ich ihm nicht nur meinen Vornamen, ich zeige ihm gleich meinen Fuhrerschein. Hier bitte einmal ein Facepalm einfugen. Aber der Spass geht noch weiter. Am selben Abend geht Sky dann joggen und trifft naturlich rein ZUFALLIG ihren Stalker. Der kann ihr auch fehlerfrei runter rattern wo sie wohnt und bringt sie nach Hause. Es folgen viele viele Seiten, die ich so ein bisschen verdrangt habe, weil da eh nix wichtiges bei rumgekommen ist. Sky und Holder streiten sich alle paar Seiten nur unterbrochen von endlosen Passagen, in denen Sky uber Holders Aussehen schwadroniert. Sie findet es auch uberhaupt nicht bedenklich, dass der Junge nachts durch ihr Fenster steigt und sich zu ihr ins Bett legt oder so, ne? Wieso sie ihm nicht mit einem Baseballschlager eine uberzieht? Weil er so heiss ist naturlich! Ne, ich krieg da Ausschlag von! So viel Dummheit auf einem Haufen. Die erste Halfte des Buches ist also nur eine Aneinanderreihung von damlichen Szenen in denen Sky und Holder sich anzicken oder anschmachten, manchmal auch beides zeitgleich. Wir erfahren, dass sky adoptiert ist und beim Kussen nie was spurt. Sie hat die Angewohnheit dabei die Sterne an ihrer Zimmerdecke zu zahlen. Ausser naturlich bei Holder. Der kann mit seiner flinken und super geschickten Zunge Dinge in ihr heraufbeschworen, die naturlich niemals irgendein anderer Mann geschafft hatte. Ich wusste nicht, dass es neuerdings nur noch einen Partner fur jeden Menschen gibt, der irgendeine Art von Gefuhl in einem Menschen auslosen kann, aber gut. Was weiss ich denn schon? Ich kenne ja auch keinen Dean Holder, ne? Und weil es auf Skys Seite noch nicht genugend Potenzial fur die nachste Folge "Mitten im Leben" gibt, hat auch Holder eine ganz tragische Geschichte. Seine Zwillingsschwester Leslie hat sich ein Jahr vor Handlungsbeginn das Leben genommen, seine Eltern sind geschieden und er wird auf der Schule nicht so gerne gesehen, weil er mal einen Jungen krankenhausreif geschlagen hat. Gut, da muss ich ganz ehrlich zugeben bei so einem Spruch hatte ich auch jemandem eine reingezwiebelt. Endlose Seiten voller Geschwarme und Gelaber und Geschmachte und wir kommen zu der zweiten Halfte des Buches die alles an Realitat totet, was noch irgendwie da gewesen ist. Sky erfahrt, dass sie eigentlich Hope heisst. Ich habe schon wieder vergessen wie sie das rausgefunden hat, war wohl beleidigend unrealistisch. Und Hope hat fruher im Nachbarhaus von Holder und Leslie gewohnt und war mit denen als Kind befreundet und wurde dann entfuhrt. Da war sie so ungefahr funf Jahre alt. Holder hat seine Sandkastenliebe naturlich nie vergessen und nach ihr gesucht und sich deswegen wie ein Irrer im Supermarkt aufgefuhrt. Ich glaube, ihre Erkenntnis hatte irgendwas mit einer Panikattacke kurz vor dem Sex zu tun. Also, sie und Holder waren kurz davor und dann hat sie voll Panik gekriegt und ihre verdrangten Erinnerungen sind wieder aufgetaucht. Daraufhin erzahlt Holder ihr dann dass sie eigentlich Hope heisst und fahrt sie nach Hause. Sie sagt ihm ausdrucklich dass sie alleine sein will und was macht der Junge? Richtig! Er legt sich zu seiner Freundin ins Bett, wahrend sie schlaft. Skys Adoptiv mutter findet das nicht lustig, als sie nachts ins Zimmer kommt und die beiden gehirnamputierten Goren packen ihre Sachen und verpieseln sich. Es wird dann mal das angesprochen, was jeder Leser mit maximal 3 Gehirnzellen sich schon seit 200 Seiten denkt Sky wurde als Kind von ihrem Vater sexuell missbraucht. Und weil sie es nicht aushalt, dass ihr Vater ihr und Holder das erste Mal geklaut hat fleht sie Holder an mit ihr zu schlafen. Er soll die schlimmen Erinnerungen durch schone ersetzen. Der will erst nicht, tut es dann aber doch. Hort aber nach funf Sekunden wieder auf. Es wird kurz geredet, Holder gibt wieder das kitschigste Liebesgestandnis der kitschigen Liebesgestandnisse von sich und es wird diesmal Liebe gemacht. Bing und Bong haben also in einem dreckigen Motelzimmer, Minuten nach der Erkenntnis, dass eine der Parteien als Kind brutal und unmenschlich und bestialisch vergewaltigt wurde, erstmal 'ne Runde gepimpert. Holt die Schnapsglaser raus, ich geb' einen aus! Am Tag darauf fahrt unser Traumpaar dann zu Skys Vater und konfrontiert ihn mit den Vorwurfen. Der gibt alles zu, spielt aber alles runter und sagt es ware nur einmal passiert. Als ware es dadurch besser oder verzeihlich oder nicht ganz so schlimm. Ich verabscheue sowas. Ich muss aber ganz ehrlich zugeben, dass es mir gefallen hat dass Colleen Hoover hier nicht komplett schwarz und weiss gemalt hat. Sie lasst Sky ihren Vater verabscheuen und hassen und Angst vor ihm haben, aber sie gibt Sky auch eine andere Stimme. Eine andere Erinnerung, eine gute Erinnerung. Einige Gefuhle, die zulassen das man irgendwie verstehen kann dass sie ihren Vater liebt bzw. geliebt hat. Den Vater, der ihr ein Gutenachtlied gesungen hat als sie klein war. Nicht den Vater, der seiner Tochter viel mehr als die Kindheit und Jungfraulichkeit raubte. Meine positive Uberraschung ich mag's dunkel und aussichtslos ist aber schnell abgeklungen, als der Vater zugibt dass er, als junger Mann, auch seine Schwester vergewaltigte und nach Skys Entfuhrung die Nachbarstochter. Also Leslie, Holders Schwester. So grausam das auch ist, genauso vorhersehbar war das. Holder ist kurz vorm ausrasten, als ihm klar wird, dass das der Grund fur Leslies Suizid gewesen ist. Bevor er dem alten Perversling aber mal so richtig gehorig und verdient die Fresse spitz hauen kann, erschiesst dieser sich mit einem Kopfschuss. Und auch die anschliessende Szene im Motel, als die beiden gemeinsam in der Dusche stehen und sich Blut und Gehirnmasse abwaschen ist gut geschrieben. In dieser Szene hat man richtig bemerkt dass Colleen Hoover schreiben kann und vor allem die ruhigen Momente nach einer Tragodie unglaublich emotional heruberbringen kann. Und das war es auch schon mit der Verbesserung, denn kurz danach schlafen die beiden miteinander, diesmal muss nicht Holder Sky heilen, sondern Sky muss Holder heilen. Also werden wortwortlich die Probleme weggebumst. Anders kann man das nicht beschreiben. Das wird zwar als unglaublicher Liebesbeweis und grosse romantische Szene verkauft, aber im Endeffekt ist es nur eine Sache sie reitet ihren Kerl in den Schlaf. Anschliessend fahrt unser Traumpaar wieder nach Hause und Sky erfahrt das Karen ihre Adoptivmutter ihre leibliche Tante ist, besagte misshandelte Schwester des Vaters. Sky soll entscheiden, ob sie zur Polizei geht. Macht sie nicht, weil sie die ganzen dreizehn Jahre gut von Karen behandelt wurde und sie halt ihre Mama ist. Die beiden setzen sich hin, reden uber alles und umarmen sich in Dauerschleife und ich kam mir vor wie bei ,,zwei bei Kallwass". Und naturlich hat diese Geschichte nur eine Zeitspanne von einem Monat, die zweite Halfte des Buches spielt sogar nur an einem Wochenende. Die Liebe heilt alles, Traumata werden weggesteckt wie ein Papierschnitt und die Einhorner konnen wieder uber die pinke Glitzerwiese galoppieren. Danke, danke, ich musste Regenbogen kotzen und Glitzer pupsen und erstmal eine rauchen gehen Das Traurige ist, so wie sehr oft, dass das eine richtig schone und gute Geschichte hatte werden konnen. Voller Tragik und den Abgrunden der menschlichen Seele und einem tiefsitzendem Trauma, Verdrangung und der Heilung von solchen Ereignissen. Und ja, von mir aus auch mit der ganz grossen Glitzerliebe. Aber doch nicht so ... Fazit Ich bin bisher von Colleen Hoover enttauscht worden. Die erste Halfte war unterirdische Kindergartenkacke, die zweite Halfte war zwar gefuhlvoller und ernsthafter, aber durch die sich uberschlagenden Ereignisse und die Reaktionen der Protagonisten auf diverse Situationen einfach nur extrem unrealistisch. Schade, wirklich schade. Colleen Hoover und ich werden wohl keine Freunde werden. 1 5 Sternen

I read somewhere that this book these books, I suppose came out in the '90s, and let me say, it makes sense! Not that the story is bad or anything, it's just that.... there were so many things I expected to happen that didn't, and I think that's because I am so used to reading newer, more recent books. I actually liked the storyline. The whole setting, with the gigantic 'starscrapers' and everything... That was really cool! I'm not sure how well I'd do in it, though.... I'm moderately afraid of heights.... Anyways, I liked a lot of the plot. I wish, though, that we would have gotten to meet some more advanced hexes- come on, Raven can't possibly be THE ONLY ONE. I think it would have made the story more interesting.... It would have put it in perspective. And I wish that there had been a little more character development with basically every character. And also, I wish the laboratory wouldn't have blown up But that's just because it's sad... It fit with the story........ But what REALLY bugged me about this book books is the style of writing. Ugh. It seemed really fast paced... Like the author didn't want to sit down and get in to everything. There seemed to be a lot of encounters where there could have been a lot of character development, or a lot of emotion, and there just... wasn't. Even in the places where I felt like the author WANTED there to be a lot of emotion, there wasn't. And when there was character development, it felt really awkward. If the plot line wasn't so interesting, I probably would have dropped this book as soon as I noticed it. Sorry And finally..... Raven. Not my favorite character. There was absolutely no character development about practically anything. She put a lot of effort in to saving Rachel in the first book... But the second starts off and she doesn't even give a crap. What? Also, when they blow up the lab.... Raven is totally like, whatever. Who cares, but a lot of innocent children just died. It's not that she's not sad... I don't care that she is not emotionally affected. But she never even says that what happened was wrong. It's just like they died, and that's too bad. It made it really, really hard to relate to her, and also really, really hard to look up to her. Ugh. But all in all, it was an interesting series. Go for it.

Endlich mal wieder ein Drachenroman und dann auch noch einer der vom Autor der Eragon-Reihe Christopher Paolini in hochsten Tonen gelobt wird, das kann doch eigentlich nur gut sein, oder etwa nicht? Genau dieses etwa trifft leider auf den Roman Serafina - Das Konigreich der Drachen zu. Der Einstieg in diesen Roman ist mir so gar nicht gelungen, es gibt zwar nur relativ wenige Charaktere, die auch noch einmal in einem separaten Personenverzeichnis aufgefuhrt sind, trotzdem viel es mir sehr schwer, mir die einzelnen Charaktere und ihre Aufgaben zu merken geschweige denn mich mit ihnen ansatzweise zu identifizieren. Die Geschichte kommt leider nur sehr schleppend voran und es ist anfangs kaum ersichtlich, wohin die Reise einmal gehen soll und als es dann doch endlich klargeworden ist, kann man schon ziemlich gut erahnen, wie dieses Buch enden wird. Daruber hinaus konnte ich mit der Erzahlform ich-Form nicht sonderlich viel anfangen, es wird mir fur meinen Geschmack einfach viel zu viel geheult, sei es nun aus Trauer, Liebe, Gluck oder ahnliches, es ist auf Dauer sehr nervig. Leider konnte ich auch mit dem von Serafina wohl gepflegten "Kopfgarten", eine Art Gedankenkonstrukt, um mit ihrem wohl gehuteten Geheimnis besser fertig zu werden, nichts anfangen. Es kam mir einfach unnotig und vollig fehl am Platz vor. Zugegeben, das Buchcover ist wunderbar gestaltet und sowohl die letzten rund 80 Seiten als auch das Finale trosten uber grosse Durststrecken hinweg, nichtsdestotrotz tauschen diese positiven Aspekte nicht uber einen schlechten Roman hinweg, der mich mehr gelangweilt als gefesselt hat. Die Umsetzung war leider sehr schlecht, obwohl die Geschichte mich wirklich interessiert hat. Fazit Dieser Roman hat mich leider insgesamt mehr als enttauscht. Die Geschichte kommt viel zu langsam in Gang, die Charaktere sind langweilig gestaltet, es wird zu viel geweint und die Handlung ist alles in allem zu durchsichtig. Ich kann diesen Roman leider nicht weiterempfehlen!

My prior observation with Collins writing style in the first two books of The Hunger Games trilogy seems to be less of an issue with Mockingjay. There seems to be a bit more personality infused in the way Collins uses words and sentences. Of course, writing style is still a secondary skill--primary is her plotting, which refuses to take a break in Mockingjay--as well as the intimately linked skill in having characters act in a way pivotal to their personality. While I doubt if anyone stuck around if they didn't like the first book, those who kept plugging away may find Mockingjay to be more palpable. It is a concentrated revolt against the Capitol and President Snow, which itself may sound typical, but I really liked the way Collins works with the issue. Few people acknowledge the good and the bad when it comes to politics, but Collins does this realistically and naturally. Also, when they make a movie of this book and Catching Fire, for that matter , they totally need to get Juliette Lewis to play Johanna Mason, preferably re-channeling her role from Whip It. Because from the moment Johanna opened her mouth that is who I saw.

This was a pleasant surprise. I was all ready for your run-of-the-mill YA story about a girl with some kind of paranormal power and a love triangle and hijinks....and instead I got a sneak attack of a story. So yes, there is a love triangle...but it isn't really a love triangle...and the way its done is so refreshingly new and keeps you guessing about what's actually going on in the characters' heads. Sadly, most of the cool parts of this story reside in the plot. And the reason why this book kept my interest and is so FUN is because of the way the plot slowly unfolds there are clues galore about the bad guys and what they're doing, there's clues galore hidden in the way the heroine, Addie, feels about both boys, and there's a point near the end where you run back through events in your mind and have to acknowledge how clever the author was to implant those clues without tipping her hand. So I can't really tell you the parts I loved without giving stuff away that you should really figure out on your own. The beginning was a bit slow and confusing-- and I almost gave up until I figured out why things felt so disjointed. Then I was intrigued. Addie can see her own future-- she experiences the two results of any given choice like a memory. It's real for her. Her best friend, Laila, can erase memories, and she says she's never done it to Addie before, but what if Addie has seen something in her future she wants to forget? There is young-YA appropriate kissing and hugging, and there's some murdered girls offstage thrown in the mix, so I wouldn't mind my elementary school aged daughter reading this. But don't get me wrong, keeping track of what's going on, figuring out the clues, and matching them to future events keeps even adults intrigued. The ending manages to tie together everything while showing Addie made a choice-- and setting up a cliffhanger for the next book. Which I must go buy now.

I was about half way done with this when I got to questioning why I felt like I had read this before. As it turns out, I read the first book in the series about 7-8 years ago. I barely recall anything about Boys that Bite except the name, cover and the whole twin sisters that are as different as night and day. I guess I should have looked more closely before starting this book but considering it took about an hour to read, longer if you count the break I took to bake brownies, no harm done. I was taken back by the extreme juvenile tone of the book. Even if I had read this at 16 or 17, I would have mocked the childish tones. Each character played a perfect cut-out role. Everything was black and white, no gray. Such trivial teen drama played out with vampires. Ugh. On a end note... just how many different breeds hybrids can one sister be? Half-vamp, vampire slayer and now her family heritage? Really? I'll skip books 2-3 and anything that came after 4, thank you very much.
Loved that the ending left them in a somewhat good place.

I really loved this... even after the late, late twist. It's probably one that is best read twice and if you're confused, look to the chapter headers with the dates and before after at the top of the page. It's pretty helpful since you have dual narrators and two main timelines - before the accident and after. Still a good family drama with a big heap of suspense.

I'm pretty sure this book wasn't worth wasting my Saturday off over. I hate saying this, because I don't like to think of reading a book as a waste of time and I don't like it when I don't click with a book. I enjoyed the science fiction-y aspects of Nobody - that there are people living hidden among us with special powers - and the main characters' plot to uncover the secret plans of a shady institution. That sort of thing will probably never get old for me, no matter how many different books in which I read it. The characters, though, they were a different story. The self-loathing in Nix was like Edward Cullen times 77. Logically, I could see why he was like that, as The Society has ingrained in him from a very young age how insignificant he was, that his only worth was in his ability to take out his designated targets. Despite understanding this with my head, Nix's "I'm not worthy, she should hate me, because I'm a killer" stint got old quickly. The speed in which Claire and Nix supposedly fell in love made me want to roll my eyes a bit. Once again, I can understand the thrill of finding someone else in the world who actually registers your existence, but to be spouting off I love yous after only knowing each other for a few days? To this realist, that seems to be pushing things a bit. And don't get me started on the whole "you tamed me" bit Nix ganked from The Little Prince. That just takes the saved by the love of a good woman trope to a whole other level and makes me want to bring back the ever delightful nineties expression "gag me with a spoon."

This book cleverly mixed the actual history of World War I with steampunk elements for a read that would appeal to anyone from older kids to adults. My son and I both read it and enjoyed talking about the story and it brought on a discussion of the "real" WWI.
Chilling and exciting. And the ending left me wanting more. A fun new novel that kept me up half the night until my husband demanded I turn out the lights and go to sleep.

Absolutely, i was touched. almost got teary eyed. It was written beautifully especially the ending. I enjoyed the relationship Cage and Low had, its bitter sweet. All about the story has a touch of being imperfect, and how does this end so perfectly? At first Marcus reminds me of my bf, but on the later part I think he's gaining the upperhand hahaha! Anyway, im reading other books alongside with this, but I gain more interest in this than te other I dont really know if Ill continue reading the others . I want to read more of Ms. Abbi's book! Its incredible and addictive. totally LOVESICK.

Very disappointed in this sequel. Will and Layken were even more immature than in the last book and their characterization was very inconsistent, I did not enjoy Will's POV at all - in fact, he's a bit of a sexist asshole, and even though some things did happen in the novel I still feel like nothing HAPPENED. There were literally only two maybe two and a half important plot points the entire book. This book was butterflying awful.

I am absolutely in love with this book series. Words can not describe the feelings I have each time I read them. I remember picking up this book shortly after finishing Twilight. It was recommended to me by Borders.com and at the time I didn't have any suggests on what to read next. Let me just say that after finishing the first one it blew my mind and I had to rush to the store to pick up the rest at the time Blood Promise was just being released . After reading Twilight, I really began to dislike for Bella Swan's lack of a back bone. All she did through out the whole series was play games, and get rescured...Enter Rose. This was not the case for Rose Hathaway. She is funny, clever, and a complete smart-ass qualities that I absolutely adore. Rose is very refreshing, because she never places herself to play the role of the victim. She would rather die than miss the opportunity to fight back and protect the ones she loves. The romantic interest, Dimitri, has to be the hottest character I have come across in a long time within any fictional story. Who would not go for a tall, dark, and sexy Russian man, who happens to be slight older and forbidden? He was a great element to throw Rose's world upside, since he must be her mentor. Lastly, the bond between Lissa and Rose reminds me of my own friendship with my best friend. They are willing to do anything they can to protect each other, even if it means dying or getting into typical high school trouble. All I have to say is Richelle Mead is an excellant author. She is not the type to talk down to you, and is not afraid to throw in hard topics like sex, self-cutting, and other related topics. Overall, Vampire Academy delivers everything from humor, action, mystery, suspense, and of course, forbidden romance. What more could a person ask for?

Honestly, I wasn't the biggest fan of this book. The story had absolutely no point. The only purpose of the entire thing was to cause a love struggle in the third book. There was no real growth of Lena's character, and to be honest I wasn't the biggest fan of Julian. Alex was such a better character, an I felt like Alex better helped Lena in both her growth as a character and her maturity. Julian does none of that. I feel like the third book is going to be reminiscent of a Twilight love story in the amount of times Lena says she's ready to die and then miraculously got saved and has this horrible love triangle to figure out. I guess I'm just a big fan of Alex and knew from the beginning that he was going to come back so the entire relationship with Lena and Julian annoyed me from the start because I knew they'd end up falling in love.

This is the first book in the Hush Hush saga by Becca Fitzpatrick. The book is filled with suspense, mystery, and action. This book is basically about a girl named Nora Grey, who is a top student and she worries about her grades, and then she meets Patch who is the recluse of school and he is the bad boy. Nora and Patch get paired for a biology assignment and then the novel takes off from there. There's so much going on in this novel and it's absolutely AMAZING!! If you haven't read this book or series, then you should definitely pick them up. It's a page-turner that I literally could not put down! I found myself reading the book every minute that I had! It's full of suspense and action, and mystery! If you want an amazing page-turning novel, and series that you can't put down and that you want to be able to fly through, that makes you think, pick up this book! You will not regret it. Basically it's about Nora trying to figure out why Patch is different, and why she's so drawn to him. If you are looking for a book with the ultimate bad boy, than you should definitely pick it up. Hush Hush by Becca Fitzpatrick is my 3rd favourite book series I have EVER read!!

it has alot of " I did not see that coming " stuff but still brilliant anyway I LOVE IT

Read this book in a day so my head's a mess, I have so many thoughts! Initial reaction I liked it a lot. As a sucker for a happy ending, I was really rooting for a happier conclusion, especially as we find in more detail what transpired between Leonard and Asher. There's no closure here and I feel like Leonard deserved better, but the final letter gave me hope that he's going to work towards the future he deserves. I've never read anything by Matthew Quick before and he writes well, but I can't help but wish that Leonard tried to execute so to speak his plan in the beginning half of the book, so that the second half could've been about the fallout. The message of the book is important and I think it would've been great to see how this very serious situation should've been handled, because similar things happen today and they're often not spoken about as much as they should be! I liked Herr Silverman throughout the entire book UNTIL we get to the last time he's ever mentioned. Leonard told Silverman literally everything that he did, everything he was going to do, everything that happened with Asher, has an idea of the kind of woman Linda is and yet. In his final voicemail he says 'I have to say i'm disappointed in you bla bla bla you've put me in an awkward position.' I just think that after finding out about everything Leonard was going through, it really wasn't the best thing to say to a very clearly suicidal teenager who still had a lot to work through. Silverman comes across as very empathetic throughout the book so this didn't sit well with me. But I still liked him a lot more than Linda! Anyway, I thought that overall the book was a real page-turner with some real poignant moments, I just wish certain aspects were explored in more detail.
I probably would have liked this better if my expectations hadn't been so high for fans of Supernatural!? You bet! and the narrator audiobook had been a little better.

I like the book but not the cliffhanging ending. I wish the author stated that the book had a cliffhanging and second book. I still would have purchased it but I would not have started to read it until the remaining book s were published.

I really liked this. The descriptions were magical, the charters were really likeable and it was original. I'm not saying it was particularly believable, I don't know many urban teenagers who can name artists, make glass art and read art books but there we go, maybe it's just an Aussie thing. Or maybe the author is just being hopeful. I can't say it was particularly gripping, the plot wasn't exactly intense but it was well thought out and the ending sort of came together well. Everything could have been a bit darker and more dramatic but I'm bias because i like dark and dramatic books and this is probably aimed at a slightly younger audience anyway. But it was worth a read, i'm glad I did, it inspired me to get drawing again because, as the book points out, art is a beautiful form of self expression.

The last time I read this book was more than 10 years ago... I never read the last book so I knew I needed to reread the first ones. It's very short but it took me a long time to read it. It wasn't as great as I remembered it to be. It's rushed and the writing style was changing from time to time. Marie-Lune speaks with a big quebec style but when she narrates the things she see and do it's almost poetic. Also I don't understand why her mother or her father or even her grandmother couldn't tell her about her mom's cancer. I mean she was dying and Marie-Lune never knew about it... I think the author wanted to do a suspense or a surprise for the reader but it's not realistic and it bothers me. I will read the other books but now I know I probably never read them again.

Review posted on The Eater of Books! blog All Our Pretty Songs by Sarah McCarry Book One of a trilogy Publisher St. Martin's Griffin Publication Date July 30, 2013 Rating 1 star Source eARC from NetGalley Summary from Goodreads Set against the lush, magical backdrop of the Pacific Northwest, two inseparable best friends who have grown up like sisters--the charismatic, mercurial, and beautiful Aurora and the devoted, soulful, watchful narrator--find their bond challenged for the first time ever when a mysterious and gifted musician named Jack comes between them. Suddenly, each girl must decide what matters most friendship, or love. What both girls don't know is that the stakes are even higher than either of them could have imagined. They're not the only ones who have noticed Jack's gift his music has awakened an ancient evil--and a world both above and below which may not be mythical at all. The real and the mystical the romantic and the heartbreaking all begin to swirl together, carrying the two on journey that is both enthralling and terrifying. And it's up to the narrator to protect the people she loves--if she can. What I Liked Literally, nothing. I'm sorry, I don't say this a lot, but this book appealed to me in absolutely NO WAY. Just the cover, I suppose. And the glowing synopsis. Gosh. I really, really wanted to like this book, but it totally fell flat for me. What I Did Not Like There isn't much to this book. It's extremely short something like 240 pages, which seems even shorter on a Kindle , and it's not what I would call dense. I'd seen a few things about this book before reading the book - that the author has a beautiful writing style, beautiful prose, a really beautiful way with words. Also, the synopsis leads us to believe that there is some powerful romance, an amazing friendship, and some mythical aspect to the novel. Sounds great, right? Well. I'll start with the writing style. I really don't see what's so beautiful and amazing and gripping about it. I found the writing style and the narration boring and repetitive and not at all engaging. I was expecting something fabulous, something dynamic that would sweep me off my feet - and instead, I got flat, boring, lifeless narration, brought on by a not-so-awesome writing style. Then there's the fact that this book is really short, and not that dense, and not a lot happens in this book. Literally, all that happens is the narrator describes her life with her best friend, then Jack appears, the narrator falls in love with Jack, but then Aurora the best friend does too, and then Jack and and Aurora disappear, and the narrator feels the need to save them. TRUST ME when I saw that my cute summary above is more interesting than the entire book. NOTHING HAPPENS. The first part of the book WITHOUT Jack is the narrator describing how not-hot she is, and how gorgeous and perfect Aurora is. She describes how Aurora barely remembers her dad, and how she the narrator doesn't know her dad. Then Jack comes along, and sweeps the narrator off her feet. That really irritates me - that Jack appears and the narrator and him just fall in love. It's total insta-love, insta-lust, whatever. There is no powerful love story in this book. I don't see or feel any all-encompassing pull between Jack and the narrator, that makes them soul mates, or something. It's complete insta-love, with a giant dose of lust. Seriously. They cannot keep their hands off each other, and all the narrator can think about is Jack, so much that she can't see straight. So much that she doesn't realize when her best friend falls in love or lust with Jack as well. Assuming I understood that correctly from the story. There is a good chance that I didn't understand the entire story. I originally thought that Aurora and the narrator had the same dad - which would make the constant "close like sisters" references make sense - but I never got an explanation on that surprise! . I kind of hated the narrator throughout the entire story. She acts like a tough girl - she even thinks she's tough - but she bows to whatever Aurora wants. She runs off with Jack at every chance. She blindly tries to get Aurora and Jack from whatever hell they put themselves in I seriously mean hell - that's the mythological part . She constantly tells Aurora that no one means more to her than Aurora, but when Jack comes along, we know that's not true. Everything is Aurora, Aurora, Aurora, and Jack, Jack, Jack. I expected some sort of threesome to happen at some point in the book - in which I would have STOPPED, and clocked in my first DNF. I don't know about your sexual preferences, but threesomes are NOT for me. So, there is a love triangle, sort of. And I hate all three people in the love triangle. You know it's bad when you disliked hate all of the main characters in the book. The only character that I could stomach was the narrator's friend who saves her at the end and I cannot remember his name, for crying out loud! . I touched on this, but the plot is ridiculous. It feels like NOTHING happens, and then at the last couple of percents, the narrator goes on some life-changing quest to get Aurora and Jack, and that all in itself is so confusing and pointless and UGH! Can the author at least TRY to explain ANYTHING?! I don't understand the "mythology" part of the book. I'm putting it in quotes because I don't even know if it's mythology, or the narrator is doing drugs or drinking alcohol, or the narrator is off her rocker. No characterization the narrator does not grow up AT ALL , no plot, no explanation, crap romance... how did I even finish this book?! Thank goodness it was so short - because I remember getting violently angry on so many occasions while reading this book. Good thing I love my Kindle. I think that the people who say the author's writing is beautiful must have a better understanding of how to muddle through confusion nonsense nothings that make absolutely NO SENSE. It's rare that a book confuses me. It's rare that an author twists a story that I can't figure out. It's also BAD when I meet a story that I can't understand, because I am not stupid, and yet, I cannot make head or tail of this book. I'm done. I apologize to the author, the publishing house, and the team of people who worked hard to get this book to where it is. But to me? This book is absolutely awful and a complete waste of my time. and we all know how many books are out there... Would I Recommend It No. Nonononononono. Do NOT make the mistake of thinking that there is a pretty cover, a wonderful romance, and a mysterious story waiting for beneath that deceptive cover. Like I did, unfortunately. I had really high hopes for this book, and it ended up being an utter disappointment. Rating 1 star. Trust me when I say that I would have given it 0 stars, had I the chance.

Here's the deal with this book Its plot is lacking, everything is revealed in info-dumps, and there's no dialogue. The most you get is the main character telling you about what was said. This had a lot of potential. Kids created from the DNA of serial killers? To me, that sounds AWESOME. But the execution was underwhelming. Th beginning is fairly uneventful and the way that everything unfolded just didn't use the cool idea to its fullest. On top of that, the writing style just didn't work for me. This is a preference thing, but I found our main character extremely annoying, and the info dumps on every other page just about killed me. Never before has so much USELESS and sometimes false information been thrown at me. You can see other 1-star reviews to see examples such as telling us how the character feels about snow, fish, and blonde-haired women. Not. Necessary. Also, the info dumps would throw too much information, and it's like the author would forget he already told you it. Because then, twenty pages later, it would be treated like a big reveal, even though it had already been told to the reader. Either that, or Jeff told us everything twenty times like I couldn't remember it the first. And his thoughts are so. freaking. annoying. This may be the book for you, but the style didn't work for me, that plot was lacking, the characters were annoying and unrealistic, and insane amounts of useless information was given to you. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone.

I couldn't decide if I liked this as well as Graceling or better! When I discussed this with friends we agreed to disagree, but I loved how the author set so many things up and at the same time it only made me hungry for more.

I was in a bind and needed a quick and easy read. I had seen this book several times at the library and decided to grab it and go. I'll start by saying that I love love love young adult books. However, this one was way too juvenile for my taste. Also the verbiage that was used is completely annoying. It reminded me of valley girls conversing back and forth with each other. It was a lot of "then she said...then I said...then he said" It drove me insane. Plus the whole "One World" jargon was a bit over the top for me. Don't get me wrong...I'm all for reduce, reuse, recycle but seriously. The main character Lani was not your normal teenage girl and I believe she struggles with anxiety pretty bad. Some of her quirks were mentioned throughout the book but nothing in-dept on her dealing with them was ever explored. I think that take may have made the book more enjoyable. In my opinion the ending was lacking as well. I did finish it even though I had considered giving up but I stuck in there because I did want to see what the characters decided to do in the end.

After waiting two years for the conclusion of an extremely drawn out series, I expected something epic. Instead, there was nothing but disappointment. I don't know if it was the long wait that made disconnect with the characters or lose complete interest in them, all I know is that I did not enjoy reading this one bit. It felt like chore picking up the book to read and that's not because of its large size.

Unfortunately, since I knew there was a twist ending, I was looking for clues and figured it out less than a third of the way through. I still enjoyed the writing style and I'm sure I would have really liked it if I hadn't already been suspicious!

As much as it pained me to turn the last page knowing the series ended there was still joy in my heart for the way things worked out. Yes we lost a beloved character but one that lives on in the minds and hearts of both readers and Ethan and his family and friends. It has been a grand journey for almost a week of reading, staying immersed in the world with these characters was very emotional all across the board from joy to sorrow and back again with everything in between! This was truly pleasure reading for me from start of book one Beautiful Creatures to end of book 4 Beautiful Redemption, I savored every scene and the story will stay with me for a long while.
Was really liking this book and then half way through started not liking it as much. Probably won't continue the series.

So, I was more than reluctant to start the predecessor Bloodlines, my obsession with Dimitri would mean that reading the spin-off would be like breaking up with him! Ha! But when The Golden Lily came out, I had to face facts, Me and Dimitri were over.. But Me and Adrian? There was still hope! This is wonderful thing about Mead's writing. The characters become a part of you, haunt you even! It took me a while to warm to Sydney after Rose and her gutsy ways. But I found more of me in Sydney than Rose, there's something vulnerable and real about Sydney that I can identify with. Not to mention the fussy eating! This just left me all fuzzy and desperate to read the next part! Adrian is no Dimitri and I lived for every small cameo Dimka had but I think he grows more as a character than anyone else in this book. He's a luvvie! Cannot wait for The Indigo Spell, but it's nearly a year of waiting.. sobs If you loved Bloodlines, or the Vampire Academy series, then you are sure to love this. Richelle Mead never fails when it comes to YA fiction! .

Great conclusion to the series. Still, I feel the power of the first book was overshadowing this one. But I feel satisfied that this book did not change Katniss' character too much. She struggles with her own feeling for most of the part, and I think the climactic part where she lost someone dear to her was a good choice. It, for one thing, makes her able to make the final decision on her future.

I received this book for free through Goodreads First Reads. To be honest, I usually try to avoid cancer books. They are practically guaranteed to be sad, and since I bawl like a baby at the slightest thing then maybe they're not such a good idea. The only cancer book I've ever read before this one is the majestic The Fault In Our Stars, and that was only because I felt like the only person in the whole world who hadn't read it. But as soon as I saw In Bloom listed on the Goodread Giveaways page, I changed my mind. The blurb seemed positive and optimistic in comparison to the backs of other cancer books that I've looked at and that intrigued me. And, mostly, it lived up to the expectations of it I had. It wasn't a desperately sad book that made me cry and cry for hours on end, which is good. But, unfortunately, it didn't make me laugh or smile for hours either, nor did it make me want to go out and change my life. It was definitely funny and there was definite optimism along with some sadness, but it just didn't grab me in the way I wanted it too. I wanted a book that would make my heart swell and this just didn't. However, it was still a lovely and memorable read. I think my main problem with this book is that I didn't like Francis. I've read a lot of reviews saying that he's a real teenager and that he's really funny, but I didn't get that. The way he narrated events made him seem unrealistic and detached to me. He was certainly funny, but I just didn't care about him in the way I wanted to. He kind of bored me, to be honest. I think I would have liked this book a lot more had it been written in third person or in Amber's point of view. I also thought that Francis's feelings for Amber were completely over-the-top, but I kind of understand that because I was fifteen not too long ago and I knew plenty of people who acted the same way that Francis did. It's just that I was expecting a heartfelt, beautiful love story and when I didn't get that I was slightly disappointed. However, I loved Amber as a character. I also loved all of her family and all of Francis's family. The family scenes were probably the best part of the book to me along with the ending. To me, the ending had all the bittersweet optimism that I'd longed for when I requested a copy and that most of the middle of the book had lacked. It was the only point in the novel that I cried, and it'll probably be the part of it that stays with me for the longest. I suppose you could say that the ending was a little predictable, but that's a stupid comment because it's a cancer book. Cancer books are only ever going to end one of two ways and I'm glad this one went the way it did. Overall, I'm very glad that I read this novel. I wouldn't say it's the greatest book I've ever read in my life, but it's a nice read and I enjoyed it. If you enjoyed The Fault In Our Stars, you'll enjoy this. There's a similar mix of humour and sadness, even if I do think TFIOS mixed those elements slightly better. But at the end of the day, it's unfair to compare. John Green was already a bestselling author when TFIOS was published whereas this is only Matthew Crow's third book. And if this novel is anything to go by, he has a promising career ahead of him and I look forward to reading more. This is a book I'd definitely recommend.

Just finished it so I could return it to my library. Not my normal choice for a read but I could still appreaciate the story. It introduced me to port-wine stains which I never knew about before. I'm glad that Jacob Terra seemed to be getting back together by the end. My favorite quoate had to be "Memento Mori" becasu eI thought it was a good theme that fit in nicely with the book. A very fast read. I finished this in one seating. In fairness, Nicola Yoon has a good writing voice. Though instead of a Young Adult book, I feel like the way it was written and those illustrations has more middle-grade feel than YA. Typical boy meets girl, they chat, they became friends, they fell in love. Only, the girl has SCID, a sickness that didn't allow her to go out of her house. She was an innocent girl who changed when she met Olly and fell in love with him. I honestly don't like the message this book is implying. That when you are growing up and you are falling in love with the opposite sex you begin to lie and keep secrets from your parents, thus hurting the person who took care of you your whole life in the process. I don't agree with that because I am personally very close to my Mom. But anyway, maybe most of the teenagers are really like that. I wouldn't know. Sure I kinda thought that will be the case halfway through reading this but hey, that was still a good twist. And the ending. I like the ending.

spoiler alert I read this book after Crown of Midnight because that's the order they were written. This one was so far.. my favourite. It brings together all the best parts that i liked about the books. It focuses heavily on Celina as an assassin rather than all the magic elements. Also it introduces Sam. After spending the first two books with fighting in my mind of Dorian and Chaol, Sam is easily the winner and probably my favourite character from the series. Each of the 5 novellas added something different to Celina's backstory and helped to shape the character. The stories of the desert and the silent assassins completely changed my opinion of those characters that are rarely mentioned in the first two novels. Even though knowing the main parts of the story, watching Celina and Sam's romance as well as the death and capture was a great read. Already recommending to friends.

I don't know how the author does it. She spins so many stories together, from so many different points of view, and it turns out amazing!!!!!! The plot keeps getting more and more complicated, and I can't wait to see how it all turns out!!

I really really struggled with this one and have to admit that I spent most of the second half of the book skimming. I went into this book with big hopes as the story line sounded like exactly my type of thing, but sadly I was left disappointed. I couldn't connect with Lucille, like at all. She was in a really bad home situation so I should have felt bad for her, but I didn't really feel anything at all. Maybe it had something to do with the way that she was just so over dramatic. I mean something tiny and insignificant happens and she would just totally over react. I really wanted to like her, I just couldn't. And the romance, I feel like it could be compared to marmite. Some people love it, others not so much. Sadly I was in the 'not so much' category. I don't normally have a problem with storylines that feature cheating but this one just seemed to really bug me. I didn't find their relationship swoony, in fact it was a bit cringey at times. FInally, I have to say that there were just WAY too many storylines going on in this short book for me to keep up with, and more annoyingly there were so many that were not tied up at the end of the book. It just felt like the book had no conclusion. It was a nice book, but not as memorable as I had hoped and just had too many annoying little things to keep me from being able to properly finish it.

Meh? Maybe a 2.75 stars. I didn't hate this book, but unfortunately I just found it to be really, really boring up until literally the last 6 or 7 pages. I do plan to carry on with the series, but not any time soon
